A beautiful, open-world Souls Like that most will probably enjoy, especially if they are new to the genre. Technically it's the entry with the most new gameplay mechanics and stunning graphics as well as amount of bosses and areas to explore/clear out, however, aside from that it doesn't have much else better from previous titles.

I played through DS2 and all the DLCs as well as NG+, it's my only experience with the series but it was a really good one. So when I entered the world of Elden Ring I had similar expectations of the bosses and enemies and general ideea of exploration, except they couldn't be applied. ER takes such a inbetween position of gameplay that it utterly annoys me how disrespectful it is to the player, it tries to stay on two stools, one which is Dark Soul's movement/dodge based wait out with punishment to the boss after their combo, and to the Sekiro's/Bloodborne aggressiveness of the enemies/the player...? 

Most notably the only real mobility change the player gets in combat is jumping, which would have been a nice addition if it wasn't for how ridiculously inertialess it feels. Finding the actual gap where you can attack the enemies and bosses freely or at least even just trade with them - is extremely tiring. The recovery time for the combo's are so short your gameplay will be 95% of the time just seeing someone's body and a bunch of metal sounds and bright flashes while constantly spamming dodge. Dark Souls at least had you use your actual positioning/walking/running and not just dodge rolling at the correct time so you had  a more balanced type of gameplay between the boss and yourself.

Horseback fighting is also extremely clunky and unsatisfying, most enemies that were designed around it are really not entertaining to fight against because they are so much easier when using the horse. It should have stayed as a mode of transportation since the springstream mechanic is quite fun and the world is already pretty big. To continue - the world being big doesnt necessarily mean it's shallow as a puddle, but I would have definetely preffered if they condensed the world by 2x and not made the curious player feel like they waste time 90% of the time. Dark Souls while linear would always reward curious players, so when i came over to ER and started looking over each nook and cranny only to get useless crafting materials - well it's just discouraging and feels like the developer trying to take out as much time out of you as possible.

Ashes of War are perhaps the only good mechanic that came out of this entry and even then from the little use that I did have with them, it seems most are extremely niche and likely to never be used in favor of other objectively better ones leaving 90% of them to never be used and be clutter. Take this with a grain of salt as I didn't use them all that much.

Overall, while the game is good and many new players will enjoy it - I wouldn't buy it if you are self respecting Dark Souls fan. The game caters rather hardly to the hardcore players and I say this as a DS2 fan which had the same allegations thrown against it. Elden Ring is through and through made to break your patience and test just how much are you ready to adapt to it's bosses and new mechanics constantly. Pros:
1. Art Direction: Breathtakingly marvelous introductions to each to new area, diverse but on-theme lighting and colors.
2. World: Very well crafted environment that looks good and has just enough mesh between verticality and open space.  Just enough random dungeons and field bosses in the world for you to find too.
3. Legacy Dungeons: Detailed and gorgeous structures as well as many rooms and pathways to explore, good enemy and item placement for the most part.  One optional endgame area stands out especially.  Pinnacle of FromSoftware's great level design.
4. Combat: What you're looking for in a souls-like!  Very well designed combat system that caters to different weapons, builds, and playstyles.  Incredibly fun and engaging to fight even the most basic enemies.
5. Bosses: Interesting and diverse movesets that reward critical thinking and pattern recognition.
6. Weapons and Build Variety: There are hundreds of weapons and you can basically play however you like as rarely is there a specifically bad build or weapon choice in this game.  This in turn gives Elden Ring great replayability.  For a souls newbie, there also are plenty of overpowered weapons to choose from.
7. Optimization: Runs really well on my low-end laptop.  You'll have a smooth experience for sure.

Cons:
1. Questlines: One of the worst quest systems of any video game out there.  Elden Ring takes confusing, obscure,  and overcomplicated quests to a WHOLE NEW LEVEL.  The game gives you absolutely no direction for what to do next in a quest.  Should I rest and come back?  Should I click the dialogue option three times or is there nothing?  Do I move on to the next area?  Where IS the next area?  What the hell is this NPC even talking about?  Worse still, Many questlines are intertwined SO deeply that you just get your quest progress halted if you don't find like 2 other "unrelated" NPCs in completely different areas and do their respective quests.  On top of that, you can also softlock yourself out of quests if you talk to the "wrong" NPC or advance beyond the game's specific intended points.  Oh and there's no quest log so you better fire up your brain and prepare to memorize every word spoken by the NPCs.
2. World: Although well-crafted, if you intend on exploring every nook and cranny, prepare for some boring and repetitive perimeter scouting.  
3. Story: You're mission in this game is practically to genocide everyone so that you become king of the land.  Quite the inspiring story.
4. Bosses: Although few, there are some bosses that are overall so poorly designed that you have to stop to question yourself whether the devs who made the great parts were even part of making this boss.  Another possible criticism could be that boss movesets are too long and that they give too little breathing room.

Overall, cons of this game are cringe but they don't take away from the awesome experience. 8/10 game, worth it for sure.

Visually, Elden Ring is stunning. Areas like Liurnia, Leyndell, and the underground cities are breathtaking and constantly made me stop just to admire the scenery. The soundtrack perfectly complements the world, making every major battle and discovery feel epic.

Elden Ring isn't just an amazing RPG—it's a masterpiece that sets a new standard for open-world games. If you enjoy exploration, challenging combat, and unforgettable worlds, this is a game you absolutely must play.

Having spent hundreds of hours in the Lands Between, I can confidently say that Elden Ring is not just a game you finish; it is a world you live in, leave, and inevitably return to. The From Software masterpiece first open world. 
While the first playthrough delivers an unmatched sense of awe, discovery, and overwhelming challenge, the true magic of this masterpiece reveals itself on subsequent runs. Knowing the map doesn't ruin the experience—it transforms it. In your first run, you survive. In your next runs, you orchestrate your journey. The absolute freedom to choose your path allows you to completely break the traditional progression, taking down major bosses in whatever order you see fit or hunting down late-game gear within the first hour.
The build variety is where FromSoftware truly outdid themselves. Replaying the game as a pure Strength colossus feels entirely different from playing as a nimble Dexterity-intelligence spellblade or a Crucible Knight faith build. Every weapon class, Ash of War, and spell school demands a completely different approach to the game’s legendary boss fights.
Combined with the unmatched verticality of its legacy dungeons and the sheer depth of the lore hidden in every item description, Elden Ring remains as captivating on the fourth playthrough as it was on the first. It is a rare triumph in gaming where the open world never feels like a chore, but rather a playground of endless tactical possibilities.

Pros:
-An open world that actually respects the player's intelligence and curiosity.
-Incredible build diversity that changes how you approach every single encounter.
-Exceptional boss design and art direction.
-Insane replay value; New Game+ and fresh characters feel like entirely new experiences.

Cons:
- Minor performance hiccups in specific late-game areas.
- The sheer scale can feel intimidating to absolute beginners without a guide.
A must-play for From Software/ Soulsbourne fans. The more I play, the more I enjoy the experience.

I was one of those people who bought it as my first souls game shortly after release. I knew I was supposed to skip bosses and explore, but I wandered into some late game zone, got bodied repeatedly, felt annoyed and just put it down.

But it's mentioned everywhere, so I had to give it another go. This time I looked up a cheesy build and didn't care - all I wanted was to actually experience it. Around the 15 hour mark it all started to click, and boyyy did this game suck me in.

The sense of wonder is something I hadn't felt in years. Going over a hill and seeing something massive in the distance, knowing you can just go there - no quest marker, no hand-holding, just you and your curiosity. Just so much hidden stuff you find that leaves you with a sense of wonder.
Honestly, Elden Ring ruined other games for me.
I still haven't touched the DLC - I'm saving it like a drug addict hiding away that one last dose.

If I HAD to nitpick: there is little to no indication how to complete quests and you will miss a lot of stuff, I read the wiki a lot because I had no idea how to finish a side quest. Levelling - some Turbo Knight you spent 20 minutes trying to beat will drop a penny, meanwhile a wolf in a wolf pack in another area that dies in 2 seconds will dump far more.

All in all really I can say is give it time. Let it click. Then let it take you away. One of the best experiences in recent gaming history.

Elden Ring is an amazing game. I am very much content in not having finished it. In case it is relevant, I reached Crumbling Farum Azula before stopping.

Right out the gate, ER makes a strong impression. Its scenery is beautiful and I love how creative so many locations are with their color palettes and concepts. Multiple times in this game I'd see some beautiful setpiece like a cave with a star-filled ceiling or the giant dragon corpse in Leyndell and sit for a minute to appreciate it. Outside of the intentionally revolting places like Caelid, many areas gave an otherwise rare sense of tranquility sorely needed in a game of this genre.

The game also does a phenomenal job (initially) of subtly funneling the player to points of interest, both with difficulty spikes and geographic obstacles to traversal. A big problem with open world games in my experience is the lack of direction they can often have, but that wasn't the case here.

Despite being singleplayer, I really liked the multiplayer integration of notes and comments. It made otherwise obtuse and annoying design, like hidden walls or split paths where one leads to a dead end trap and the other goes forward, into a communal experience where everyone cooperates. In a game as challenging as this, I loved the "we're all in this together" mindset the message system fosters.

I enjoyed the dungeons. They generally felt pretty seamless with the rest of the game, and were the highlight of the experience. That said, of the ones I explored, they felt quite unbalanced in terms of scope. It very well could be due to how much I struggled with it as the first, but Stormveil Castle felt much larger and deeper than all but Leyndell, Royal Capital. I enjoyed my time with the others, but I wanted more of Volcano Manor and Raya Lucaria than was present.

The world also felt quite front-loaded. This very well could be due to me getting tired and wanting to plow through, but the first area, Limgrave, and to a lesser extent the second major area, Liurnia, felt much denser than the other areas I explored in terms of things to do. I didn't find later areas like Caelid, Mountaintops of the Giants, or the Altus Plateau as interesting to explore, even if they arguably had better rewards for exploration. Their main routes felt clearer. I know earlier I praised the game for how it funneled the player, but early on side content was also funneled to, and I felt less interesting side content was brought to my attention as the game went on. Especially since the mini-dungeons (catacombs and mines) are very boring to explore, especially with how samey they are. Imagine the shrines from Breath of the Wild, but each one takes half an hour and they're all combat focused. They were complete slogs.

ER is ultimately an excellent game, and I would not hesitate to recommend it, but I wouldn't expect a player like myself to finish the game. Despite the immense enjoyment I got out of it, it still fell weak to the common flaws of open world design.

Also the lack of pausing made me want to kill myself. Let me pee in peace.

Combined with an incredible soundtrack, memorable characters, and some of the most imaginative creature and boss designs ever put into a video game, Elden Ring delivers an experience that is both epic and deeply personal. I adore Elden Ring. I have played it through many times, completed each ending at least once, and bought and played the dlc almost as soon as it came out. It is deeply meaningful to me, for its characters, story, and the truly beautiful world. I am not done with it and probably won't be for a very long time.
I will also, however, admit that I did mod it. I played the whole thing offline, with a modpack that made a number of changes to make the game easier for me. I have heard many times that this is not the intended experience, and that I am "doing it wrong" and not getting "the intended experience". But I played it, and I was able to play it and enjoy it, and I think that is an often missed part of this argument. I would always rather be able to play something, even if it isn't the perfect intended way, than leave it on a shelf forever because it was simply designed to be too frustrating for me.
The point of this is to say, Elden Ring is beautiful. If you want to play it because it is a challenge and you want the glorious struggle to victory after dozens of tries at a boss, you can. If you are intrigued by the story, or by everyone raving about it, and soulsborne games are just not your specialty? There's no shame in making it fun for yourself. Elden Ring is amazing, and I want people to be able to enjoy it even if they don't have the time to sink into hundreds of hours of grinding. It's a game, and games are meant to be fun. And Elden Ring sure as hell is fun.

The game refers to the Greater Will, which although ambiguous appears to refer to a literal entity that is an Outer God. It seems to be some sort of cosmic parasite, but who knows. This entity’s influence is represented by the golden light (‘grace’) that is seen everywhere. Queen Marika will come to be this entity’s vassal, who bears the Elden Ring, which is the physical manifestation of the Greater Will’s power and is made up of disparate runes (and is also the source of the power of the Erdtrees). The Two Fingers are literal emissaries that try to enact the desires of the Greater Will (not sure exaclty how the Two Fingers are created/born, are they also from space?). The Golden Order, as a human system of beliefs, eventually comes about to be to help enact the Greater Will’s desires.

Starting at the beginning, the Lands Between were first ruled by the dragons, led by Dragonlord Placidusax. The dragons were allied with an unnamed Outer God, who over time abandoned them and led to a soft decline of the Dragons power (and probably also to the crumbling of their sky city, Farum Azula, which gets subsumed in some sort of temporal vortex for some reason). Also around this time, what is now known now as the Erdtree was in a ‘primordial’ form and was understood as the ‘crucible’ of life. At some point, the Greater Will sends the Elden Beast within a star as a vassal and as mentioned Marika then becomes the vassal of the Greater Will (the Elden Beast is absorbed into her body). All that is known about Marika before this is that she is descended from the Numen race, which is a race that originated outside the Lands Between. For whatever reason, after becoming the Greater Will’s vassal, Marika goes into the Lands Between and establishes Leyndell. This will lead to many conflicts, one of which is the conflict with the dragons. As can be seen in the capital, the dragons attack (presumably for encroaching on their territory) but ultimately with the Greater Will’s power, Leyndell is able to stave off the Dragons. Over time, some individuals will join dragon cults and wish to become them. For example, the Magma Wyrms are actually humans who attempted to transform into dragons, but it only half-worked and they end up cursed to never fly. Eventually, Marika’s son Godwyn (Marika’s family tree is addressed a little later) will even befriend one of them, namely Fortissax. Another will join the magic academy and overall the dragons are clearly mostly pacified and that conflict is now over and dealt with.

Sometime around the establishing of Leyndell, the primordial erdtree is transformed into its current version. The crucible knights that defended the prior version were allowed to remain. One important falling out from this transformation is for the “omens”. Before the Golden Order was established, those born with signs of the crucible (e.g., horns, tails etc.) were seen as a blessing from the crucible. Afterwards, it is viewed as a curse (presumably because the Greater Will views it as an affront to its unity of power). In general, it is unclear how much of Marika’s actions and motivations could be ascribed to her or to the Greater Will, who uses her as its vassal. Anyways, those born with horns are shunned into the sewers and elsewhere. This would even escalate into Omenkillers deciding to hunt them down and was presumably a contribution to discrimination in general to any others seen as “impure”, which would also include the demi-humans and misbegotten, the bats (who sing a sing in real-life latin lamenting their new fate), the albinaurics, and the vulgar milita.

Noteworthy during this time period of Leyndell and the Golden Order, immortality is a power conferred by the Greater Will and the rune of death is held by Queen Marika’s half-brother, Maliketh, for safe-keeping. Well, technically the rune of death was held by the Dusk-Eyed/Gloam-Eyed Queen whose followers were the Godskin Apostles that use the blackflame and seemed to also use the deathbirds as its emissary. Maliketh slew the Queen and took her rune of death for himself/Marika’s purposes. Afterwards, it seems that beings during this time do not die up until they visit the Erdtree at which point, and this is only a theory, they are presumably absorbed into the Greater Will (or something like that).

Around this time, at the fringes, are some other Outer Gods. These include the ‘Formless Mother’ (a blood-based Outer God), a God of the Scarlet Rot, the Frenzied Flame, the One-Eyed Fell God of the Giants (essentially a fire god), and the aforementioned Gloam-Eyed Queen (essentially a goddess of death). I’ll get to most of those later, but for now want to camp out on the Giant’s Fell God, as this leads to war. Marika wages a war on the Fire Giants (led by a ‘Storm Ruler’), presumably because of the threat of their Forged Flame, a very powerful fire that emanates from the Giant’s pact with the One-Eyed Fell God and has the potential to burn the Erdtree. Marika has two noteworthy generals at this time, Radagon and Horah Loux (who is a chieftain of the neighboring Badlands). One noteworthy thing that occurs in the war is the Trolls betray the Giants and ally with Marika. They have holes in their stomachs as they removed the eye that used to be there to mark the presence of the Fell God. Marika’s forces win the war but when Marika realizes she cannot eradicate their Flame, she cursed the last fire giant to attend it for eternity, and that giant responded with a curse on Radagon to have his red hair (which is something he resents although some like Radhan view it with pride, presumably Radagon’s hair was golden before the curse). The Flame Monks are tasked with guarding this flame, although over time they are seduced by its power.

Queen Marika decides to marry Hoarah Loux, who rebrands himself and takes on the moniker Godfrey presumably to better enact the Greater Will (note this marriage may have already happened earlier). Godfrey and Marika have (at least) three children, Godwyn the Golden, as well as the twins Mogh and Morgott. Note that Morgott is also ‘Margit’ who you fight at the beginning because he is testing you. Mogh and Morgott are banished after they are birthed because they bear the aforementioned ‘omens’ (their horns) and are considered cursed. Mogh will resent this and eventually fall into league with ‘The Formless Mother’, while Morgott takes over the Capital in the long-run (as he remains a true believer in the Golden Order despite its treatment of him).

One event worth mentioning around now is the twin underground cities of Nokron and Nokstella. The lore around these cities is a little small, but it would seem what happened is certain individuals (the Nox) started messing with alchemy in a way the Greater Will did not approve. In other words, they created things such as the fingerslayer blade (a weapon powerful enough to kill the Two Fingers). This was naturally not considered okay and these individuals were essentially banished to live underground. In the past, an underground society already semi-existed with the Uhl (the minotaur people) but they were already gone or the Nox built around them. Over time, the Nox would experiment with creating artificial lifeforms and lords and also attempted to transform people into dragons (e.g. the dragonkin soldiers), presumably for power reasons. They are also the creators of the Albinaurics, who are artificial lifeforms. Eventually, these cities would be destroyed by beasts carried on falling stars (e.g. Astels). It would seem quite possible that the Astels were sent by the Greater Will to eradicate the dangers of these civilizations after they were self-contained underground (and remember the Elden Beast was itself sent as part of a falling star). Elden Ring is, in my opinion, the greatest video game ever made. It takes everything that made FromSoftware's previous games special and expands it into a massive open world filled with mystery, challenge, and unforgettable moments.

The world of the Lands Between is breathtaking. Every region feels unique, with stunning landscapes, hidden secrets, and incredible bosses waiting around every corner. Exploration is constantly rewarding because you never know what you'll discover next, whether it's a powerful weapon, a secret dungeon, or an entirely new area. Critics widely praised the game's open-world design, combat, and sense of discovery.

Combat is one of Elden Ring's strongest features. Every victory feels earned, and the variety of weapons, spells, and builds allows players to create their own unique playstyle. The boss fights are challenging, memorable, and some of the best in gaming history. Reviewers frequently highlighted the depth of the combat system and the creativity of its encounters.

The game's lore and atmosphere are equally impressive. Instead of telling its story through long cutscenes, Elden Ring encourages players to piece together its world through exploration and discovery. This makes the adventure feel personal and rewarding.

While the game can be difficult and occasionally overwhelming for newcomers, those willing to learn its systems will find one of the most rewarding experiences gaming has to offer. Its combination of exploration, combat, world-building, and freedom creates an adventure unlike any other.

Rating: 10/10

Elden Ring isn't just my favorite game—it's the standard by which I judge every other game. Few titles capture the same sense of wonder, accomplishment, and adventure. For me, it is the best game ever made.

This game deserves all of its flowers, and I want to add my piece: Limgrave is probably the smartest ease-in to an open-world I've ever come across. As soon as you leave the tutorial area, you open those doors, and the beauty of this game immediately leaves you in awe. You take your first steps toward whom you perceive as the welcome mat to this stunning spectacle, and get called maidenless. You see a Golden-armored horseman and are immediately filled with the determination to kill it, only to be stomped on like a bug. You can't seemingly fight him as you are now, unless you're willing to keep bashing your head at it, so you go on to explore. You look around and fight some enemies, only for them to kill you over and over again, and suddenly you're met with an exhaustion to put down the controller. You wake up the next day realize that whether its exploring or fighting a boss, there's no way you're going to progress unless you practice, so you take it slow and sneak up on a few enemies instead of taking them head on. you find a cool weapon and figure out how to start leveling up, and that same boss becomes trivial. That is the philosophy that is drilled into your head not even 30 minutes into the game, and yet it spans across your entire playthrough. you don't HAVE to explore every nook and cranny of the surrounding area until you level up enough to beat a boss easily, and you don't HAVE to die 40+ times until you kill a boss. That's what the game is telling you, the way you want to play is how the game is played. You can choose an int build and melt enemies with your magic. You can pick up the biggest sword you can find and make bosses to buckle easily, it's all up to you. 

I haven't completed the game more than once, but I will say I have played through at least Limgrave a few times a least. It's just that good. I would take the time to talk about the masterful level-design of Limgrave ALONE from a game-development perspective, but it would just turn into a full blown essay. Go play this game, its definitely more of a full package than any other game at it's pricing, and I've heard the DLC is its own full game, which is insane. First off, Elden Ring is not a bad game. The boss fights, visuals and world building are all cool, and while I finished the game and then some, its just... a drag. 

The world is massive, and you can really feel it. Exploration is a key to Elden Ring, and that can be fun at times. What is not fun, is the absurd scale of the game combined with a complete lack of non-filler content. Useless crafting materials, random ashes (another whole topic on its own) and grave glovewort being treated like "rewards" for exploring far off corners of the world, same one enemies in every dungeon, and half of the boss fights being "what if we did it again... but now there's two of them". Same one tree sentinel. Same one tree spirit.

With enemies scattered all over with nothing to gain from killing them, the game heavily encourages you to not fight, and just explore in the open world. What's that? John Knight patroling a random road drops a unique item, but you ignored him as he's literally a generic enemy found all over elsewhere? Oh well, thats unfortunate. Better luck next time. 

Souls games inherently will never be possible to mostly complete on a first run without some sort of guide, and quest chains even more so as they're intended to be done over multiple playthroughs, but the insane amount of NOTHING in this game that is just recycled over and over and over that you CANNOT skip without a guide because guess what, that one dungeon you chose to skip, missed or forgot was the one dungeon that didnt just have useless ashes in them. That one hill over there might have a key item for your build or quest chain, so you better go explore it thoroughly, but wait... there was nothing. Again.

As I started with, the game isnt bad. The game is mostly enjoyable. It has some crazy fights, its weapons and various forms of incantations/sorceries are very cool, but there's just too much in this game that has no place, or is recycled adding nothing but filler, for me to reccomend it before literally any other fromsoft souls game. If part of the enjoyment in these games for you is trying to explore and find as much as possible without help, the world is filled with far too much nothing, but hey, at least it will look pretty and the main boss fights will be cool.

I don't like FromSoftware games, I find them boring, they are often annoying and just suck. It is not hard to call them overrated, they are extremely popular and also quite edgy, and like in every other media, edgy titles tend to produce the most overrated works.

The game is very beautiful, areas look amazing.

The problem, however, is in the small recurring things. Annoying sequences that have become FromSoftware signatures, despite being ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Poison lakes with speed debuffs, terrible platform sections in an engine that clearly is not for that. Vague quest system that no longer works in an open world. Lingering AOEs (poison mists and fires) that you can't really roll through due to their size, despite the game being designed around roll. Bosses that keep repositioning after attacks (I played melee, ♥♥♥♥ Maliketh). Giant bosses that really don't work when you can't see them whole on camera. Some bosses just being recycled too much, like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dragons, I HATE GENERIC DRAGONS. Horse combat was ♥♥♥♥, but what game does vehicle combat well...

It's a good game, quite inconsistent, but you should play it.

As someone who's played Dark Souls 1, Dark Souls 3, and Sekiro, Elden Ring is a bit of a mixed bag for me.

The biggest difference is obviously the open world. In the older games, if I got stuck on a boss, that boss became my entire problem. There weren't a hundred other places to go or things to do. The only option was to learn the fight and beat it. I really liked that feeling of being forced to overcome the obstacle in front of me.

With Elden Ring, I sometimes end up overwhelmed by all the choices. Even on my third playthrough of the base game (my first two were on Xbox), I still find myself wondering where I should go next or if there's something else I should be doing instead. The freedom is impressive, but it can also make the experience feel less focused.

That being said, everything else about the game is incredible. The combat, bosses, build variety, world design, music, and sense of discovery are all top-tier.

I still prefer the more linear design of Dark Souls and Sekiro, but that's really just personal preference. Other than the open-world structure not being my favorite, Elden Ring is a 10/10 game and easily one of the best games I've ever played.

Attack variety and unpredictability is what makes this game fun. But having those attacks hit you for all your health is pretty lame and kind of restricts you from exploring weird builds. I think the from soft game that got its difficulty balanced perfectly was Sekiro. It was incredibly difficult but I felt like it was fair. An attack with an area of effect that could cover the surface of the moon should not be able to take all of your health. Additionally a sleeping toad that does no damage to you should not be giving over two thousand runes while a flying paladin with holy magic that can one shot you only gives you three. This almost perfect game would have benefited from some balancing. But even if they don't make that change in the future, From Soft is still going to make some of the best games on the market.

[h1]Open world yay...or nay[/h1]

Here we go another entry in dark/demon souls series. But it's elden souls now.
So this time they made dark souls open world.

Story? As always there's none, just some nonsensical characters around speaking in riddles and rubbish in general.

Open world is very static and feels dead. There are enemies copy pasted everywhere though. With some stationary npc's who apparently are immortal and not afraid of any danger. Oh wait you can kill them so they're mortal but not. Of well lets move on from the “story”.

Gameplay stays the same. Dodge, hit, dodge, hit, etc. Less janky this time though but still with a huge input lag. But this time you can jump. Can't believe such a revolutionary feature would be ever added to dark souls. So you can do a jump attack now. And on top of that another absolutely stunning and revolutionary feature – a horse. Yep you have a horse now to move through the empty world.
I wonder what's the next feature in the upcoming dark souls? Maybe swimming?
There are some nice changes though. You can use any weapon, upgrade it, respec as much as you like. Also runbacks to bosses are short.

So you roam the world of the dead and the goal is to defeat the evil lords or whatever nonsense. Most of the bosses are just reskins, they went quantity over quality with this one. Fights go from overly simple and easy to unbearably tedious and hard. There's absolutely no balance whatsoever.

No difficulty options for some reason. So it takes a lot of fun from the game and makes it a tedious, boring grind fest.
Main boss design though is good. Funnily enough the coolest bosses are the weakest. Also last boss being a huge space pe**s is hilarious.

Graphically the game is almost alright. Good for AA or indie but I thought it's a AAA game? It looks boring and same'ey. Sky is the worst, just some skybox jpeg glued on top.
Performance is who knows.Technically the game is a mess. Fps is locked to 60 for some reason which is unacceptable for and action-hack&slash game.
Obviously no ultrawide support which shows how incompetent developers are. You can enable it with fixes though. Although you risk getting banned in the game even though it's single player.

Sound is the only good thing this game has. Since there's no story line obviously there's not much voice acting besides few lines. But the music is outstanding.

In general a decent action game but it falls short in being open world, lacking cohesive story, characters, gameplay, enemy variety, etc. There are better ones. Even assassins creed is better which tells a lot.

Elden Ring is one of the most impressive open-world RPGs ever made. Developed by FromSoftware and directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game combines the challenging combat the studio is known for with a massive world full of exploration, secrets, and unforgettable encounters.

The Lands Between is a stunning setting that constantly rewards curiosity. Every region feels unique, from haunting castles to underground cities hidden beneath the world. Unlike many open-world games, exploration rarely feels repetitive because there is always something interesting around the next corner.

Combat is deep and satisfying, offering a huge variety of weapons, spells, and character builds. Boss battles are a major highlight, requiring skill, patience, and strategy. While the difficulty can be intimidating for newcomers, the game's open structure allows players to explore elsewhere and grow stronger before tackling tougher challenges.

The story is mysterious and often told through environmental details, item descriptions, and character interactions. This approach won't appeal to everyone, but it creates a sense of discovery that fits the game's world perfectly.

The few drawbacks include occasional performance issues and a lack of traditional quest tracking, which can sometimes leave players confused about where to go next. However, these flaws are minor compared to the overall experience.

Overall, Elden Ring is a masterpiece that successfully blends challenging gameplay, rewarding exploration, and rich world-building. Whether you're a longtime fan of FromSoftware games or a newcomer looking for an unforgettable adventure, it is a game well worth playing.

SILLY LORE/PLAYED BEFORE KNOWLEDGE I never played a soulslike before, and before this game the usual combat in game experiences I had were (in order) Zelda, Baldur’s gate 3, and assasin’s creed Origins. Oh, and some light dragons dogma 2. I heard of Eldenring shortly after completing Baldur’s gate 3 and was intrigued by its alleged amazing worldbuilding handled by none other than George R.R Martin. (known from ASOIAF/GOT) This is kinda how the ball began to roll, but it would take YEARS before I would give Eldenring an actual chance. Mainly: Allegedly, ER is a very massive, beautiful but challenging game. Up until joining an achievement hunter discord, where tons of folks told me just how fun it was and that I should give it a try. Before, my biggest challenge in games used to be that a villager would plant its butt down in animal crossing in the way of my terraforming and oh my, has that issue been overshadowed immensely by Elden Ring.

OVERRAL THOUGHTS ABOUT THE GAME.
DESIGN:
The game is in my honest opinion, but I don’t play many games like this very beautiful designed. The colours seem lush and lifely, while still keeping that wandering between two worlds kinda element, as if you are in a magical place beyond our world. I liked the watergraphics, the grass looked cozy as the guards knocked me face down into it, and I am sure my character enjoyed bleeding out on some of the amazingly beautifully designed bridges. The character creator was also very important to me, and I sure enjoyed making my EldenLord a few times over…maybe too many times…

THE GAME FOR ME
So as I said, the game is unlike anything I played before. From the leveling system, to the rather harsh punishments when you do lose, to the scary enemies and the darker themes this is not a classical game I would normally pick up to play. And maybe that is exactly what made playing this (eventually) so much fun! At the first few times I felt like I was failing really badly and that I’d never make it past the first boss but after help from my friends and kinda learning that soulsgames=dying and learning I slowly became more confident. Bosses that used to send me running, or jumpscares that caused me to close the game became tests to test my reflexes and with every victory (big or small) I regained more and more confidence and learned along the way. The world that once seemed so overwhelmingly big became smaller as I uncovered pieces of the map and once my weapon was upgraded, and I actually paid attention to what a boss does during a fight, I had an absolutely almost unhealthy amount of joy playing it, jumping enemies in a violent way and screaming that their time had come, making concerned neighbors of mine wonder if everything was truly alright. Is ELDENRING for everybody? I think not, but what game truly is? It was a challenge, and it did what it promised. It challenged, it changed the way I’d approach a fight in a game and maybe even me along the way. 

10/10 would recommend.

Elden Ring is one of the rare games that genuinely feels like a masterpiece.

The world design is absolutely unmatched. Exploration doesn’t feel like filler—it feels like discovery in the truest sense. Every direction you go has something worth finding, and the game constantly rewards curiosity without holding your hand.

Combat is deep, satisfying, and incredibly flexible. Whether you’re playing a heavy strength build, magic, or something more hybrid, the game gives you real freedom to approach situations your own way. Boss fights are often highlights of the entire experience, with many feeling unforgettable once you finally overcome them.

What really makes Elden Ring stand out is how consistently it delivers those “I can’t believe this is in a game” moments. The scale, atmosphere, and sense of mystery are on another level.

There are some rough edges—occasional performance issues and some repeated enemy designs—but they don’t take away from the overall experience.

This is easily one of the best games ever made. Not just an action RPG, but a landmark title that sets a new standard for open-world design.

Highly recommended.

I got this game YEARS AGO, back in college, as a gift from a good friend of mine, Jay. He got it for me as an introduction to souls-like games, and I had the blessing of having him join me for my first boss fight.

For fans of souls-like games: This is a great one, and you already know you're in for a good time with a Fromsoft title. Get the game, dog; and don't give up, skeleton.

Souls-like games are best captured, in my opinion, by this game's opening sequence. You leave the tutorial area, and right in front of you is a massive horseback sentinel. It deals enough damage to two-tap you. Your hitbox is incredibly precise, and its hitbox is incredibly precise. With enough skill, you can do some damage to it, and survive for a while. The game places it there to tell you "Some obstacles are hard enough you should go find other loot, level up, and return stronger to better deal with them; however, you will be rewarded for your skills and will be able to accomplish anything you set your mind to with enough skill, time, and willpower." With that lesson placed in front of me, I spent 9 hours straight, running on like 22 hours of being awake when I first started, beating this boss, and me and my friend celebrated its glorious defeat. And that is how I got introduced to souls-like games.

The game went on to delight, frustrate, and otherwise completely enthrall me. It's seeded a deep love of soulslike games, and has provided already 400 hours of thoroughly enjoyed gameplay, with countless more yet to come as I continue to play through the 100% playthrough I'm working on right now, of which I'm at 53% completion with 177 hours. Not including the DLC. This game rocks.

The premise of Elden Ring was really quite simple. You know this iconic series of challenging action games FromSoftware is known to make? Take that and make it bigger, grander and epic. Make it Dark Souls, but open world. Then give GRR Martin yet another excuse not to finish the Winds of Winter by hiring him to create for you a backstory full of weird incestuous genderfluid gods. Finally, add to the mix a strange horse-goat of a mount and you have something really quite unusual. That's the premise and the promise. Now whether it delivers on that promise or not that's a different discussion. One that after spending a good 200 hours on this game's expansive world, perhaps I can answer.

Let's begin with the elephant in the room. The open world. This is one damn big elephant, truly ginormous. It goes on and on. Mountains, swamps, frozen over lakes, caverns, vast underground locations. This is one of the bigger games I have played and it's filled with details. It's also terrifyingly beautiful. The rich use of colour, the stunning landscapes, the dramatic vistas, the incredible heights. The game's art direction is top-notch. I would argue it's era defining. However there is an important caveat to consider. The open world is an incredible achievement yes, but how well does it serve the game's other mechanics.

Here the picture becomes somewhat less celebratory. You see the game retains its Dark Souls bones, the nuanced, environmental story-telling, the sparse quests driven by occasional meetups. Only now this spans a vastly larger surface and becomes a lot harder to experience naturally. Put simply, a great number of quests are next to impossible to do correctly without a guide. Not because of the minimalist design and lack of compasses, but exactly because of how incongruous the quest design is when applied to an open world. You execute a step in a quest. The character moves. Where? Go figure. In Dark Souls progression was linear and this was not much of an issue. Here, it is.

On gameplay this is largely Dark Souls still. Except significantly easier. This is likely another side-effect of the open world direction. I'm not saying the game is not challenging. Rush ahead and you will be punished. However, the game rewards careful exploration, as it rewards skilful combat. Generously. And there is plenty of rewarding side-content to conquer. Do that enough and by the endgame even superbosses won't be that scary. On a smaller scale, a disappointing element was the complete lack of a swimming ability. So many inviting islands close to the coast that are impossible to reach without gimmicks. The moment your character reaches the darker shade of waters down they go, as if they reached the proverbial end of the world. Be that as it may, this is a competently made and entertaining action game. Given its pedigree, I would expect no less.

Technically speaking the game is less impressive than its stellar art direction might suggest. Its graphical prowess in particular is decent but not extraordinary. There are sloppy technical decisions present that I wouldn't expect to see in a modern game. For example the lack of ultra wide monitor support. Even Dark Souls Remastered had that. But not Elden Ring? What's worse, the game is taking anti-cheating a bit too seriously and attempting to mod the game to include missing functionality can mark you as a cheater. I ended up having to play the game completely offline and with the use of extraneous software that didn't integrate quite seamlessly enough. All so that I could make the game work properly with my setup. FromSoftware really needs to do better here.

To conclude, does Elden Ring deliver on its promise. Is this Dark Souls but open world and is that a good thing? The first question is easy. Yes, it definitely is. The minimalist story telling, the challenging combat, the well crafted world. It's all here. The second question is harder. Dark Souls is not an open world game and making it one required changes that occasionally felt like discounts to the formula. In the end this is a lovingly made game of incredible ambition. It is beautiful and it is flawed. Is it worth playing? Absolutely, it's also worth pondering. There is something truly monumental just a few improvements away.

Side note for PC players with steam decks: 
Once you get to basically end game, it's really easy to experience all three of the main endings (the ones that give achievements) without being forced to create a new save or new game+ for other endings. Make sure to have a save on your steam deck prior to choosing an ending, and set your PC to offline mode. If you move your character even an inch to the right on your steam deck with cloud save, your PC local file is now desynced from your steam deck. This causes a file conflict which you want. You can go through each of the ending, and go back to your cloud save from the steam deck so you can choose another ending.

I was excited to try this game because of the 10/10 reviews and George RR Martin's involvement. But sadly the world just feels so...empty and forlorn. I get that its supposed to be post apocalyptic dark fantasy, but you'd think there would be at least be some kind of narrative and more than a handful of NPCs that only babble nonsense. 

The game is absolutely mind-blowing in its visuals. Even in the spell animations. They're some of the best I've ever seen, in fact. The world is gorgeous and the art direction team deserves some heavy praise. But this illusion of immersion shatters the moment you realize there isn't much to do while exploring that beautiful world aside from randomly killing things to grind XP. 

It actually baffled me quite a bit. I'm not the biggest fan of Game of Thrones, but Martin obviously knows how to write fantasy lore. But I didn't see any of that in my nearly 10 hours of play. I was lost and confused and wondering what my motivation was, what I was supposed to do and why I should care about this world. 

So I did some research, and it turns out that he didn't write any dialogue or narrative for the actual game, but just the lore that happened 5,000 years before the game started, which the player has no way of accessing. I don't really see the point in this. If they were going to hire someone to create an elaborate fantasy world, why didn't we get to play in that world, instead wandering around randomly fighting stuff in an empty world of nothing?

Perhaps the gameplay could have supported the experience, but I found it quite lacking in that department as well. I elected to play a mage, and the only useful spell I could find was the generic magic missile starting spell. There were others, but the selection was very limited, I had to grind runes to get them, and even then I could only access them after fighting a secret boss that could only find by looking it up on a wiki. (Seriously, there was no clue about this in the actual game itself.) After going to all this trouble, what did I get? A handful of useless garbage spells that were worse than what I started with. 

So yeah, my impression of this game is probably tainted by the poor implementation of magic. But I don't think I would have enjoyed playing a martial-type character either. The melee combat is slow and sluggish. It doesn't feel quick and responsive at all, more like moving through a layer of mud, and evasion is awkward. 

Character progression is likewise pretty lackluster. All you get on level up is 1 point of stat assignment that barely changes your numbers. No feats, skill trees, talent points, anything like that. It didn't feel like I was making a build or learning new abilities that changed how I played, more like just grinding to make numbers go up. 

All of this only got worse when I ran into the first major boss. I wasn't strong enough to beat him despite being almost level 30. I'm not sure how much more I would have had to grind to get past it, but I was already bored by that point. 

The kicker, though, was when the game randomly deleted all my save files. I might have been halfway tempted to keep going, but not if I have to start over now on top of all of that. 

I honestly don't understand the positive reviews for this game. Even 15 year old games full of jank like Oblivion and Morrowind have better worlds, more complex magic systems, and are more creative than this.

Elden Ring was my first Soulsbourne game/Fromsoft game back on the PS5 and I have 1500 plus hours on it.  I loved the game so much that I bought it again on PC once I had a good gaming rig.  Because of this game, I recently went back and played all the Dark Souls games and enjoyed the hell out of them as well, so that's another reason I decided to pick this one up again.  

After playing those, I have some different thoughts and insights on this game.  Either way, I suppose it might be helpful to break this down into a Pros/Cons list, so here we go:

Pros:   
-Visually, this is the most beautiful game I've ever played.  I wish it had a legit photo mode because I've taken so many screenshots, it's not funny.  Unfortunately, most of those have health bars or something in them.  The views often look like a painting and are truly a work of art.  And, no, it's just the skyboxes, it's the architecture, overall building design, and locales as well.  

-Best exploration of any open world game I've played - there aren't any icons or checklists, you just explore, get some visual storytelling, and you are frequently rewarded with cool items, lore, and/or visuals.  I played FF VII Rebirth after this and as fun as most of the game is, the open world was... mostly unpleasant.  I wish they could have learned from this game.

-Weapons, armor, and items - oh my.  This really creates a big part of the replayability of this game as you can come up with so many new "builds" and new ways to play. 
-Replayability - Continued from above, but yeah... it's hugely replayable between getting different endings, finishing up questlines you missed, and just being able to play through it completely differently.  The latter was my favorite part as I played through the first time with a Dex/Bleed build and had several struggles toward the end, but when I played as sorcerer I breezed through some of those areas and struggled in different places.  

-Challenging, but rewarding (most of the time) - At first, the combat was painful for me.  I had never played these games before and it just wasn't clicking.  It took way longer than it should have and I tried to play it like a Skyrim stealth archer, so you can imagine how that went.  Still, once it began to click, it became more fun. When you do overcome an obstacle or a tough boss, you feel good about it.
-Spirit Ash Summons - I'm so glad these exist.  I'm currently trying to play without them, unless it's like a reused boss or something just to add some variety, but these helped so much on my first few runs since this was all new to me.  I'm not sure if I would have finished the game without having them as an option.  Of course, it's pretty clear after playing the other 3 games that the bosses here were designed with their use in mind.

Cons:

-Most NPC questlines are borderline impossible without guides - This goes for all of the Souls games, but this one the most.  I completed some of them by accident, but for most of them, I didn't even realize they were quests.  I don't think we need a detailed quest system or anything, but a basic journal would be great. I played Shadows of the Erdtree with some hand-written notes and it helped, but this game is just too big to remember all these NPCs, what they want, and where they're going.  Well, you never know where they're going...

-Endgame difficult spike - Mountaintops of the Giants and Consecrated Snowfields are just unpleasantly difficult. Part of it is the enemies and bosses just have huge health bars, but also they hit ridiculously hard even at high levels.  In addition, some of the catacombs are almost a joke with their difficulty such as when they include some of the difficult early catacomb bosses as regular enemies throughout.  I found myself getting frustrated a lot and in subsequent playthroughs, I skipped a lot in these areas unless I'm looking for specific items.

-Reused bosses - I noticed this more after playing the DS games and coming back to ER, but it is just not fun running into your 4th, 5th, or 10th Erdtree Avatar, Ulcerated Tree Spirit, or Crucible Knight.  I hate it even worse when they just become a regular enemy.  It's not quite as bad if they don't respawn, but it's still just boring.  Shadow of the Erdtree did this the worst with the Ulcerated Tree Spirits, especially in one of the coolest areas of the game.  It's like the only thing that changes is that they're stronger and hit harder.

-Shadows of the Erdtree empty areas - This expansion is beautiful, challenging, and a game in and of itself, but there are some big, empty areas.  I get that some are important for the lore, but I'm not sure why they couldn't have cut some of these down and/or added some other items worth finding.  The Finger ruins, the grassy areas outside of Shadow Keep, and the area with the red flowers are some of the worst offenders.  Again, at least they're all really cool looking, but I got an empty feeling quite often after exploring them.  I found myself asking, "Is that it?" quite often.

-Shadows of the Erdtree final bosses and overall ending to the DLC:  Just overall I would say the final bosses and overall ending were... disappointing.  I don't want to give spoilers, but Gaius and the final DLC boss are just awful.  Endless combos, bad hitboxes, and flashiness to the point of distraction.  It was just so unfun that I had no problem looking up "cheese" methods or even doing a respec just to get through the fights.

Anyway, overall this is one of my favorite games of all time.  It's easily top 5 or maybe even top 2.  I really hope there's an Elden Ring 2 that takes what this game did and even further improves upon it.  I'll be there for it, either way.

I was pressured into playing this by many people. I loved it for the first 12 hours, then I tolerated it for the other 12 I put into it, trying to be open-minded about playing an official soulslite for the first time even when I was starting to realize it wasn't for me. I was holding off on posting this review as I KNOW there will be fans out there prepared to counter any points I could make before I'm actually understood. Regardless of the backlash I'm sure I'll face for daring to downvote Elden Ring, I feel like there are multiple elephants in the room around this game that are still critical to one's enjoyment of it. If you like Elden Ring / FromSoft games, I don't intend on changing your opinion, I just ask that you respect mine.

I'll get the positives out of the way first:

-The exploration is gorgeous, the map is big and adversity is around every corner; it reminds me of the original Legend of Zelda, where you (mostly) have access to everything the game has to offer from the beginning and it entirely lets you dictate the pacing of it. Combat is accessible, you don't need to be good at mashing buttons or remember complex combos to learn this game's controls; it's really easy to pick up where you left off.

Now for all of the negatives:
-Enemy placement and design in Elden Ring consistently resorts to what would be considered cheap in any other game; enemies killing you from around corners / off-screen, inflated damage and health bars, unexplained debuffs, mechanics and attack patterns that're literally impossible for even the top 1% of eSports players to react to.
-The open-world and the stealth mechanics are a necessary waste of time to eventually overcome boss battles. Some bosses are literally impossible unless you grind for stats in a game about hacking-and-slashing.
-The 60fps lock is a design choice to prevent you from ever having the ability to react to particular fatal hits from bosses. It is not even theoretically possible for a fresh player to complete this game without some kind of memory or knowledge of the bosses patterns.
-Dying boots you to a really long loading screen, even on a gen 4 SSD, that reloads every enemy back into the map. I'm sitting on the loading screen of this game about as often as I am actually playing the game and then wasting further time, fighting the same enemies again, to get back to where I was before.
-Class variety can change your experience of the game from a brutally difficult experience trying to fight with sticks and stones to a breeze with purely ranged magic attacks that bosses are completely helpless to.
-The general design of this game is very hostile and manipulative. Playing Elden Ring is like being a young person trying to survive in America; you need experience you can't get and you need money / runes you can't earn; choosing the wrong career path / class will ruin your life / game. When you beat a boss, you can't tell if it's because you actually mastered it's pattern or if you just didn't die that time. You don't get to fight all of them again to know for sure, at least not within the same save file. A game that provides enough content as-is doesn't need all of this fluff to justify it's usually $60 price tag; playing Elden Ring became a chore, whether you repeatedly fight the same boss or you spend hours farming for runes you could very easily lose.

I'm going to list some games that Elden Ring reminds me of and why I like them over this:

Castlevania (1 and 3 on the NES) Fights are hard, but not drawn-out. You don't need a memory of patterns / where good stuff is to progress, but they do help. it's all entirely possible with what your character starts out with. No save points, but it's quick to get back to where you were before you had to shut off the game.

Zelda BOTW: The exploration, side-quests and puzzles are guaranteed to help you progress through the game even if they're not what you primarily play BOTW for. You don't bend over backwards for a weapon / move that's weaker than what you already have and enemy variety is much more interesting than "hehe bird with a barrel haha look at this loading screen some more." Upgrading your character and farming Rupies isn't contingent on you keeping your character alive, you're permitted to make mistakes while you're still learning the game.

DOOM (2016, Eternal and TDA): Brutal difficulty you can always dial back or shut-off and come back to as you please. No bloated leveling system or big world designed to waste your time, progression is consistent; if you get past a hard part, you have confidence that you could pull it off again. The game doesn't let you just barely survive; enemies you fight come back and are compounded by newer enemies and patterns, so progression is made clear to you through demonstration, even if it's harder that way. Boss fights are not drawn out to the point where you die because of human error, but they're challenging enough to where you still have to learn them.

If all I have to do is git gud to enjoy any video game, then what responsibility do developers have in designing it? Why is $60 no longer a good enough accommodation to know you'll enjoy the game? If I just want to understand the world of Elden Ring and experience the story, if I just wanna see what the other 200+ bosses look like, why do I have to commit a bunch of time into the ones I'll see only once, maybe twice?

Why am I not allowed to pause in a singleplayer game? Yet another hostile design choice against those who may not have the option to play the game uninterrupted. I don't want every game I play to be super difficult and demand more out of me than my own work does; If you're a master Elden Ring player, yeah this game brings you clout, but it brings you clout by making others regret buying something that apparently wasn't for them

more onto the game:
Ive wanted to play this game since it released on my 18th birthday, however put it off until earlier this year, purely because at that time i only really used to stick to games like fallout, cod and fortnite, I then bought Dark Souls 2 when it was on sale towards the start of this year and ended up really enjoying souls like games, after 100% Scholar of first sin I immediately decided I was finally going to buy this game, managed to hold out long enough and picked up base game for £25.

map detailing is incredible, and the game manages to look amazing at almost any frame rate, boss fight arenas are well designed and usually you can guess what kind of attacks to expect by the arena you're in, I havent had any issues with this game as someone with aracnaphobia, but when the crawling hand things attack you, it is incredibly spider-like and did freak me out, If you survived dark souls 2 spiders, theres nothing to really worry about in terms of that. Elden Ring is a high fantasy game and a "what if Dark Souls and Skyrim had a baby". The combat is very high paced comparable to Bloodborne while keeping the clunkiness (realism) of Souls game, have a wide variety of arsenal from magic, faith, blood, and swords. Although while the weapons and magics seems to be balanced around PvE, the PvP is is still enjoyable to various degree with the addition of Arena. As for the exploration, the player is able to ride a horse to travel around the huge Lands' Between, similar to Skyrim.

The bosses' fights are top notch, ranged from a huge old man who filters the player with its difficulty, an epic raid boss, to a gigantic alien with cosmos inside its body. The players may encounter some bosses with numbers advantage on them, which comes the time when co-op comes in handy. Some of the bosses' fights also encourage the players to try different built which makes the game very diverse.

The visuals are very stellar. It doesn't come with a lot of NVIDIA enchantments aside from the ray tracing, but the grasses, scenic locations, weathers, gravity and special effects are enough to activate the neurons of the players. Even better, the weathers and locations affects the gameplay, adding more realism to the game.

The lore comes in various angle and up to players' interpretation while keeping the original writers style. For example in layman's term, the players started with nothing (just like when they're born), then they met someone who told them they're unfortunately maidenless (telling the players to get laid) and told them to become Elden Lord (encouraging the players to become the King of their own, and start a family perhaps).

All in all, Elden Ring may be a complete game that people have been wanting for a decade, especially for Souls and Elder Scrolls fans. Just play it in a healthy manner as to not forget the message of the game (such as stuck in Lands' Between and forgot outside the mum' basement).

main bosses here are [h1] gravity [/h1] and [h1] curiosity [/h1]

the [b] actual bosses [/b] are underwhelming for the most part, lacking variety in both movesets and designs, while some of their attacks are nearly broken.[spoiler] elden beast is just too vacuous and shallow for a final boss. we're taking inspiration from naruto now, besides berserk? [/spoiler]

this time they implemented spirit ashes so players could bring some help into fights offline and get past difficult obstacles. sadly, this mechanic is either useless or drastically lowers the difficulty of a fight, making victory feel somewhat hollow if you're looking for a good challenge. some broken attacks make you rely on a lucky attempt where they either aren't used or don't catch you, especially when playing melee (waterfowl dance, hoarah loux's earthshaker, claw barrage, etc.). so when you're given the option not to waste so much time waiting for the perfect attempt, you're most likely going to use it, and that takes a lot away from the experience. I'd choose a really good fight without one-shot attacks over spirit ashes any day

[b] open world [/b] is very flawed. there are too many unused or copy-pasted fields, activities, and enemies scattered across the map, along with a huge number of counterintuitive obstacles. even the level design in the more linear locations is in decline compared to the DS series. it's especially noticeable in places like farum azula and even leyndell

[b]quests[/b], including the important ones, don't bring anything particularly interesting or emotional to the table. the only questlines I really admired were Iron Alexander's and little Jar-Bairn's

[b]music[/b] could've been far more interesting and memorable, but that's been a recurring weakness of their games for a while now. maybe they should've borrowed a little more from ICO in that department as well

overall, the game feels like a mix of all previous FS titles, but with a much less challenging twist and what some would call quality-of-life improvements. this is the most popular game they've made, and it shows, because the floor messages here are the most useless and mediocre I've seen. it actually makes you want to play offline, which I find ridiculous for an FS title

[spoiler] the ending was comically short and uneventful after all the grand, ambitious ideas the game spends so much time talking about. I'd have been happier with no dialogue whatsoever, just show me something I actually had an impact on by the end of it all, if there was any [/spoiler]

[h3]A generational game, but not without flaws[/h3]

To preface this review: my only experience with any souls-like was 'The First Berserker: Khazan', and I never finished it.
Actually, I almost never finished Elden Ring either. A few hours in, and I was ready to quit, but the sheer number of players glazing this game was bugging me. "What do they see, that i dont?''
I couldn't tell you exactly when I found my answer; it was more of a gradual experience. But I do now understand, even if I don't fully agree.

The [b][i]world[/i][/b] that's built here is amazing. The ambience and overall vibes made me feel like this was a living, breathing realm full of despair and danger. Even without many cut scenes, I could still grasp the severity and gravity of the events that had taken place. (even if most of the time i had no idea what was happening in the story)

The [b][i]combat[/i][/b], while at times was a little frustrating, is still one of its best features. The build diversity and scope are something special that I can't really find a comparison to in anything else I've played before it. 
The bosses, too, were imaginative and challenging, and more than a few times I found myself jumping out of my seat and slamming my desk in excitement after I defeated them.

There's more I could praise, but I won't, because so many reviews have already done that. So instead ill bring up a few of the [b][i]negatives[/i][/b] that i dont see mentioned very often.
The target locking in this game is dreadful. I swear I died more times to this than actual bosses. It's mostly fine when you have a single enemy to deal with, but as soon as there are multiple targets, it fails miserably.
The other massive flaw I feel this game has is with its in-game systems/mechanics. I can't think of a single game I've ever played that required me to tab out and Google as many times as this. It really was ridiculous. There is just so much that isn't explained or explained well, and most players will miss out on a lot of content or waste a lot of time without Alt-tabbing and turning to guides. 

Overall though, I'm happy I put the time in and finished it. It was a great adventure.

80% of the game is optional, and that optional content is basically cut and paste, so it's not very enjoyable... you'll find so many Erdtree Minors, Ulcerated whatevers, Wyrms, Tree Sentinels, etc.  Yes, that's how the previous games were, but I don't think to this extent.  It's also funny to hear Elden Ring enthusiasts complain about things in Dark Souls 2, when those same things exist in ER, to an even higher degree.  See also gank squads and discontinuity between areas.

The other thing I've realized is that Souls games have essentially evolved to be a memory game, where enemies move 1,000 MPH, hit incredibly hard, do ridiculously long and comical windups, have infinite combos/stamina, and have a minimum of 2 phases per boss.  So you have to memorize all their tells, the gimmicky long delays between hits, and so on.  It's exhausting and not fun.

I really don't know what this bigger "open" world gives the game... sure, more content, but when it's cut and paste, it's not really interesting.  Like a lot of the caves end at a boss, with some useless trinket.  I very much preferred the limited open world aspect of the previous games.  Also, some of the bonfires have weird spacing... it's definitely way worse in this than DS3, but it makes the pacing feel weird.

Scarlet rot is the worst, and you can tell they were so proud of it by adding it in a ton of places.  Did we need 2 areas that were like Swamp of Sorrow from Demon's Souls?  No, absolutely not.

Another thing they seem to be proud of is how obscure they can make things... from finding bosses, different areas of the map, etc.  I swear one of the ways to progress something was talking to an NPC 3x, even though they said the same thing all 3x.  Unnecessary and annoying.

Some more minor things like when you're fighting multiple enemies, it's hard to target the ones closer to you, and sometimes the target would just be downright awful.  What other open world games do is give you a journal... this game does not, which is typical FromSoft fashion, but it's honestly kinda annoying.  Like, we get it, you're pretentious.  Cool.  So what is there to like?

Graphically, it's a very lovely game... I do wish there were more colors?  Or less saturation?  I don't know, but it does feel monotone at times.  The performance of it is fantastic.  The infinite stamina when not in a fight is such a good addition.  The movement of the character feels fluid too, and adding something as simple as a jump button makes a pretty big difference.  I have had fun with some of the boss fights, not so much the repeats... I think Margit is way too hard as a 1st real boss.

Finally, as an achievement hunter, I do appreciate that the achievements didn't require the DLC, honestly shocked by that, and could be done in 1 playthrough, as long as you don't miss one of the legendary items, and I think there was something else.  You can save scum after beating Elden Beast and trigger the 3 endings that are needed... don't care, not gonna be playing this game again, maybe ever.

I almost wish they had added Nightreign as an alternate way to play this game... maybe you start as a scrub, and over time, the permanent stat increases help for when you have to start the run over because you died to something... this would make exploring the caves better too because the trinket at the end would be a list of items you could pick from.  Also just increase the movement speed and give you a bird to fly around on for even quicker travel.

This is my first Souls game where I'm honestly perplexed and mixed on it. [i][b]Review EN/RU (Firstly in English / Затем на русском)[/b][/i]
Review first and foremost for those who haven't played Soulslikes before, or who tried them and quit.
If you're a fan of the genre, you don't need this review.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3716232166
I can't say I recommend the game unconditionally, but it does many things very well.
And some things very poorly.
I'll share how I see it, and the decision is yours.
[h2]What I really liked:[/h2]
[list]
[*] [h3]The open world is probably the best I've ever seen.[/h3]
Very beautiful. Diverse. Packed with things to discover.
Every area differs significantly in visuals, enemy types, atmosphere, and overall feel.
Outstanding art direction.

[*] [h3]A huge variety of weapons.[/h3]
Whatever you're looking for, you'll find it.
Awesome unusual models, animation sets, unique and standard weapon skills, enchantments...
I can't think of another game that offers so much for weapon enthusiasts.

[*] [h3]Some bosses are genuinely awesome.[/h3]
Not all of them, and not all the time (more on that later), but there are several truly spectacular encounters.
[/list]
[quote]I should note, however, that some of my favorite weapons and bosses came from the DLC.[/quote]
[list]
[*] [h3]The most accessible FromSoftware Soulslike for newcomers.[/h3]
I'm excluding Sekiro and FromSoftware games from other genres (like Armored Core).
It looks great, runs well, doesn't have too many bugs or technical issues, and includes plenty of quality-of-life features.
And thanks to the open world, if you hit a wall somewhere, you can always go exploring, find better gear, level up, and come back later.
[/list]

[h2]Mixed impressions:[/h2]
[list]
[*] [h3]Reuse of optional bosses and dungeons.[/h3]
This will depend on your personal tolerance and preferences.
For me, the game ended just before it became annoying, but the issue is definitely there.
Many dungeons use the same gimmicks (and visually they're almost identical).
The game contains lots of dragons, tree spirits, and knights — especially if you're clearing everything, you might get annoyed. Many other secondary bosses will also appear more than once.

[*] [h3]Online play and cheaters.[/h3]
I'm speaking from second-hand information here — I know there are currently people who use cheats during invasions to completely ruin someone's playthrough.
Personally, I played offline for most of the game (because of mods — even visual mods will force you to play offline!), and thankfully the game is perfectly playable that way.
[/list]

[h2]What I didn't like:[/h2]
[list]
[*] [h3]Platforming.[/h3]
I died from the game's platforming sections more than from everything else combined.
I'm pretty sure I had at least 200 deaths from falling.

[*] [h3]"Quests."[/h3]
This is a special kind of madness that somehow became a staple of the developers' games.
"My thimby toves..." You know the memes.

[*] [h3]The RPG mechanics.[/h3]
The system is fairly simple and JRPG-like, inheriting one of the genre's worst traits — everything is hidden.
Damage formulas, stat scaling, soft caps, actual talisman values, and so on.
[/list]
[quote]When it comes to quests and mechanics, you'll have to make a choice: either play blind (and definitely miss or misunderstand something), or rely on an external wiki.
Personally, I hate when games fail to properly explain their RPG systems internally, forcing players to research them elsewhere.[/quote]
[list]
[*] [h3]You can't replay bosses through memories.[/h3]
It's not exactly a major downside, but I really liked this feature in Sekiro, and its absence here is disappointing.[/list]

Overall, though, I had a great time.
It took me 170 hours to complete two playthroughs and earn all achievements, and many of my friends became completely obsessed with the game.
The DLC was also a lot of fun, but that's a story for another time.
