Elden Ring — это великая игра, которая споткнулась о собственные амбиции. Попытка Миядзаки натянуть выверенный годами соулс-дизайн на гигантский открытый мир привела к закономерному результату: бескрайние поля оригинальной игры и пустоты DLC утомляют. Повторяющиеся подземелья, одинаковые боссы-камни и тонны бесполезного мусора в качестве награды за исследование (особенно в DLC) бьют по динамике. Спасает ситуацию лишь гениальный, вертикальный левелдизайн ключевых замков, где FromSoftware по-прежнему нет равных.

Системный кризис механики:

Главная объективная проблема Elden Ring — это критический дисбаланс между возможностями игрока и агрессией боссов. Разработчики предоставили колоссальную свободу выбора: сотни видов оружия, щитов и заклинаний. Однако на поздних этапах игры и в DLC вся эта ролевая глубина натыкается на стену: боссы стали настолько быстрыми, а их комбо-атаки — бесконечными, что половина вашего арсенала становится неэффективной.

В итоге игра сама подталкивает к абсурду, превращаясь в соревнование «кто кого сильнее сломает». Чтобы игрок не сошел с ума от духоты, разработчики щедро насыпали в игру легальных способов аннигиляции всего живого. Сборка билдов на кровотечение (Bleed) или обморожение (Frost) позволяет взрывать полоски здоровья боссов за секунды, игнорируя их дикие фазы. Добавьте сюда перекачанные Пеплы Войны вроде «Львиного когтя» или «Богохульного клинка», спам которых превращает грозных полубогов в беспомощных манекенов, и картину закроет прах Ложной Слезы. Использование всего этого «полома» — это не читерство, а объективный ответ игрока на сломанный геймдизайн. Это инструменты, которые FromSoftware сознательно оставили, чтобы компенсировать собственную перекрученную сложность и дать игроку возможность наконец увидеть финальные титры.

Звуковой молот: Музыка войны

Если вы играете в Elden Ring без наушников — вы теряете половину атмосферы. Саундтрек здесь — это не просто фон, это триггер для мурашек. Radagon Theme (она же главная тема игры) — монументальный шедевр, который буквально вколачивает игрока в кресло. А трагичные, величественные мотивы в темах Малении и Ромины идеально подчеркивают их лор и заставляют прочувствовать всю эстетику увядания.

Общий вывод:

Elden Ring со своим дополнением — это монументальный памятник кризису масштаба. Миядзаки доказал, что FromSoftware все еще умеют делать гениальную музыку, потрясающий визуал и образцовых боссов. Но они впервые запутались в собственных размерах. Это великая, изматывающая и глубоко несовершенная игра. Она заслуживает свои 8.5 баллов, но оставляет после себя тревожное послевкусие: студии пора прекращать раздувать масштабы и возвращаться к истокам — к компактному, выверенному до миллиметра геймдизайну.

P.S.Продираясь сквозь пустые поля, сгорая на душных боссах и проклиная геймдизайн Миядзаки, я все же дотащил свой измотанный силовой билд до финала. И знаете что? Когда после всей этой клоунады со щитами, бесконечных смертей и призывов праха ты наконец активируешь концовку Рани и наступает Век Звёзд — ты понимаешь, что всё было не зря. Эта четырехрукая чертовка и ее холодный космический финал — лучшая награда за сотню часов ментального насилия. Мы уходим в темноту, но уходим красиво.

This game is nothing but hard. Yes that's a skill issue, HOWEVER that's not the complaint. A stupidly hard game can be fun. Elden Ring is not.

The Story it has is so scarce, you have to actively look for every last scrap of it to get SOME idea of what's happening in the world. Except for some random dialogue with NPCs and a cutscene every 15k deaths there is simply nothing. And the bits you get are more confusing and vague than your average politicians speech. Even if you like vague storytelling, it doesn't change the fact that it's told in a really boring way. Cutscenes made from a few still images with voiceover, clicking a button at a specific site of grace for 2 minutes of Monologue (and yes it's ALWAYS Monologue, because the MC has either pulled the Kimiko move or forgotten how to talk, leaving you with only an occasional grunt or scream of pain).

So yeah, the story sucks, the storytelling sucks as well. Lets move on to the world you move around in.
It feels empty and dead even though there are enemies everywhere. These enemies however are completely silent, stand around until they die of dehydration or walk their set path. Over and over and over... Which wouldn't be so bad if there were other things that made the world interesting. So let's see... There are a few NPCs, that are ALL COMPLETELY stationary (unless you try to kill them, then they remember they have arms and legs) and remain - just like the enemies - completely silent. They don't react to you, they don't talk to you unless you talk to them first and when they talk, they all sound the same. Boring monotone voices, that make listening to these NPCs more of a chore than an enjoyable part of the game.

With a boring story, a dead world and badly designed interactions there is progression.
You basically follow the "guidance of grace", which is just a beam of light pointing towards the next lost grace. You can do some side bosses, which mostly awards you with mid items. You can also do quests. Which brings me to the part i hate most about Elden Ring
There is NO WAY to keep track of progression. There is NOTHING that help you find your next point of interest. If you get a "quest" from an NPC, you gotta do some sometimes really complicated stuff (or find some item in some cave after killing some random boss) which is explained so vaguely or not at all by whoever you talk to, that even on your first playthrough you kind of NEED guides to help you understand what you gotta do. And if you take a longer break from the game GOOD LUCK finding out what quest you were on, what you had to do next and so on. The game provides ZERO Info which makes progression a tedious act of walking and scouring every part of the map just so you could complete one assignment. And after you do that you don't get your reward, because the NPC has moved to a completely arbitrary spot on the Map, which means you gotta go look for them. Again. No indicators, no Info on anything. I'm not asking for a Quest Marker that tells you where to go at all times, but at least SOME Info would be nice. I wanna do my quest, win hard fights against many enemies or a strong boss, not backtrack to every part of the map looking for a chest i might have missed or an NPC that moved. I also don't wanna play a game that needs guides for every Interaction you have. I wanna figure stuff out myself, but doing so shouldn't involve 16 hours of walking around playing hide and seek.

Last thing I wanna mention is the Co-op. Calling it that is kind of an Insult to every other Co-op system out there. The so called "Co-op" let's you call your buddy into your world, where you fight together, get invaded constantly. You can't turn these Invasions off. Sometimes you get lucky and your invaders aren't too strong. But usually you get hardsweats, that kill you and you friend in a few hits so you gotta re-summon them. Your buddy is extremely weakened while fighting alongside you, and if they die, they return to their own world, meaning you gotta call them again. If you beat a boss, they auto-leave, so you gotta call them again. There is no cross progression, meaning if you beat the boss in your own world, you gotta do the same ♥♥♥♥ in your buddies world. I genuinely only enjoy this game when I'm playing with friends, which needs a mod, because the base-game Co-op is a mix of bad ideas and worse concepts.

TLDR - Game is really hard but even more so really dull and stupidly annoying

Second, the camera settings being set to auto-follow (ESPECIALLY on Torrent) can cause motion sickness, so I would recommend turning those settings off if you are prone to motion sickness in video games. 

However, despite these two critiques the gameplay and feelings of satisfaction after defeating bosses feels really good. 

Last statement: This game is nothing like the Dark Souls trilogy and should be treated as a separate entity from prior FromSoftware games. Personally, I prefer the Dark Souls games, but I can respect Elden Ring for what it is.

Elden Ring took everything that made Dark Souls great, dialled it up a bunch of notches, and set you loose in an open world.

I wasn't initially sold on the idea of an Open world souls game, but I can honestly say that I think it was a fantastic move to make the genre accessible to new players. Far more so than in the souls series, if you hit a wall you can often pick another direction very easily, find new dungeons or encounters, and hunt for loot and runes without specifically banging your head against a wall. Pair this with the spirit ashes allowing summons in almost every boss fight that you can level with you, and this is a great starting point for newcomers to the genre.

If you're a veteran, the game has you covered too, since there's no NEED to engage with summons if you don't want to. The fights escalate a lot as the game goes on, and really make you feel rewarded for learning the dances in a way I feel is only beaten by Sekiro in the Genre.

There is beautiful visuals, fun gameplay and fighting mechanics, almost something to do in every corner of the map and most of the bosses are a lot of fun, imo. The world itself is also enjoyable to explore because there is stuff to find almost anywhere like castles, forts, caves, catacombs, npcs and bosses. Experimenting with different weapons and builds is enjoyable. The soundtrack is amazing, so good that I sometimes listen to it outside of the game. There are a few tedious parts but the rest of the game makes up for it. There's also repeat bosses so just a heads up if that bothers you. And as I said before, this is a really challenging game, especially for beginners, like my self when I bought it, so if you don't want to fight tense, hard bosses, then this probably isn't for you. It took me a lot of tries to beat the hardest boss in the game, and that was with a summon. I would be lying if I said I didn't get a bit frustrated with this game a few times lol. And this isn't a review on the dlc but I would like to say that it's also great and if you enjoyed the base game, you'll love shadow of the erdtree. It's basically elden ring 2 full of new stuff to find and new bosses to fight. It also adds a lot to the story. So if any of this sounds appealing to you, then I recommend checking this game out for yourself, this review doesn't do it justice.

Elden Ring is a breathtaking action RPG developed by FromSoftware and directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, with worldbuilding contributions from George R. R. Martin. The game takes the classic Souls formula and expands it into a massive open world filled with mystery, danger, and discovery.

Set in the Lands Between, players explore a dark fantasy universe packed with hidden dungeons, terrifying enemies, and unforgettable bosses. What makes the game special is the incredible freedom it offers. Instead of forcing players down a single path, the world encourages exploration and rewards curiosity. Every area feels unique and full of secrets waiting to be uncovered.

The combat is one of the game’s strongest aspects. Battles are challenging but fair, requiring patience, timing, and strategy. The huge variety of weapons, spells, and builds allows players to create their own playstyle, whether they prefer fast melee combat, heavy weapons, or powerful magic attacks.

Visually, the game is stunning. From ruined castles to golden forests and underground cities, every environment feels artistic and immersive. The soundtrack and sound design also enhance the epic atmosphere, especially during boss fights that feel both intense and cinematic.

However, the game is not perfect. Some players may find the difficulty frustrating, and certain late-game areas can feel repetitive or unbalanced. The story is also told in a very cryptic way, which may confuse newcomers unfamiliar with FromSoftware’s style.

Despite these flaws, Elden Ring is a masterpiece of modern gaming. It successfully combines exploration, combat, and atmosphere into an unforgettable experience that sets a new standard for open-world RPGs.

After spending a massive amount of time in the Lands Between, I can easily say this is one of the best gaming experiences I have had, especially with friends. 

The Good: 
Fantastic Co-op: Playing this game with a friend completely changes the dynamic. Taking down massive, punishing bosses together makes the victories feel twice as rewarding.
Build Variety: You can play exactly how you want. Magic, massive swords, spears, axes, and katanas—now even with exploding perfume bottles—everything feels viable and fun.
Incredible Atmosphere: The world design, art style, and boss encounters are top-tier. You get legendary moments like a boss shouting "Bear witness!", a literal wrestler who suplexes you mid-fight, an infamous swordswoman everyone already knows, and a brutal DLC final boss dropping literal flashbang orbital lasers on your head.
God-Tier Voice Acting: The voice acting is stellar across the board. There is one specific companion NPC whose absolute rage and jaw-droppingly intense performance during a major dragon fight sticks with you long after the battle ends.

My Personal Critique: If I have one minor issue, it is the open world. It isn't that I dislike open-world games in general—some games suit it and some don't. However, for this series, I prefer the more traditional, linear style of previous titles. To be specific, I really like the freedom to "go in any direction" found in games like Dark Souls 1, but Elden Ring's massive open scale felt a bit much for my taste. 

Conclusion: There isn't a game out there that doesn't have some minor flaws, but despite my preference for the older style, I still thoroughly enjoyed my time. Whether you play it solo or dive in with a friend, it is highly recommended.

Elden Ring has a reputation for being hard, which is honestly confusing, because the bosses are unbelievably easy.

Every boss fight is basically a friendly conversation where the boss lets you take the first swing, the second swing, and then immediately reminds you that you are nothing. Attacks are super readable, especially the ones that come from off-screen, behind you, and directly through your hopes and dreams. Healing is generous too—the boss always waits until you’re at full vulnerability before launching a perfectly timed combo.

The difficulty curve is incredibly smooth. You start weak, get stronger, and the bosses scale accordingly by learning new ways to invent violence. Sometimes they even add phase two, which is very thoughtful because it gives you more time to reflect on the mistake of buying the game.

I especially appreciate how fair everything feels. If you die, it’s clearly your fault for blinking, breathing, or thinking you had an opening. The game teaches patience by making you watch the same death animation over and over until you achieve enlightenment or uninstall.

Overall, Elden Ring is a relaxing, beginner-friendly experience where bosses gently guide you toward humility, anger management issues, and the realization that you were never as good at games as you thought. 10/10, easiest game I’ve ever played.

First of all: I bought ELDEN RING expecting another great Dark Souls-title or successor. I was disappointed. That is not to say ELDEN RING is an objectively bad game - it just didn't click for me, coming from the Dark Souls-series.

It really pains me to give a thumbs down for ELDEN RING. I really wanted to like this game, so at first I tried it alone, but found myself aimlessly wandering around, wondering: "Where do I go?" - "What do I do?" - "Why is what and where is who?" and so on.

Then I played together with my girlfriend so we could at least experience the chaos and wonder together... But I was constantly checking the wiki, looking at game-progression-routes, stumbled into dead-ends. That took the fun away quick - having a to look at another screen, just to find out, you've skipped or passed an important part of the map or must do this and that before doing that and this.

Where Dark Souls succeeded in taking me into its world by doing exactly that - developing lore by showing, not telling - ELDEN RING just falls short for me with its ambitious, yet chaotic and not well thought-out attempt to lead and pace you.

Where Dark Souls left you wondering, who the NPCs were, but still had a game-route for you, that you could follow even withput completing any NPC-quests - ELDEN RING throws you into this world, gives you NPCs, that are cryptic as always, which is fine for Dark Souls, but are your (only) way to get information where to go and what to do.

Where Dark Souls paced you by offering you 2, 3 or maybe even 4 paths, that you could, based on skill/items/knowledge/... , take - ELDEN RING just throws this massive open world at you, that you can wander around.

Where Dark Souls Bosses were built up, felt unique and rewarding to beat, so you could continue the path - ELDEN RING Bosses were sometimes like "Oh... Apparently I'm in a Boss-Fight now...". Some Bosses seemed all too similar and I had the feeling they locked onto you, no matter their orientation and it was all just a "Dodge at the perfect time, then attack - rinse and repeat"-game. Which Dark Souls kinda is, but it just felt too repetitive and non-rewarding.

Where Dark Souls gave you weapons, armor, spells and many more items to explore and try out - ELDEN RING gave us 3 maybe 4 armors after hours and hours of playing.

For some this "open-world Breath of the WIld-inspired hype-train" might be something to enjoy - For me it was (just as Zelda) trying to be too much: An RPG, an Open-World-Game, a Dark-Souls-Game and so much more. But in trying to be everything (or at least more than before) it fell short and became nothing for me.

My only real qualm is that most of the things you find under those rocks aren't terribly interesting, or even all that useful. Some of those rocks are quite heavy, too. So, you just don't turn over the boring rocks, right? Unfortunately, these functionally useless rocks make exploring a significant portion of the vast, wonderful world that is The Lands Between a chore and waste of time in service of the important rocks, which makes a lot of your later runs feel very scripted. This can get pretty boring if you don't enjoy challenge runs or exploring different weapon classes. Also, some of the bosses are just so. so terrible. really poorly done. Few of them are mandatory, but many of them gate content much more engaging than themselves.

I consider Elden Ring a must play, just like pretty much every game in the modern FromSoft oeuvre. Peak of peak, buy this game and play it. If they did that "ultimate game of all time" thing that Dark Souls won a few years ago today, I can't think of a game better suited for the title.

This is the long awaited spiritual successor to the Dark Souls series, maintaining many mechanics like the equipment and communication interfaces. Players of these games should find themselves right at home, though new players will find it a little more intuitive. However, at least for me, this game was much harder than From's previous third person RPGs. The scenery is beautiful, the areas are wide open, and the thematic elements are masterfully done.

However, as a long time fan of their work, I do have a few complaints. 
*The game world, while very detailed, is still ultimately semi-linear. Each area is very wide, but eventually to progress you'll need to invade a castle and kill a boss. It can feel empty in some areas, and many dungeons aren't as uniquely crafted as well as they once all were. This can make the game feel repetitive in certain ways.
*The difficulty feels kinda all over the place. I'm not against having strong enemies you encounter early or a surprise increase in difficulty, but many bosses can feel like a brick wall that the previous fights haven't prepared you for. I feel like the difficulty curve in previous games was far more reasonable.

In short, it lacks focus. This can be a good thing in many ways, if you're getting frustrated there's many other things you can do to pass the time productively. There's many good options for making a unique character, and the main dungeons and scenarios are well crafted. However, at times you may feel lost or discouraged. I think everyone should at least try this game, though I think relatively few of them will manage to finish it. You should be able to find a playstyle that works for you like many other RPGs, but it's unlikely you'll find the perfect build that makes you feel omnipotent.

My main build uses an enormous brick-on-a-stick that I bless with incantations that I flail with disturbing speed, a basic shield, the occasional bolt of lightning, and a holy bow with holy arrows. With my blue cloak and many bottles of varied liquid protecting me, my confessor spreads his word. 

Even shorter, I can't recommend it enough!

Elden Ring is a generation-defining masterpiece that successfully translates the punishing, rewarding DNA of Dark Souls into a breathtaking, seamless open world. It offers unparalleled exploration, deep lore, and unmatched build variety, though its extreme difficulty and lack of hand-holding require immense patience.The World & ExplorationThe Lands Between: The world is an absolute triumph of design. Every time you look at the horizon and think, “I can go there,” you actually can.Zero Hand-Holding: There is no traditional quest log or waypoint system. You learn the story by talking to NPCs, reading item descriptions, and getting lost.Environmental Storytelling: From the golden, majestic capital of Leyndell to the rot-infested, nightmarish plains of Caelid, the art direction is astonishing.Combat & GameplayMasterful Mechanics: The combat feels incredibly weighty and responsive. The addition of guard counters and jump attacks opens up new offensive and defensive strategies.Unforgiving but Fair: You will die—a lot. However, if you get stuck on a difficult boss, the open-world nature allows you to simply ride away, explore elsewhere, and come back when you are stronger.Build Variety: Whether you want to wield a massive greatsword, cast glintstone sorceries, or summon spirit ashes to fight alongside you, the game accommodates almost any playstyle.The Flaws (Because nothing is perfect)Obscure Quests: Sidequests can be incredibly frustrating to track without a guide, as NPCs move around the massive map with little to no clues.Balance & Pacing: Some late-game bosses can feel cheap or overtuned, and the repetition of mini-bosses in optional dungeons can wear on you after 70+ hours.No Pause Button: If you need to step away in the middle of a dungeon, tough luck!The Verdict: Elden Ring completely revitalized the action-RPG genre. Reviewing Elden Ring is tricky. Objectively, it’s probably the pinnacle of the genre. Performance-wise, it ran great with my current build.

However, it didn't hit the same high notes for me as Dark Souls 3. I realized during my playthrough that I just don't love open-world games. While the freedom is impressive, I missed the dense, interconnected, and deliberate pacing of DS3's legacy dungeons. It's a fantastic game, but the shift to an open world means it won't be for every traditional Souls fan. Definitely recommended, but linear Souls still wins out for me.

This game is not for those who hate losing. It's for those who take every death as an opportunity to learn, and grow.
Because you will die.
A LOT.
For this is a souls-like, and dying is part of the experience. There's no point in complaining about how hard the game is, when that is what you signed up for. So do not buy this, if you don't like the idea of dying so much, the sound (dunnnn...) replays in your head when you sleep. But this is an amazing game. The characters are well fleshed out, with questlines that tie in well to the lore, and don't feel like pointless side quests. The music always fits the atmosphere, and almost every moment in the game is screenshot worthy, with stunning landscapes that I find almost always integrate well into the gameplay, art that fits the mood of a souls-like well, and models that that look well when you swing it at a giant more detailed than my facial structure. There's also the freedom with weapons that some games do not give you, with many different staffs, katanas, and hammers that keep the game feeling unique, and differentiate every playthrough. They are all (mostly) well balanced as well, so that you don't feel as if you are choosing to lose with choosing different builds. But sometimes, the level progression can feel a little bit slow, but it is for the best, so as you don't over-level, which takes the fun out of the bosses. Oh yeah, the bosses. All previously mentioned pale in comparison to the bosses and combat which this game truly excels at. These bosses will not feel like a challenge of who has more firepower, but will feel like a dance, every dodge and attack feeling fluid, and learnt, requiring discipline and (previously mentioned) dying. So unlike other games where beating a boss simply means getting good enough gear, for Elden Ring this is not enough, and you will need to beat these bosses with sheer skill. But obviously, levelling helps too. But something I do have to say, is that the weapon levelling system does sometimes feel a little bit trapping, as sometimes you feel forced to only use and upgrade one weapon, because it is the strongest you have, leading to less freedom, which is a shame for all of the previously mentioned weapon choices there are available.
So, finally, time for the scales.
Art: 8/10. Not outstanding, but definitely great.
Music: 8/10. Again, great, but not why it shines as a game.
Performance: 7/10. Chugs sometimes, but works fine.
Gambling (Y/N): N. No luck involved whatsoever. 
Gameplay: 10/10. Definitely the best bosses i have beaten in my life
Difficulty: 9/10. Other Souls-like games are harder, but this is a behemoth of a game to conquer.
Progression: 9/10. The growth throughout the entire game feels amazing, but there is the slight levelling and weapon levelling problem previously mentioned.
Overall: 10/10. Genuinely one of, if not the best game I have ever played, but not for those who don't like losing. Why are you still waiting. Buy Elden Ring now.

I have played through 3 playthroughs of this game on seamless co-op and started a single player run of this game where at time of writing this I have reached the altus plateau; just to set the scene. This game has one of the best combat systems of any game I've ever played with lots of different types of damage and with every enemy having different resistances which follows set patterns with who they are. There are many many weapons and different magic systems and each boss has unique move-sets and is really challenging. This game also does not shy away on looks or music either both being really good in certain parts. 

So why is this a negative review you may be asking. It is not the "skill issue" that people often quote when players are struggling with the game. As I see it if you like to grind away memorizing every possible attack and corresponding dodge timing and direction that is fine by me and obviously a lot of people are as 10% of you have completed all achievements in this game which means getting the three main ending therefore completing the game a minimum of three times. 

Really my gripe with Elden ring is motive and its endings. In Elden ring you are a tarnished a undead and are hated my many and I do mean many, everywhere you go enemies will flock towards you like moths to a lighthouse and try to kill you. Furthermore, you are expected to kill many bosses with little to no reason other than to get Melina to the Erdtree. Once this is done you continue on with the game ultimately killing more enemies and bosses until finally reaching one of the six endings to the game. 

The thought that often fills my head with the Elden ring endings is that you sit upon a throne of the corpses from a kingdom which you have slain. Each ending often finds you picking between the least worst and all have drawbacks and a range of people arguing which is the quote on quote "best ending". One of my friends thinks the "frenzied flame" ending is best whereas I know several other people online argue that the "age of order" ending is best. There is no right answer and all could be interpreted as incredibly bad from certain point of views. This wouldn't necessarily be a problem if the game was easy but and I pray most of  you can agree with me on this that, at least when you start out, it isn't. 

The great combat I was talking about early is good if you know how it works and what bosses are resistant to and are able to do simple math by looking at your weapons statistics and are good at getting runes and upgrade materials for your character and knowing what to prioritise. This often involves looking at a wiki page which can also be very easy to get side tracked on given how large the game is. While this may not even still matter if you need to get a certain item in a late game area not realising that said late game area needs you to fight another boss to get there. 

This overly complex system is very good for people who get into it but can be quite overwhelming for newer players which will just usually result to the default, fight boss, learn move set, die, repeat until boss is dead. This can make Elden ring and other souls-like and souls game along with it, feel in my opinion at least more like a chore or job than a fun experience also know as a game. However, if you are under the status of unemployed and/or have too much free time then this could be a good game for if that is you just like to play it for the sake of it given my previous comment on how the ending motivation is practically zero. 

Also the game's fundamental story is huge but it is more or less a modern more realistic fantasy re-take of a Shakespeare tragedy and I do NOT like both Shakespeare and this game's story. It is not pleasant to listen to and reflects this game's apocalyptic, sad, depressed, undead state throughout all NPC quest lines which almost always result in them dying at the end by some sad unfortunate means, if not you killing their family or friends is the other common thing.  

Elden ring does have Co-op but I wouldn't even try it because it allows players to "invade" you which means another real life player will come to try and kill you and upon kill the host all co-op players will be banished from your world. However, a mod on nexus mods called "seamless co-op" removes this issue and also allows for removing of invaders and curses allowing for a true co-op experience. However the game still fundamentally hasn't changed and the amount of health each boss has scales with the amount of players. 

I have enjoyed some of the moments from my seamless co-op playthroughs with my friends but even then I shouldn't be having to recommend that you install a mod to make a already ambiguous game in my eyes more bearable. 4/10

Elden Ring has great world, exploration, sound design, item filling - and if this is only thing you care about, you will find it relatively good, but bosses and combat are worse than even in Lords of the Fallen. Unfortunately, studio moved combat design from ds3 into "elden ring" direction instead of fully adopting Sekiro combat and philosophy. This is not "get good" game, like previous souls or Sekiro, or good "soulslike" action games, but "learn all the timings perfectly and buff properly" game.
Years ago I fully completed this game with the sorcerer/summonner build, I was enjoying it, azuring and rocking all the bosses through the way, then figured out about souls-likes, really liked concept, completed many of them (including whole dark souls series) with great enjoyment and now I returned here to complete game properly (no summon, no chease). I would better not. Maybe games with top-notch combat, like Nioh, Sekiro, NG, and  Khazan influenced me too much - but Elden Ring combat for me is now absolutely unbearable slow-mo and not because of the slow animations. Most bosses, and all in the end game are glued of delayed attacks, delayed followups, delayed aoe attacks and delayed aoe followup attacks - and all this goes in relentless spamming sequences. Timings are carefully crafted so, that you often cannot heal in "attack" window and one mistimed roll leads to eating all the combo (almost all attacks stagger character). Tens years old bug with delayed roll input is still there (and it is not just "it works on key release" - character starts to roll when finger is already far from button). Bosses do not respect spacing and have input reading to instantly reach you regardless of the actual distance. Basic fight (using only r1, l1, r2 and roll) here feels like moving through jelly filled space and is totally not enjoyable and boring. Godskin duo, Maliketh, gideon, Godfrey second phase, Radagon and elden beast are easily worst from bosses, worse than bed of chaos and most of ds2 bosses. No emotions after most bosses beating ("right way") at all - neither satisfaction nor even relief - maybe, only regret for time I lost doing it. Through every boss could be seen an intention to somehow make things harder, but the only hard thing in the end is delays - atrocious and unnatural. Good designed bosses are few - Godrick, Rhadan, and first encountered tree sentinel.

And few words about Malenia - if you ever see such poorly made enemy in other random souls-like - you will name it garbage, but it is boss in Elden Ring - so everybody is in queue to praise it. 180 degree tracking, baseless rotation in air, input reading, multitude of "jump from hanging in air" moves, random absolute armor (hit connects, but no damage is made), strange hitboxes (ones where you getting hit - are bigger than should be, but when you hit - you can miss her because weapon hit exact space between body and arm), multitude of instant reach moves which look especially idiotic when full attack with close up happens in half of time you need to drink estus - this one fight actually shows where limits of animation locked combat are. But all this is manageable, it is common set of low-key moves in modern games, and understandable why it is here - anybody will make such boss when refusing evolution and stuck in aged approach to combat. What actually makes it unfair trash - one-shot combo you cannot dodge from if distance from her and position on arena is unlucky wrong. And her baiting for you to close up when she does nothing for minutes, but should you close up enough to have it not dodgeable - combo will follow - is some huge level of trolling. We did it, because we can, eat this. I might be wrong, and there is a way to roll it from any position but there is no way to learn it by own experience. Imbuing it by rot in the second phase and hiding attacks behind visual noise does not help to make it better either. (second phase adds also another moves with similar properties - you cannot avoid it if she decides to execute it right over your head) So you have long fight glued of low-key design elements, generic, boring, and non-respecting what you learned. You reach point where first phase is finished no-hit or 1-2 hit only, but then random dance at the moment you have no room to avoid id - and welcome re-spawn. This is absolute disrespect to players from developers in kind of game where you are supposed ideally to correct each mistake after falling for move once at most.

With all honesty, It is a step back from the souls formula, from my perspective and way of playing.

To me this, and other Dark Souls, are RPGs and I will always abuse on my own way and gameplay style the mechanics and possibilities I am offered.

In the Dark Souls, I feel encouraged to and gladly explore the map and spaces, even look for secrets, but Elden Ring's map to me feels like a massive, extremely big "To do" list, and that discourages me.

I don't like having access to the full world at start, I do not enjoy having access to whatever item I want to use from the start because that makes me want to spend whatever amount of time I need to spend to get the item I want to use and when I get the item I am burned out and just don't want to even play anymore.

I don't know when we turned from having a good experience in a videogame to having a long one, I feel that is not the way.

Be ready to kill 10 times the same boss, because actually developing a game with different 3D models for each boss/enemy takes time and money they decided not to spend. But hey, if it is Hidetaka Miyazaki reusing content we forgive him, right guys? and only him.

I enjoyed the designs, Items, bosses, but they are not better than the soul's. 

How it feels generally, the jump adition, it is dark souls 3 on steroids. Riding around feels nice but I got over it quickly, to the point I wish to get places quickly so I can unmount and actually play the game.

The amount of extra stuff I will never use, which is not neccesarily bad but it is also the same thing about feeling like I should use such things but I don't feel like putting the time into it. Flask of Wondrous Physick for example, or 99% of the ashes of war.

Some of the songs in the soundtrack are extremely good, others I feel like I heard them repeatedly.

Finally, the Yggdrasil style story is too common in media even if it has not much to do with the game's actuall story, but the Erdtree do have a great impact upon what the story is build on. I would take any of the soul's story over this one.

Honestly, I enjoyed the Dark Souls saga so much, I don't feel this game does any good to it, it feels more like a "Nintendo" take on the souls genre.

I write this review fully knowing this game is what most fans, and most non-fans of the souls wanted, but the game is just not for me, and I can't recommend it to my past self, in fact, I would be desapointed to know this is what Elden Ring came out to be. This was for FromSoftware the "big hit", and they developed it with that in mind.

Unlike previous souls games, the huge open world and new mechanics make it much more beginner friendly without compromising the overall progression experience.

The graphics, controls, animations, landscapes, music, voice acting, atmospheric storytelling, platforming, Torrent mount, plus the wide selection of weapons and armor and spells and skills and items, add up to something that is even greater than the sum of its parts. The way the map expands and new builds you can try as you play through the story honestly blows my mind. Even if you miss all the optional quest and secrets, it's just huge. The gameplay can be challenging but it almost always feels fair and keeps you coming back for more.

The most glaring flaws in my opinion are: (1) It's impossible to understand or finish half the quests without referring to internet guides (2) I attempted to play co-op with my friend, and we tried all the summoning statues and fingers but it never let us summon each other. And even if that worked seamlessly, the way this game handles summons in such limited areas is subpar.
But those concerns are not overly detrimental to the overall enjoyment, because the game is that good. And depending on your platform, there are useful fun mods to try.

[b]Games fun, [i]very casual (non-derogatory)[/i] souls game, open world feels like an afterthought; lots of really generic catacombs, caves and mines that makes Oblivion dungeons feel fun to explore.[/b]

   [b]Few gripes[/b]
[list]
[*] Bosses aside from the main ones are just regular enemies but large and there's a lot of repeats.
[*] Most enemy types will already be encountered before you beat your second main boss.
[*] Boring exploration, as stated before all the dungeons are very dull and primitive, you'll get one or two items out of them, sometimes it'll be good.
[*] Game heavily focuses on using the horse for things but it cannot be upgraded at all, not even cosmetics.
[*] Souls NPC Questlines, if you know you know, now add an entire open-world of sequence skipping on accident.
[*] Crafting mechanics.
[/list]
   [b]Couple Positives[/b]
[list]
[*] Co-op is massively streamlined, you get the ability to touch statues to make it yourself available to be summoned to that location remotely, not only that it adds it to a pool of potential places to be summoned, insane upgrade from having one static summon sign, wish you could use both at the same time though.
[*] Posture from Sekiro, practically all enemies can be staggered from beating the living hell out of them, leaving them exposed to critical finishers.
[*] Heavy attacks matters, in the old games heavy attacks were usually a waste of time since light attacks would out-dps them and leave you a lot less vulnerable, in this, heavy attacks on most enemies will knock'em out of animations so you can pulverize them (can be a negative since it can easily be abused)
[*] Sorceries look a lot cooler, that's pretty all there is to say, they still boil down to press the win button from across the map but they look really rad.
[*] Miracles got a glow up, lots more offensive and cool abilities for priest players
[*] Prop hunt is a re-usable item
[*] Invasions are locked behind co-op, you will never be invaded by a real player unless you're playing co-op. making invading a lot more intense since it'll always be a 1vs2 situation at least (can be a negative especially since the rewards is not all that great at times and the invasion items sparing until you get your hands on the re-usable one)
[*] Crafting mechanics.
[/list]

Elden Ring is one of those games that feels more like an experience than just a video game you would play for leisure. The world is MASSIVE and there's so much content packed into this game that never feels like filler or is just there to add play time. There are so many unique weapons, and spells, and enemies, and bosses, etc that makes you constantly question just how much **** is in this game. Combining this with the incredible worldbuilding, from the creative level design of all the unique locations in the game to the intricate lore that gets woven into every aspect of the game, creates a truly immersive experience for the player. As you journey through The Lands Between it never feels as if you are just exploring some generic fantasy setting, but a world with deep history and life that is very detailed such that it doesn't leave the impression of being artificial. On top of it all the game is stunning and incredibly cinematic. 

Although Elden Ring can be very brutal and punishing, the difficulty has never felt unfair due to the freedom given to the player. If an area or boss seems too challenging at the moment, the open world allows you to just go elsewhere and come back later with better gear or at a higher level. However it doesn't take away from the challenge of the game and some bosses are just hard and you just have to git gud. Despite that, the satisfaction and sense of euphoria you get from finally beating a boss after hours of attempts, creates such a strong high that you end up forgetting all the suffering you went through.

Elden Ring ruined open world games for me. Every time I thought I had seen everything, the game casually revealed an entire underground civilization, a hidden legacy dungeon, or some horrifying creature waiting to humble me in 0.3 seconds.

The combat is brutal but fair (except the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cat statues in catacombs, those things can go to hell). Exploration feels genuinely rewarding because the game trusts you to figure things out yourself instead of turning everything into checklist content.
One minute you’re feeling like a god after beating a boss first try, the next you lose 60k runes because you got greedy against a giant murder cat. Peak gaming.
What I love most about this game is the atmosphere. Everything feels ancient, tragic, mysterious, and deeply intentional. Half the time I feel like I’m wandering through the remains of a dead myth. The world feels lonely in the best way possible — like every castle, ruin, and frozen mountaintop has history buried inside it. Even random NPC interactions feel weirdly profound or unsettling.

The enemy and environment design is insane. I’ll walk into an area and just stop moving because I’m too busy staring at the scenery or some horrifying monstrosity looming in the distance. Then five seconds later I’m getting violently flattened because I forgot the game punishes awe.
I also genuinely love that the game doesn’t hold your hand. It lets you be curious. It rewards exploration, experimentation, and even failure. Some of my favorite moments have been completely accidental — finding hidden elevators, getting teleported somewhere terrifying way too early, discovering entire areas underground that made my jaw drop, or randomly stumbling into bosses I absolutely had no business fighting yet.
And weirdly enough, the difficulty makes the victories feel emotional. When you finally beat a boss that’s been destroying you for an hour, it feels euphoric. The game constantly pushes you into this cycle of “I’m a god” immediately followed by “I am the weakest creature alive.” It’s addicting.

I can’t recall when, but I’ve always seen people play Souls-like/FromSoft games. I thought they looked aesthetically cool, but I was never interested in playing them as they looked boring, old, and other than the stiff-looking controls, how could they possibly be challenging? Outside of Sekiro, until playing Elden Ring, Bloodborne would be my first and last introduction to the series (that game made me rage, lol). Yet, outside of GTA 5, Persona 5, RDR2, and Minecraft, Elden Ring is the only single-player game I have more than 500 hours on that's actually tracked. 

I was introduced to Elden Ring by some YouTubers I watched at the time, who got to play the beta. The game would eventually launch in early 2022, garnering a lot of success, but I was still put off on buying it, as I had no real reason to. I’d eventually pick up the game later that summer after going on an insane gaming rotation with the boys. I had already completed it, but we were supposed to play RDR2 to see who could complete the game the fastest. Unfortunately, these guys bailed and started messing around in RDR Online. My friends, Kyron and Lucas, got bored with the story and wanted a new game. Kyron recommended Elden Ring, which shocked me because a game like that is out of his gaming vocabulary. Kyron bought the game and gameshared Lucas, and I would ask my sister for $90 and bought the game (still haven't paid her back, smh). All I gotta say is you just had to be there. I started off pretty slow, being behind everyone until I killed that giant white dragon, gaining a bunch of runes. I was now the strongest, and everyone wanted to know the method. I had to guide them and lost a lot of progress in the process. One by one, people got the game, and again, I had to help them with the dragon method. My friend Daniel would eventually give up on the game, as games like Elden Ring were too sophisticated for a “ball and gun gamer” such as himself. In the end, there were only two true new players who joined the squad: My brother and Kyron's girlfriend's (Stussy) little brother, Ahmed. I game-shared them both the PS5 and PS4 versions, with the rest of the GC begging for game shares or for us to buy them the game.

Like I said before, you just had to be there. We all stayed up fighting bosses and helped each other via “share play” or summoned each other to help with bosses (I really hated how co-op was implemented in this game). We also all have extremely different play styles, with my favourite being Ahmed's. He used the Vagabond build, and despite taking the longest and struggling the most as he didn't have alot of spells and magic, his boss fights were by far the most entertaining outside of myself, of course. My brother and Lucas turned into complete fiends, with Lucas gatekeeping methods being ahead early on. Then, my brother out doing him, making an insane magic/spellcasting build (and of course, gatekeeping as well). I swear, those last 3 to 2 weeks of August and September were therapy. We were also public enemy number one, as most of us refused to play other games with the rest of GC. People in the GC would beg us to hop on Siege, and we just refused. Sometimes we would join to make teams even, but for the most part, we didn’t join. It was also hilarious because it felt like that Family Guy “You Guys Always Act Like You're Better Than Me” meme (and we were)...

Most of us stopped playing as it was now September, with some of us focusing on school and others focusing on NBA 2K (I swear that game is a cult). Over and over again, I would struggle to kill Malenia and my brother with Radagon. Getting the game using FitGirl (IYKYK), my brother and I beat the game when everyone moved over to PC in 2023 (because of it, by the way :). After beating it, I would try a lot of Souls-like games, like Bloodborne, Demon's Souls, and Dark Souls, which I'm currently playing. My brother would try non-FromSoftware Souls-likes like Lies of P, Shadow of the Colossus, Lords of the Fallen, and Mortal Shell. None of FromSoftware's games aside, you really start to see what walked so Elden Ring could run. Elden takes a lot of elements from its predecessors and improves on them. It’s basically a love letter to FromSoft's past games. The game doesn’t hold your hand, and neither does the story and its rich lore. A lot of people have it at number one or in their top 5; I personally don't have it there, but it’s definitely close. It was annoying and tedious since you can't have multiple saves, but I would finally platinum the game on PlayStation 5 after 3 years and 2 months. Oh, and despite being playable, I refuse to play it on the Steam Deck. I officially bought it on Steam for that reason and regret it. I genuinely question people who complete games like that on that device and have a great time. I hate replaying or rewatching media, but I plan to play it again on a more powerful handheld, most likely the Asus Rog Flow Z13, since this game is very poorly optimized.

[b] (Cue the Vince McMahon crying meme): [/b] Since the move to PC, 5 people have been introduced to the game, but they just can't hang with the OGs! Like I said before, YOU JUST HAD TO BE THERE! Looking back, it’s wild to think I almost skipped this game entirely because I thought the genre looked old and boring (thank you, Kyron, I guess). Again, it might be terribly optimized and out of my top 5, but Elden Ring gave me an unforgettable experience. Whether it was helping each other, discovering new places or items, gatekeeping, or laughing at each other, gaming with the boys that summer was therapy. Also, shoutout to Daniel and Lucas for being terrible cheaters, and Jorden for spelling cookie with a "K" during trivia while we were farming (I couldn't stop laughing). I’m not dissing your intelligence, but that slip-up is a core memory tied to this game. And a big thanks to FromSoftware and Miyazaki, I can't wait for what you have in store next.

The best way I can describe this game is it is a bad GREAT game. There is no doubt that the game is great, however as far as great games go, I think this one is bad at it.

Starting with the negatives, the main one for me is just boss repeats. I don't want to fight 3 Margit's or 5 Demi-Human's or whatever. So there are somewhere around 200 bosses I think? But maybe only about 50 of them are unique? And I understand that you can't really have a game with over 200 unique bosses, but I just find it quite lazy and honestly a bit of a turn off. Why are there 2 Godrick's or 3 Morgott fights or whatever, to me it just doesn't make sense and where yeah, you get more overall boss fight time (which is the fun of the souls games) repeating it in this way? No fun.

Another issue I have is the game feels more like a dodge simulator, some bosses feel like they give you no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ room to attack. It takes me back to DS3 Pontiff where you just never get a damn turn and honestly, I hate that. I'm not saying I want 5 second long openings to get free staggers, but I don't want to have to do 8 dodges, 1 attack, another 6 dodges, 1 attack, but I also don't want to have to trade damage just because I want to attack. I think some bosses aren't balanced well at all for this, and I think the DLC makes it more of a prominent issue.

That said, that's the main negatives for me, a couple small gripes could also be things like I don't find the Catacombs fun, just felt lengthy imo, I didn't really like the whole underground in Siofra, the area was just a bit tedious, and I do wish you could navigate the map a bit faster especially in NG+, going for graces again takes so long. Add a Surge Sprint into this just like Nightreign, would honestly help so much.

All that said, I still think it's a great game. There really is an endless amount of things to do. And one thing I really love is the weapon variety. In Dark Souls, it felt like you could just get a Uchigatana and be set, but in this I actually wanted to try new weapons. Godskin Peeler with Black Flame Tornado was so much fun for me, then things like the Fallingstar Beast Jaw also has such a cool and unique skill to it, I do love the variety in that and love how almost all weapons feel useable. And then there's magic to swap things up even more, even though I think melee is way more fun, the spells were cool and you could get creative. 

Back to bosses, for what fights are actually unique, I think they are great. Some bosses are just obnoxious, like Red Wolf just running away and spamming Glintblades, it does get infuriating but every game is gonna have annoying bosses like that. I think pretty much all Great Rune bosses are cool, I love the final boss, love Radagon, love Godfrey, they are some very enjoyable bosses. 

Overall great game, definitely has potential to be a great great game, but for me the negatives of it really do take it down quite a bit, but that said the game itself is so good that I would still recommend it 100%.

Before Elden Ring, I had never played a soulslike game. Now, after 59 hours in my first real playthrough, I finished the game. First thing I’ll say: the hype was deserved. The game is well made and my journey through [i]The Lands Between[/i]  a TON of fun. The difficulty did not hold me back at all, thanks to the generous help the game gives to the player. Are you a gamer and do you think Elden Ring will be too difficult for you? Don’t worry, just get the game. It’ll be fine.

Bullet points first, then my full spoiler-free review.

- Graphics: 8.5/10
- Exploration: 10/10
- Combat: 9/10
- Bosses: 9/10
- Audio: 9/10
- Story: 8/10
- Fun: ~9/10
- Difficulty: tough but doable

I know everyone always hypes up Elden Ring’s bosses and combat, and while they were incredibly good indeed, my personal highlight of the game was its exploration. There are so many unique areas in the game, and exploring them never feels dull: there’s LOOT everywhere, there’re QUESTS everywhere, there are DUNGEONS everywhere. The whole world is just so meticulously filled with details and things to do, that I just never got bored. My personal favorite area HAS to be [spoiler] Liurnia (duh)… Unfathomably fun. I was obsessed. [/spoiler]

My favorite part of the game is honestly just that the gameplay loop is so fun. It’s just a constant change between exploring, fighting and questing; it never gets boring. The messages people leave behind are also very fun: many of them are very funny or incredibly useful. I’d have missed so many secrets if it weren’t for messages leading me to them… It’s a wonderful replacement of using google to find your way around in the game.

The story and worldbuilding just add onto the pure EPICNESS of Elden Ring. I truly felt like a dark fantasy hero in a broken world. And the way everything matches up, everything works together towards the narrative; it’s just fantastic. 

The world itself is beautiful, we know that already, but also just incredibly BOMBASTIC and OVERWHELMING. It’s honestly a good example of the feeling of the Sublime; certain areas and places are just beyond magnificent, are just awe-inspiring on so many levels, and just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gigantic. Oftentimes I wanted to go take a screenshot of some landscape but everything is just so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ big so the screenshots never truly do the game justice. 

And now: the difficulty. The bosses are definitely hard, but thanks to the many tools the game gives you, I could beat almost every boss with less than 15 tries, often averaging 3-5 tries. And that’s not because I’m an experienced soulslike or competitive player; it’s thanks to the buffs and the loadouts you can get & thanks to the summons of the game. Otherwise I would’ve probably quit the game way before finishing it. Long live [spoiler] Moonveil & Skeleton Soldiers :)! [/spoiler]

I played until completion to leave this review, finishing through spite rather than enjoyment. My playthrough was late and apart from knowing about Ranni and Rykard through memes, I went in completely blind as a big Dark Souls 1 and 2 fan. The game wasn't what I expected and for the first few days of playing, I went where I thought I was supposed to go and just hit wall after wall after wall. Whether through the luck of it being open world, but I roamed around until going north and just felt powerless against everything. I'd tough it out against what I thought were boss looking enemies in the overworld only for them to not drop anything after trying to kill them for an hour. Or randomly get ambushed by a pack of something, which I learned is the games favourite thing to do. It took a long time to realize enemies were meant to be avoided unless progression was blocked.

My intent to not look anything up and play a dex build was tossed when I genuinely felt like stopping, because I was endlessly frustrated at nothing being consistent and the general gameplay. Enemy poise and my ability to parry was completely up in the air, I'd break poise against soldiers in armour but an emaciated ghoul with a knife could have super armour in or outside attack animations. Enemies I thought I could parry, were unparriable so I'd end up dying trying to get a pattern down and thinking I was failing. Even when successful, it was just too risky for the fact that from start to finish the game is a one-two hit kill fest if you're not specifically built for each threat, which I wasn't. This is made even worse from the fact that so many enemies in the game have multiple moves with 3-8 hit strings, whether a knight or some sort of boss. It felt so oppressively designed, not in a fun to overcome but sheer irritation to perfect dodging one attack only to be hit by a follow up attack designed to hit if you did. Then if you do manage to avoid getting hit, the enemy immediate acts again with no delay, no breathing room whatsoever. Shield the attacks instead, you get staggered and killed first combo.

This is why despite really liking all the different weapon arts and weapons themselves, there was little point. Mobs tended to die easily to anything yet anything a stage higher only let you hit once between combos or leaping away to do a ranged attack or summoning 8 of its mates to swarm you to death. Unless you use a Greatsword, then a few more enemies than normal can be staggered easily. I assume that's why I saw to many shadows use them and why enemies with them were so strong. I grew to hate the open world and the endless one note ambushes and beginners traps that were no different to each other just so frequent you got numb to it. Spirit Ashes being a requirement annoyed me at the start because I wanted to have that 1 on 1 challenge. Then they annoyed me even more when it regularly became a 2v2 race to try and kill one enemy before the spirit was killed. I can't honestly tell you a boss I liked fighting, for the first half of the game as a dual thrust wielding/twinblade dex build, to the Dark Moon Greatsword INT build I switched to at the end because I couldn't deal damage anymore. I didn't feel like I overcame a challenge, only kept trying till I got a pattern each time that let me succeed. I only stuck it through to the end because I paid for this and wanted to see Ranni's ending for myself. I assumed this game would be like Dark Souls, slow, consistent and methodical. Complete unfairness would be kept minimal and bosses were fair but challenging once you understood. Exploration would be rewarded, not met with 1000 ambushes to a crafting item. No, it's an action game with an open world and no leniency. I felt like I was in Devil May Cry but I wasn't Dante, I was the random mob he styled on. If you like that sort of thing, good for you. This isn't the souls gameplay I was looking for.

First of all, I did not like the game, I loved it!

I am writing this review as someone who has played Skyrim for quite a long time. I will also compare the game to Skyrim from time to time. Of course, they are structurally very different games, but in terms of open-world exploration, atmosphere, and the feeling of making the player wander around the map with curiosity, I could not help but compare it to Skyrim.

I finished the game without using Mimic even once, relying completely on my own hands, reflexes, learning process, and gameplay. This made me feel the difficulty of the game in a more naked way. My comments about the boss loop, build progression, and the challenging sides of the game mostly come from this experience.

Elden Ring is truly a great game. But it is NOT FOR EVERYONE! This needs to be understood.


MY POSITIVE THOUGHTS

I do not want to go on and on about the positive sides everyone keeps repeating, but to put it briefly: the open-world design, graphics, sense of exploration, music, and atmosphere are top-tier. Very few games can compete with Skyrim. In my eyes, Elden Ring is one of them.


-The boss loop is incredibly satisfying.

Dying to bosses, understanding their moves, reading when they are going to attack, learning to react better, looking for a talisman suitable for the damage they deal, coming back a little stronger, and finally beating that boss that once seemed impossible… It is an incredibly satisfying loop. The game is really strong in this regard.


-The map constantly keeps your sense of curiosity alive.

The exploration side works just as well. You see a ruined structure ahead and think, “I wonder what is there?” You go and check it out. Suddenly, an NPC there gives you a critical quest, or you open up an area you never expected. In this sense, the game flows like butter. There is something in almost every corner of the map that makes you curious.



MY NEGATIVE / INFURIATING THOUGHTS


-The interface is really clunky.

Despite loving the game this much, parts need improvement and seriously drove me crazy.

Skyrim had a similar problem, too, but at least it could be made great with mods. Elden Ring needs improvement in terms of interface, and it definitely does not feel like a game meant to be played with a keyboard and mouse.

Item switching is torture. Pressing "I" does not open the inventory. You must press Esc, then go into Equipment, and change things from there. You cannot change items from the Inventory section. You have to scroll in the equipment menu, find the new item you dropped, and only then compare its stats.

Not being able to set favorite weapons is another problem. When you want to switch a weapon, you have to search through all your weapons.

Another missing feature is a list of bosses you have not killed yet. In a game this huge, with so many optional bosses and hidden areas, not having a checklist feels like a big omission.

Esc not working properly is another problem. It does not take you back in many places. Even after 60 hours, I noticed myself instinctively spamming Esc, which does nothing. You have to use E and Backspace. Getting used to this is really hard. At some point, it feels like you are not fighting the game’s difficulty, but the stubbornness of the interface.


-There is build variety, but in practice some weapons stand out too much.

When it comes to build variety, there is definitely variety in the game. In fact, on paper it offers quite a wide build space. But in my experience, this variety does not fully feel noticeable until you reach the later parts of the game.

Especially weapons like Bloodhound’s Fang feel so efficient that the player naturally stays with the same weapon for a long time. It is also possible to sense a similar tendency from the ghost-like silhouettes of other players around me. Of course, there are different weapons, different build paths, and different playstyles, but in practice some weapons feel so strong and useful that at some point you start thinking, “Why would I even drop this?”


-The armor system and variety did not satisfy me much.

Armors cannot be upgraded, and most of them feel very close to each other. Some armors have meh-level differences in poise, weight, resistance, and appearance, but for someone expecting a clear Skyrim-style armor progression or feeling of getting stronger, the system is not satisfying.

There is no clear sense of difference at the level I expected between the armor I had at the start of the game and one of the heaviest armor sets I wore at the end. I can even say that if you finish the game with your starting armor, you do not really feel a serious difference.

In Skyrim, this was very different. There were many different levels of weapons and armor, you could make different combinations with the enchantment system, and you could upgrade sets. Whether you were a mage or a warrior, whatever job you played, there was a feeling of almost endless combinations. Elden Ring has build variety, I do not deny that, but especially the armor system does not give the same progression satisfaction.


-No offense, but: THERE IS NO QUEST MARKER!

The thing I generally dislike in Souls games is here as well. There is no quest marker. This looks like a very cool feature and is defended like crazy, but at some points you get stuck and then have to Alt+Tab to check documentation, wiki, videos, etc. Unless you are part of the top 1% elite gamer crowd, of course.

In my eyes, this is a big immersion killer. Hold my hand a little, man. In Skyrim, there is even a special skill just to show the direction of the active quest. In Elden Ring, following the progression of some quests without looking at an outside source is seriously difficult.

I think the quest marker issue should be left completely to the player. Put the markers in, make them off by default. Let us see what percentage of players will go and manually activate them. Let us choose whether to turn them on or off. There is no need to act cool.


-The input reading issue is not fair at all in my opinion.

Another serious criticism I have is the input reading issue in the game. I definitely think input reading is happening, and I do not find this ethical from a game design standpoint. Some enemies and bosses react early depending on which key you are spamming on the keyboard. There are way too many moments where it feels like bosses are directly reading your input and acting accordingly.

You use a flask, an attack comes instantly. You cast a spell, and you get punished before the animation even properly starts. Of course, I have no objection to the game being hard. In fact, I respect this difficulty. But in my opinion, there is a serious difference between difficulty and reading the player’s input to punish them.

The first gives a feeling of learning and mastery, while the second sometimes creates the feeling that the game is straight-up cheating. Challenging the player is one thing. Reacting reflexively according to the button the player presses is another.


-Some normal mobs feel way stronger than they should.

The damage balance of normal enemies is also exaggerated in some places. I am not saying bosses should hit harder or be turned into damage sponges. The problem is that some regular mobs feel way too strong for what they are.

A random bird, dog, or normal enemy on the map can sometimes tear you apart in two hits, even when you have solid armor, talismans, and buffs. The infamous rune farm bird is a good example of this kind of absurd scaling. These are supposed to be regular enemies, but some of them end up feeling more threatening than they reasonably should.

This does not make the game feel more balanced or more fair. It just makes certain mobs feel overtuned.


-So

Elden Ring is special to me. Its flaws annoyed me, and I still disagree with some choices, but its exploration, boss loop, atmosphere, and world are unforgettable. Not for everyone, but an amazing game.

Elden Ring as a game has many baffling design decisions, many of which somehow work. Typical of Souls games, the story is not straightforward and instead told primarily through the environment, flavour text in items and the enemy designs. In terms of visuals and storytelling, the game rewards exploration, attention to detail and perseverance (be prepared to do many awfully designed quests for your lore!)

The quest design is some of the worst we've seen in any Souls game. Anyone who thinks the quests are well designed in Elden Ring I am convinced they have not tried to do a quest without a wiki. Several NPCs will hint to where they will be next, but the location is so generic and nonspecific you could actively search for them and miss them because, SURPRISE they were tucked away in this little corner behind this rock you forgot to look behind. If the hardest part of your quests are figuring out where to find the next parts to continue it, your quests are badly designed.

It's strong points in gameplay are the high levels of build customisation, including large varieties of weapons, skills, talismans and armour. Unfortunately, there are many points where it feels like player choice was not prioritised to the detriment of the game. Several weapons are seemingly stuck with skills that aren't even unique to them. Many skills are badly designed, clearly meant more for show than actual practical use, and if they were made better they would make for interesting additions to builds.

Although I really like skills and spells in Elden Ring, they cause a majority of the balance problems, despite how fun they are. Many skills/spells can easily be slotted into any build for immediate power due to low stat requirements. Any build is just a few steps away from broken territory, even the simplest, most basic ones. If you're just using a big bonk stick, you'll quickly realise that jump attacks are insanely overpowered in PvE, easily staggering large enemies and bosses. There are a handful of "no-brainer" talismans that are so strong you might as well always have them equipped unless you really need to squeeze in something for your build.

This ultimately leads to my point that Elden Ring is a very unbalanced game with many overcentralising mechanics. It's no wonder the community is so uptight about how you play this game. Ultimately, I think balance of single player games still matters. I would prefer more balanced options that are competitive with each other, and also less "no-brainer" choices that are just the obvious picks.

In the end, Elden Ring is a Souls game, and in Souls games knowledge is power. Practically every Souls game has mechanics where if you know how to use them you can utterly break the game, but Elden Ring is so full of them it's very easy to just accidentally happen upon them.

Elden Ring completely pulled me in from the moment I first stepped into Limgrave. Seeing that massive world open up for the first time was honestly overwhelming in the best possible way. I remember just standing there, trying to decide where to go first, immediately making the questionable decision to wander off and explore [spoiler] before arriving at the first church [/spoiler]. That feeling of freedom is what makes this game so special. Every road, ruin, cave, or suspicious corner felt worth checking out because the game constantly rewarded curiosity. Even after hundreds of hours, I still kept finding hidden items, new paths, or entire areas I somehow missed before.

The bosses and world design were easily my favorite parts. Getting destroyed by the Tree Sentinel early on was humiliating but hilarious, and it perfectly taught me what kind of game I was facing.

Finally defeating Malenia after all the frustration, scarlet rot, and repeated failures felt incredibly satisfying. The game feels difficult, but fair, and every victory actually feels earned. I also loved diving into the lore, (even if most of it came from outside sources rather than the game directly - which is a personal choice in the end) 

Compared to Dark Souls III, this game takes everything I loved and pushes it much further. The open world, the freedom to explore, and even small quality-of-life improvements like traveling freely between Sites of Grace made the experience feel bigger and smoother without losing the soul of a FromSoftware game. Elden Ring may not be the hardest or fastest Soulslike ever, but it absolutely feels like one of the most memorable. It is one of those rare games where getting lost is not frustrating because it is the entire point.

The level design is masterful, each region has its own identity and mood, and legacy dungeons like Stormveil and Leyndell are some of the most carefully crafted spaces I've ever explored in a game. 
The cutscenes are genuinely stunning, the art, the lighting, the scale and the Soundtracks ofc.

If you want to start a FromSoftware game, Elden Ring is your go-to, It's far more beginner friendly than people make it out to be, yes there are hard parts, but the summon system is there for a reason, struggling with a boss? Call for help, It genuinely makes the experience more accessible without taking anything away from it.

And the DLC, At 40€ Shadow of the Erdtree is a steal, the amount of content, new areas, new weapons, and bosses it brings closer to a full sequel than an expansion, If you loved the base game, this is non-negotiable.
