Elden Ring (Elden Ring) is one of the most ambitious open-world action RPGs ever made. It takes the core “Souls” formula—methodical combat, challenging boss fights, and cryptic storytelling—and expands it into a vast open world that genuinely rewards curiosity. Exploration is the game’s biggest strength: stumbling onto hidden dungeons, optional bosses, or entirely new regions often feels organic rather than scripted, and the sense of discovery is consistently strong.

Combat is deep, flexible, and highly customizable. Whether you prefer heavy melee builds, magic-focused playstyles, or hybrid setups, the game gives you meaningful tools to approach encounters in different ways. Boss fights are a major highlight, often visually spectacular and mechanically demanding in a way that feels rewarding once you learn them. The world design also supports experimentation, letting players tackle challenges in multiple orders rather than forcing a strict path.

That said, Elden Ring isn’t without flaws. The difficulty can be uneven, with some bosses feeling dramatically harder or more polished than others. The open world, while impressive, can occasionally feel repetitive in its side content (similar dungeon layouts, reused bosses, etc.). And the game’s storytelling remains intentionally vague, which some players find immersive, but others find too opaque or emotionally distant.

Overall, Elden Ring is a landmark game that successfully translates the Souls formula into a massive open world without losing its identity. It’s not perfect, but its sense of scale, freedom, and challenge makes it one of the most memorable RPGs in years.

# 🎮 Why *Elden Ring* is worth your time

Imagine stepping into a massive, haunting fantasy world where **every hill hides a secret, every ruin tells a story, and every enemy could destroy you**—unless you outsmart it.

That’s *Elden Ring*.

Developed by FromSoftware and shaped with worldbuilding by George R. R. Martin, this game takes the brutal combat of *Dark Souls* and drops it into a **fully open world called the Lands Between**, where you can go almost anywhere from the start. ([Wikipedia][1])

It’s not just a game—it’s a **challenge, an exploration sandbox, and a mystery you slowly unravel**.

---

# 🌍 The Core Experience (What You Actually Do)

* Explore a **huge open world** on foot or horseback (your mount “Torrent”)
* Fight enemies and bosses using **precise, skill-based combat**
* Build your character however you want (magic, swords, stealth, hybrid, etc.)
* Discover hidden dungeons, secrets, and lore without hand-holding
* Optionally play **co-op or PvP** with other players ([Wikipedia][1])

There are no quest markers telling you what to do next—**you figure it out**.

---

# 🔥 The Pros (Why people love it)

### 1. A truly massive, rewarding open world

This isn’t filler content. Exploration constantly pays off with weapons, bosses, and secrets. ([GameScribe Daily][2])
You’re encouraged to wander—and you’re almost always rewarded.

### 2. Deep, satisfying combat

Combat is **deliberate and skill-based**—timing, stamina, and positioning matter. ([TechRadar][3])
Every victory feels earned, not handed to you.

### 3. Huge build variety

You can play however you want:

* Heavy knight with a giant sword
* Spell-casting mage
* Agile rogue
* Weird hybrid builds

The flexibility is massive and replayable. ([Play Versus Games][4])

### 4. Rich lore and atmosphere

The story isn’t spoon-fed. Instead, you piece it together through:

* Item descriptions
* NPC dialogue
* Environmental storytelling

It creates a **mysterious, immersive vibe** unlike most games. ([GameScribe Daily][2])

### 5. Tons of content

There’s easily **100+ hours of gameplay**, with more than most players will ever fully complete. ([Trusted Reviews][5])

### 6. Genuine sense of accomplishment

Beating a boss in *Elden Ring* feels like:

> “I earned this.”

That emotional payoff is one of the game’s biggest selling points.

---

# ⚠️ The Cons (What might turn you off)

### 1. It is HARD—very hard

There’s no easy mode.
You will die. A lot.
That’s intentional design. ([Trusted Reviews][5])

### 2. Minimal guidance

The game barely explains:

* Where to go
* How quests work
* What stats do

New players can feel lost or overwhelmed. ([My Blog][6])

### 3. Story is vague

If you want a clear, cinematic narrative—you won’t get it.
You have to **interpret and piece things together yourself**.

### 4. Some repetition in side content

Not every dungeon or boss is unique—some reuse ideas or layouts. ([TechRadar][3])

### 5. Occasional technical issues

Minor performance hiccups or pop-in can happen, depending on platform. ([My Blog][6])

### 6. Not very accessible

* No difficulty settings
* Limited accessibility features
  This can exclude more casual or time-limited players. ([My Blog][6])

---

# 🧠 Real Player Perspective (from the community)

From Reddit, one player summed it up bluntly:

> “The feeling of wonder and triumph… is like nothing else” ([Reddit][7])

But others note:

* It can feel confusing or frustrating
* Some bosses or systems feel unfair or unclear ([Reddit][8])

So yeah—it’s not universally loved.

---

# 🏆 Final Pitch

If you want a game that:

* Respects your intelligence
* Doesn’t hold your hand
* Rewards persistence and curiosity
* Gives you unforgettable “I DID IT” moments

👉 *Elden Ring* is one of the best modern RPGs ever made.

But if you want:

* Relaxed gameplay
* Clear direction
* Easy progression

👉 This might frustrate you more than entertain you.

---

# 🎯 Bottom line

**Buy it if:**
You like challenge, exploration, and deep gameplay systems

**Skip it if:**
You hate dying, getting lost, or figuring things out yourself

If you’ve ever thought, “I’d love a game that humbles me, confuses me, and still makes me say ‘one more try’ at 2am,” then Elden Ring is basically your soulmate.

This game drops you into a massive, mysterious world with almost zero hand-holding. There’s no “go here next!” flashing sign. Just vibes, danger, and the distant glow of a giant golden tree judging your life choices. You’ll wander, you’ll get lost, and you’ll absolutely walk into places you have no business being. And that’s kind of the magic.

Combat feels incredible until it doesn’t, which usually means you just got flattened by a boss the size of a small building. Every defeat somehow feels like a lesson, even if that lesson is “maybe don’t roll off a cliff next time.” When you finally win, it’s not just satisfying. It’s victorious in a way most games can’t touch.

The world design is honestly unreal. One minute you’re exploring peaceful fields, the next you’re in a nightmare dungeon wondering who approved this emotionally. And the bosses? Equal parts terrifying and cool, like you’re fighting living legends with anger issues.

The only “downside” is that the game expects patience. If you want something easy and straightforward, this might test your sanity. But if you’re up for a challenge and love the feeling of slowly mastering something tough, it’s incredibly rewarding.

Final verdict:
Beautiful, brutal, confusing, and completely addictive.

What a weird game - exceptionally high highs, really low lows.

If this is your first FromSoft game (as I imagine it was for a majority of its players), this game will be an undisputed masterpiece.

For Soulsborne veterans, not so much. The game is still great, but its "merely" great.
If you've played your fair share of FromSoft games, you will inevitably feel how derivative Elden Ring can feel. 

"What's this spell? Oh its literally Lightning Spear. Hey look, its the Claymore! Same moveset and everything. And this item? Ah its Red Tearstone ring with a different name". Elden Ring is essentially Dark Souls 3 with some of Dark Souls 2's design ideology, wearing a Breath of the Wild costume. The open world is a fun addition, but I personally don't think it adds anything exceptionally meaningful to the formula. Having to scrounge around for resources to craft a basic fire pot is not mechanically interesting enough to warrant the extra time wasted doing so when in previous games you can just buy them off a merchant.

Then there's the balance. Of course brainless mongoloids will mindlessly yap about gitting gut (which is sometimes completely valid), but this ignores the problem the game has. Some builds will tremendously struggle and some will breeze through due to the design ideology of the enemies and bosses.

Enemies are fast, often use ambushes, and have combos that can almost 100% to 0% you. This goes X2 for bosses. Late game bosses are caricatures of themselves - they have a stupid amount of HP, they are insanely fast, they jump around the map while you impotently try to catch up, they are almost always huge so that locking on while they do their anime dashes makes it hard to keep track, and they can easily combo you from full to dead unless you have 50+ Vigor. 

UGS enjoyers will struggle immensely, UGS + no summons is basically unviable. The game very much seems to have been designed with summons/co-op in mind, which can be either good or bad depending on your preference.

The game at least looks phenomenal - not graphically, textures/effects/lightning basically haven't improved since DS3. The game looks incredible aesthetically. The Liurnia landscape is a painting (literally), and Nokron is one of the most breathtakingly beautiful spaces I have ever seen in a video game.

The endings are underwhelming, but of course they are - that's GRRM's signature move.


TL;DR - a masterpiece of normies, a pretty good if flawed entry for seasoned FromSoft players

Elden Ring is different from previous Souls games, but it is as amazing - the developers achieved expanding the Souls gameplay fomula without destroying the core.

If I had to describe the game in simple terms, I would say it is a bit like Dark Souls + Far Cry. There is a ton of exploration that gets rewarded, lots of POIs and map objectives and it all sits on top of the core Souls combat system.

The game looks AMAZING, it is stylish and still keeps a dark and brooding atmosphere.
The game is HUGE compared to other Souls games, there are so many placed to explore, they all look great and different and there is always something to find there - NPCs, bosses, loot, ... The first playthrough (whole map explored, most of the loot, almost all achivements) took about 100hrs + ~30hrs for a NG+ playthrough to unlock all missing endings and doing all NPC quest lines.
The game brings a lot of QoL improvements compared to older Souls games, the gameplay overall is very smooth. Stakes of Marika alone save so much time and frustration. And there are some new features like Ashes of War, Spirit Summons and crafting.
The music is good, but I would rank it below all 4 Soulsborne games, not by a lot, but still. A lot of the soundtracks are "generic epic music", but it has two or three special tracks.
Bosses overall are more difficult compared to previous titles - the bosses are more aggressive and active and a lot of them have mutliple phases.
The boss design in this game sometimes is quite lazy though and can be very frustrating:
- Input reading
- Unnaturally delayed attacks
- Very, very long attack combos that leave very little time to attack yourself
- Attack combos that look the same but add extra moves when it is convenient
- Animation & stagger cancelling !!!
The game was entirely completable with a purist solo melee-only build, but quite frustrating at several points. There is one boss in particular that was very frustrating to beat. And its not that the boss is just difficult, it is simply unfair (read issues above, especially the stagger cancelling is unheard of - the boss staggers but cancels the stagger animation to instead hit you before you can finish your own attack trying to take advantage of the stagger - wtf).
But at the same time, the game is also completable for casuals and players new to the series - there are dozens of buffs that can be applied before and during a fight, there is a ton of strong ranged options and players can summon Spirit Ashes and other players for help. 

And this gets me to the few negative aspects (on top of some lazy boss design).
While I applaud the effort to make the game more accessible to new players, I think the difference between using and not using the tools the game provides you with, is too big - there is just too much "possible" help in the game and it really trivializes most bosses - many bosses can be soloed by your summons. When I summoned a Spirit Ash for the aforementioned boss fight, I suddenly managed it first try, without changing anything else.
The game feels less tight and a bit less well designed compares to other Souls games - towards the end the game started to drag a bit and a lot of map design decisions feel a bit random and less deliberate. But thats to be expected when the size of the game increased so much.
And as always, there are some issues with input lag/ignoring, but combat overall feels very fluid and smooth.

Elden Ring is one of those games that doesn’t try to impress you — it just throws you in and lets you figure things out on your own. There’s no proper direction, no step-by-step guide, and no one telling you what to do next. At the start, it feels confusing and a bit unfair, but slowly you begin to understand how everything works… and that’s when it clicks. You die a lot, you get stuck, and you question your build, but every time you come back a little better. And when you finally beat something that once felt impossible, it actually feels earned.

The freedom is what makes it special. You can play however you want, build your character however you like, and explore at your own pace without being forced into a single path. The world is quiet, sometimes beautiful, sometimes unsettling, but always interesting — every area feels unique, and there’s always something hidden waiting to be discovered. It’s not an easy game, and definitely not for everyone, but if you stick with it, it becomes something unforgettable. After finishing everything, I can confidently say it’s one of the best games I’ve ever played.

Elden Ring is a good game. Extremely overrated and overhyped but still a good game.

The game is praised for its open world but the world has nothing to offer besides Legacy Dungeons and pretty views. The rewards you often get for exploring is combat. You can't even use so many spells and weapons because your build doesn't allow for it. The starting open area is the best one but every thing that comes after is a dip in quality. The starting Legacy Dungeon is also the best and densest. FromSoftware's fixation on making everything vague just for the sake of it harms the game rather than making it more immersive, fun and enjoyable. Most of the time you are running across an open area hoping to find something good but again, all you are rewarded with is the beautiful art of this game and not something that immerses you in the world.

Going from level-based game design to a fully fledged open world also requires you to add some interesting content in the open world. Hiding a large area that you accidentally found whilst exploring is fun until you realise that area had basically nothing and you just rode across your horse for a boss fight. There are so many areas with books scattered around so why can't I read them? Why do I always have to read item descriptions to understand what's going on? Those items often provide only a line or two worth of lore. This stupid game design needs to change if they are making an open world game.

The smaller dungeons follow a very basic formula. You go in, explore until you find a lever, that lever unlocks the boss room, kill the boss. That boss you fight is either the easiest part of the dungeon or the most stupid enemy-type that ever graced your screen. Often times you can just trade blows with the boss but sometimes they put a boss which is too big for that arena, has no stagger or duo bosses which are not designed to be a duo. There really are no good small dungeon bosses in this game.

The first Legacy Dungeon, Stormveil Castle, is the best one. The second one, Raya Lucaria, is also good but not as good as the first one. The third one, Volcano Manor, had a lot of potential but it's quite short. The fourth one, Leyndell, is huge but again, not a lot to do there except kill enemies or find something that doesn't go well with your build. The last one, Elphael, is also good but it's not close to Stormveil. There are no Legacy Dungeons (or at least they are not good enough to be called that) in two main areas. 

I am not too happy with the bosses in this game. Many ♥♥♥♥ bosses have been copy and pasted in different areas. You fight the same ♥♥♥♥ boss multiple times. I have no idea how they thought that THIS boss is good enough that players won't mind fighting them for the 5th time. Most of the main bosses are good and it's fun to learn their moveset but some bosses have complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ attacks and hitboxes. The first main boss you fight is infamous for his delayed attacks and relentless combos. I think DS3 found a really good balance between the player speed and the boss' speed but Elden Ring is more in favor of the bosses rather than the player. I don't enjoy dodging a 5-10 move combo for 5-10 seconds just to land one attack. There are not many dodge and attack windows in this game (unlike DS1 and DS3). You dodge,  dodge, dodge, dodge, attack, dodge, dodge, attack. Not fun.

All of this criticism doesn't mean the game isn't good or fun. I had a blast on both of my playthroughs but Elden Ring, in many ways, is a step back for FromSoftware and it not as great as everyone makes it out to be.

One thing Elden Ring excels at is build variety. You have so many options to go for and change your playstyle. There are so many different types of weapons like swords, greatswords, colossal swords, daggers, katanas, whips, axes, greataxes, freaking perfume bottles, wands and even shields to play from. Not to mention all the cool armor sets you can mess around with to create a pretty unique looking character. 

Despite all the negativity in this review, I will still give Elden Ring a 8.5/10. It's a good game but not the pinnacle of open world games. Not even close to that.

This was my first Souls game ever, it had its ups and downs, cause this type of game is bound to tilt you sometimes, wether a hard boss or mechanics that you struggle with in particular, sometimes traps where a mob will push you off a cliff, etc. BUT, all in all, this was an amazing experience. There's no greater feeling than struggling with a boss for a bit and finally managing to kill it. The first boss you find when arriving to Limgrave, the famous Tree Sentinel, it's generally supposed to be skipped, it teaches you that sometimes a boss is a wall and you should get more powerful before attempting it, as a true gamer, you go for the challenge and no better feeling than managing to kill it. The journey is awesome, i'm not a fan of the little mobs around to confront or elites, i much prefer the boss encounters but it's still fine and Elden Ring just allows you to mostly avoid all that, you can just skim pass riding Torrent or running sometimes. In my first playthrough I killed almost all bosses of the base game + dlc (in total i'm pretty sure i'm missing less than 10 bosses), ofc in a way this meant some bosses i found later, i was a bit overleveled making it a bit too easy but ye, I just wanted to "catch them all".
It's a game you should really blindly explore and enjoy and don't stop just cause you get stuck at some boss, it can be frustrating, just go do something else, explore a different zone, take a break, because after killing it, the more you struggled the more you enjoy the fact you passed that obstacle.
This was pure yap, just play the game, it's a 10/10, not the hardest souls game according to the genre veterans but if you're new to that type of games, this is one of the best experiences for a new souls gamer. Some other details:
- Lore: It's okay, it's not bad but a bit confusing sometimes and A LOT of it, has tidbits in quests, bosses, scrolls, making it a bit complex, it's nothing crazy but I still think it's a pretty nice supporting plot for the game and with enough important secrets for the lovers of lore diving, there's a lot of good youtube videos that expose you to the deeper lore of the game and they're a nice watch
- Graphics: the view is amazing, you feel how giant the world is, insane sized areas with massive structures, one of them pretty early in the game, it's very good for players who love "old fantasy aesthetics", everything is really beautiful, bosses designs also, the weapons, "arenas", legit everything
- Audio: Just like the massive feel of the world, the soundtrack also gives that idea, with a very "epic" feel to it, one of the best games in this regard also, it's pure joy
- Performance: Super fine for when I started playing it (was a decent time after release I guess, like 2y after?) and my PC is already super old CPU wise (Intel 6700) with a good GPU (AMD 7800 XT), there were maybe 1 or 2 zones and bosses where the visual effects would tank my FPS a bit but since that was pretty rare, it was wtv, plus again, my fault having such an old CPU.
- Bad stuff i can remember: Questing in this game is definitely a bit of a challenge sometimes, for the main importanty storyline I think it's fine, but for side quests it's hard to know what to do sometimes or how can affect rewards or outcomes, sometimes I just used google, didn't really ruin my experience but something to keep in mind
Think that's about it, just play the game, it's awesome and gives you a good amount of hours, especially if you buy during sales. Think base game is an average of 55-80h maybe? Really depends on how much exploration and side stuff you do.

The game is not terrible but it is just not good enough. I 100% all Dark Souls/Sekiro games and as a successor to this franchise it is exhausting, boring, it feels off.

What is dislike:
- The main selling point - the open world - is actually its biggest flaw. Everything i remember in a positive way are the legacy dungeons like Stormveil Castle which is a closed off area that has nothing to do with the open world. It was fun exploring, but riding through generic forests or small castles or mini dungeon etc. is so boring, you just run past everything. Stop with the open worlds, you have nothing to tell, nothing to fill it with, it is not "a revolution in gaming", stop it.
- 90% of the items you find are useless, it feels underwhelming to explore anything after 20 hours ingame
- Too many recycled bosses (that giant space mantis whatever at the end of that one cave had me laughing, absolutely terrible decision to reuse that boss)
- The camera is a disaster again. It is the - I dont know - maybe 7th iteration of this kind of game and camera still sucks like in the first Dark Souls. Make walls transparent when you are forced into a corner and move the camera back, make the camera zoom out when fighting giant bosses, I want to see more than a foot of the enemy, I must know what he is about to do. I know what my character does, I do not have to see him up close.
- Generally too many giant bosses, too many dragons, towards the end of the game they put 2 dragons in an area and to top it off, another optional boss battle - a dragon - yay! Sorry but fighting a dragon in an action game has always been terrible. It is no fun, it is meant to be fought with heavy machinery or something, not in a sword fight. Stop making 1 on 1 dragon vs human fights every 2 hours. It is exhausting. Put one dragon fight in there and make it special, not generic.
- A lot of the bosses have too long combos and they also change up the attack patterns so I cannot really learn the boss because the openings are sometimes there, sometimes not, so I always have to assume there is no opening to get a hit or two in. It felt more of a gamble most of the time, or trading blows
- The balance is off. I wanted to solo the game and I did until the late game super bosses, there I was stuck and after a few attempts I tried summoning spirits for the first time. It was ridiculous, it made the game so easy that I beat almost every boss from that point forth first or second try. Having a companion is too overpowered but solo it felt impossible (e.g.: one boss turns the arena in a constant bleed build up, solo I felt there was no way as a melee class to do this fight. Maybe with more practice it is possible but I felt too tired to try it more often solo)
- There are so many checkpoints in the world so they had to turn up the damage of common enemies. Some generic dog in the late game area hits you? Say goodbye to half of your health bar. Just run past everything until you find the next checkpoint
- Too many convoluted questlines intertwined with eachother. Do not talk to this guy if you have not spoken with this guy somewhere in the south and before killing that boss! Annoying, exhausting. Dark souls had this too but it felt more possible because the characters appeared at locations you definetely come across and in order. Yeah open world ruins this too.
- Crafting is such a weird mechanic in the game. It is nice to have but you do not need it at all but because of crafting there are thousands of worthless items to collect in the world. Mushrooms, berries, twigs... sorry but just a waste of time again. Why should I create a firebomb if I can just run up to the enemy and punch him in the face?
- I used an Xbox 360 controller and the input delay was bad. The game had a real problem with accepting new inputs from me in fast fights. Lets say I used a heavy attack with a long attack animation and then pressed the button for heal during the attack animation but then realize "oh no, I cant heal i need to roll" so I keep spamming roll the game still thinks I want to heal although there were at least 3 new "roll" inputs after the heal input.
- I do not want to spoil but the final boss is the perfect metaphor for this game: boring and generic - even the name.

What I liked:
+ The first 20 hours of the game felt great, gearing up, exploring two legacy dungeons. After that it went downhill fast.
+ Music is alright I guess
+ Many builds, weapons, spells and armors available
+ Some decent and memorable boss battles (but not too many)
+ The hitboxes are actually not that bad, I remember them being quite bad in the Dark Souls series but they have improved, not a lot of instances when I thought that an attack should have hit or not have hit me
+ The scenery and cutscenes can be nice to look at

I still have to play the DLC but I cannot bring myself to play it, I am burnt out, bored.

Sort of janky with horrible platforming segments and shoddy controls at times.
The story and questing is done perhaps more poorly than any other game I've ever played.

A love letter to old school games that also had all those same issues, truly a game that is gameplay first.

Anywhere you go, there is something to find, a vista to enjoy, and a story to piece together, if you care to.

One of the things I enjoy about Fromsoft games when I first played DS2 was finding hidden routes, new areas, and quests that I never even thought to look for or was oblivious to the whole time. That has never been more true than in this game. You can think you know this game inside and out, and then you'll be like me and stumble across an entire area that you never even knew was there.

I also at times found myself thinking "man, as gorgeous as this game is, some of these areas only have a few bodies and a mushroom or two..." and then if you care to look closer you'll find a story in the arrangement of the bodies, the other items around, and also begin to enjoy the open areas that are serene in their existence, as horrifying as some are. Because while you are fit to become the Elden Lord, the universe does not care about you, and this land has existed for millennia longer than you, but may not last much longer after. You are at the tail end of the world-shaping history of this land, and while the pretty settings and grandeur are staggering... 

This world is old. It has been built upon centuries beyond centuries of kingdoms and nature and gods and goddesses and fighting and celestial conflict. You are but a speck in the glory of Grace and its many enemies.

I like making a battlemage, using a shield and sword and yet also wielding some of the most powerful spells known to Tarnished. I love this game and look forward to trying out many others of the hundreds of possibilities for a build in my future hours.

For all the praises I will lavish upon this game, the horse mechanics are just almost not perfect. They work amazingly most of the time, until you're in a fight and suddenly Torrent just *poofs* out from under you, landing you on your back and getting you killed. If you somehow survive, you can call him again... and he's obviously not dead. You don't even have to use a flask 9 times out of 10 to summon him after he disappears. And this poofing he does makes the whole Rowa fruit mechanic to feed fruit to Torrent actually pointless and proving that for everything they nailed, some things were just not executed well, and it's sad they made it through to the final product. Of course Torrent deserves all the berries, but the mechanic itself was described as decidedly combat-focused and not immersion.

By the Guidance of Grace, I found the will to fight. May you also take up the call to become the Ruler of All that is Golden, the Elden Lord.

Elden Ring: A Masterpiece of Art
Score: 10/10

Now time for the essay.

There are games you play for fun. There are games you play to be challenged. There are games you play to change you. **Elden Ring** is all of these things, and more. It’s not a game. It’s a work of art – one that is bold, brilliantly executed, and deeply rewarding at every turn. Calling it a game would be like calling the Sistine Chapel a building.

The first time you walk into the Lands Between, the world FromSoftware has built takes your breath away. Gold fields, volcanoes, crystal caves, swamps, a coliseum in the sky – all set in this magical land. Every biome is a painter’s dream. Every inch of this massive world is filled with secrets, secrets hidden behind every cliff, every crumbling ruin, every hidden underground passage.

The story of the Lands Between is the story of the archaeologist. The tale is told in pieces and shards. It is a puzzle for players to assemble, and an epic and heartbreaking myth as compelling as any you’d find in Greek literature.

We’ve known what open-world games were. Maps full of icons, waypoints and linear objectives leading to the next big moment. Elden Ring isn’t that game. There are no quest markers, no arrows on the minimap. It’s your journey. Two people could play 100 hours in the Lands Between and have completely different stories.

I love that. The best part is it scales problems to curiosity. It trusts the player completely. I can't think of a game that does that these days.

It is a game where every battle is a conversation. A timing, a positioning, a patience. Bosses are not just hurdles to jump over. They are dances to learn. The Margit that kills you 20 times becomes your dance partner and you learn the rhythm of the dance on the 21st time. Few media give you that sense of achievement when you finally get a challenge.

You’ll have more arrows in your quiver, Ashes of War, sorceries and incantations, but Elden Ring is arguably the most expressive and accessible FromSoftware game to date, while still retaining that difficulty.

"Boss Design as High Art" “Radahn, the Starscourge,” a knight so powerful that he holds the stars in place with gravity sorcery, rides across a beach as a symphony of guitars and violins fills the heavens. “Malenia, Blade of Miquella,” might be the most technically demanding and artistically beautiful boss ever dreamed up. Maliketh, Morgott, and Rennala aren’t just enemies; they are stories, tragedies, and secrets. The encounters aren’t just hard, but they’re also heart-wrenching.

The game is a hit, but it’s also created a culture. The asynchronous multiplayer aspects of messages inscribed on the dungeon floors and the ghostly presence of other players means that your lonely adventure isn’t a lonely adventure. And the DLC expansions like Shadow of the Erdtree show it’s not a ceiling, but a foundation. For many, it’s the best DLC in gaming.

Elden Ring is bold, beautiful, hard and deeply moving. It doesn’t coddle the player. Instead, it delivers one of the most immersive and emotionally satisfying experiences interactive art has ever delivered. It’s not just the best game of its generation. It sets a standard for all future games that will be judged by it for years to come.

Definitely the greatest game I’ve ever played. I’ve put more hours into it than any other game I own, and it almost always has something new to show me. Just the other day despite being on NG+13 I discovered that you can use a telescope in Limgrave and several other zones to get a bird’s‑eye view of the area. I have no idea how I overlooked that for so long, but I did. I even found a super weak Deathrite Bird or whatever it’s called in Liurnia that I somehow missed twelve times in a row.
I’m only mentioning this so that anyone who hasn’t played yet understands just how much game there is to play. There’s a bit of a learning curve for newcomers, but the game does a great job teaching you the basics in the first zone. It shows you the core controls, subtly guides you with eye‑catching landmarks and architecture, teaches you how to find map fragments without treating you like an idiot, introduces NPCs without forcing unskippable dialogue, and gives you the freedom to go wherever you want without punishing you for doing side content instead of the main story.
It’s also one of the few games I’ve played that genuinely rewards curiosity and punishes it just as often. One chest might give you a useful item, while another might teleport you to a cave across the map. Sometimes that glowing blue item at the end of a corridor really is that easy to grab, and other times the floor collapses right before you reach it. There are plenty of surprises and unexpected events, and there’s a ton of fun gameplay for just about any preferred playstyle. There’s lots of room for experimentation and an abundance of items, armor, and weapons to discover.
I could go on for hours about the creatures, environments, spells, incantations, the subtle lore hidden in item descriptions, and the overall worldbuilding. If anything I’ve mentioned sounds appealing, then I think you should give it a try.

I really want to like Elden Ring as I loved the Souls series and I have tried many times to like it but it has so many issues that I personally have with it that make it not click with me like Demon's Souls or Dark Souls did.

I think my biggest problems are that the open world while it seems cool just doesnt work with Elden Ring so well, if you explore it with no direction, you can end up in areas that feel just straight up unfair and it can be really frustrating to find where you are supposed to go at whatever level you may be at and sometimes you just have to wonder if its a skill issue or if you are genuinely in the wrong place. Ontop of this, if you are a completionist like I am with souls games then it can be really hard to find bosses or areas that you may have missed without needing to pull up a guide every 5 minutes which just feels annoying and tedious for no reason.

Another big problem I have with the game is that the boss designs are just horrid. It feels like they upped the speed of the bosses since Dark Souls 3 to match how quick they were in Sekiro, but the problem with that is that in Sekiro, players were given a parry to avoid damage and tools to exploit any bosses weaknesses, in Elden Ring, you are given nothing to help and while majority of the bosses arent too bad with how spammy they are, they have other issues. Some are way too overused, some are just straight up stupid gimmick fights and some are just straight up boring. Its hard to find bosses in Elden Ring where I sat there and thought to myself "okay this was actually good"

Another issue I have with Elden Ring is the fact that base game co-op is straight up just unplayable and takes away many features without using the seamless co-op mod, they disable your horse in base game and block off a lot of areas so that open world that was a big selling point of the game is just completely gone if you are like me and are someone who loves exploring open world games with others.

Its not all bad though, Elden Ring has some very gorgeous places and backdrops and I genuinely think that the amount of content you get is wholeheartedly worth the full price of the game even if you just played it once. Some of the characters have some very interesting storylines and the replayability is really high with how many weapons, builds and ending you can get. And thats not even counting the DLC.

All and all, I think that Elden Ring is a DECENT game, but I will NEVER understand how people glaze it and say its the best game of all time or anything like that, and if I could I would leave a maybe review but I cant and I personally dont like the game and don't think it lives up to the scores it has or the hype around it.

My review of Elden Ring
After 100 hours!!! And after completing the game 100%

I can say it’s not just a game — it’s a legendary masterpiece! At the very least, it’s a complete game. A world with this level of beauty, scale, depth, and visual variety — from lush, green natural lands to desert regions and volcanic areas, from snowy realms and dragon-infested worlds to even an underground world. From the moment you enter the game, you realize you’re standing before the greatest game of the century — perhaps even the greatest thing ever created in gaming.

The world design is carefully crafted and precise, but nothing surpasses the mastery and precision of the boss fights. Literally, Souls games are the only ones that have perfected boss combat — where you must memorize the boss’s moves, learn their fighting style, and master dodging with the correct timing. And since we mentioned timing, how can we not bring up parrying with shields — a unique and excellent feature in Souls / Souls-like games.

The story has a depth that pulls you into deep thought, and the soundtracks transport you to another world, making the experience even more incredible. The variety of weapons — from magic, swords, bows, and spears — along with the diversity of skills (Ashes of War), adds even more richness. By the way, the game isn’t primarily based on magic, yet it contains hundreds of spells — meaning it even surpasses games that are built around magic, like Hogwarts Legacy.

I don’t even know how to describe the greatness of the bosses to you. You’ll face some of the greatest bosses in Souls games — I’m talking about General Radahn, the Starscourge, descendant of war, the Red Lion, breaker of kings, shedder of blood. And I’m talking about Malenia, Lady of the Sword, the undefeated Blade of Miquella, the lone flower of the Elden. And not to mention Godfrey, the first Elden Lord, warrior of kings, breaker of thrones, the White Lion, the embodiment of raw power.

The game is difficult and gives you nothing easily, but it rewards every effort you put in and every skill you learn. Every step is calculated, every decision carries weight, every moment is full of excitement, and every minute you spend in the game is a unique experience.

Elden Ring is the crown of gaming. It doesn’t just deserve Game of the Year — it deserves Game of the Century.
They made this masterpiece in just 5 years, which is honestly insane. Even the biggest studios couldn’t pull off something like this in that time.
And yeah, I don’t regret spending a single penny on this game. Thanks, FromSoftware.

It is not perfect, and it certainly is not for everyone, but it is incredible, and I haven't played anything quite like it.

My PC playthrough has been fun, the DLC is truly amazing (although I do have some complaints), and 60fps is like taking off ankle weights, but sadly stutter is a very real issue for this game, and that is something that should've been fixed long before now. Maybe it's just my pc though.

This is one of my personal favorite games ever. I adore the way this game does combat, and how dynamic it can be. There are so many possibilities for how to overcome EACH problem you encounter on account of this being an open world game. Between TONS of different weapons and consumables, and the myriad of different skills you can choose to specialize in, you're not going to run out of new things to experiment with in combat.

If you're a Dark Souls 3 fan, the game has the fast-paced combat style of that game, with that signature style of high-octane boss battles.
If you're a Dark Souls 2 fan, you'll be happy to see how many things they carried over from that game. Like water making lightning do more damage and power-stancing weapons.
If you're never played a Fromtsoftware game before.... you're still in good hands! This game is far more accessible than any other "Souls" title before it.
If you've never played a video game before in your entire life... you're probably gonna struggle a bit, but I have faith in you regardless!

The difficulty is also relative in this game, more so than in any previous Fromsoftware game, in my opinion. Instead of reaching a boss and being unable to progress further until you beat it... in Elden Ring, you can just go somewhere else. Don't like how Margit is extinguishing your flames of ambition? Just leave. Literally go to a new area, leveling up as you fight new enemies and gather new gear, then return WAY stronger and destroy him!

It's kind of hard to write a review that's just me praising the game with no real complaints, since I think a review should show off a game's good and bad sides for the potential buyer to see. But genuinely, I think this game is phenomenal. The only complaint I would have is... by the end you'll be wishing there was more, even if that one playthrough took a hundred hours. Oh, and maybe "Malenia, Blade of Miquella" too. Not a big fan of her.

Good luck out there, fellow Tarnished.

100/10 would get emotionally destroyed again.

I genuinely love it. It’s been an amazing journey as a Tarnished so far, and I’m not even halfway through yet.

This game will humble you real quick. You’ll lose 100 times and win once but that one win? That single victory after getting your soul crushed repeatedly? Pure dopamine. Absolute cinema. Worth every desk slap and silent rage moment.

Every evening, after getting back from work, I would say, “Let's just play for an hour before hitting the bed”, which turns out to be the biggest lie. You log in at 10 PM, next thing you know it’s 4 AM and you’re fighting for your life, questioning your existence, and somehow still saying “one more try.”

Also, you will have your "oops" moments, hence, don’t forget the multiple “oops” moments where you realize you messed something up and end up restarting parts of your journey, resetting hours of progress like it’s nothing. Character building. Definitely not pain. 

Yes, I’m talking about the guy who keeps calling you “maidenless” right at the start.

Important advice from someone who learned the hard way:
This game does NOT come with a side quest guidebook. There are no hand-holding quest markers. No “go here, do this.” Just vibes and consequences.

So please, don’t jump in and start attacking every non-hostile NPC you see.
Some of them are out here offering quests, lore, rewards, and you’re out here committing accidental war crimes.

Anyway, enjoy the grind. Embrace the suffering. Question your life choices.

You came for a game.
You stayed for the trauma.

And somehow, through all the chaos, frustration, and questionable decisions, you’ll still end up smiling after a big win, proud of how far you’ve come.

And yeah it's definitely worth it, after finish up the game, you’ll probably boot it up again tomorrow.

[h1]For My First FromSoftware Title, quite the journey. 9/10[/h1]

The FromSoftware games were always something I had always wanted to play, but never really got the chance to. They are games that I have always watched people play, whose lore I have occasionally watched, but whose Soulslikes such as Code Vein, Blasphemous, and Hollow Knight/Silksong were what I generally played.

I am overall fairly familiar with the many... [i]quirks[/i] these games provide, and it was only because this game was a gift that I was able to play this game. This makes it my first ever FromSoftware title. At the time of writing, I do not own the DLC for this game. I mainly played Offline, and only really turned on Online Mode to see funny messages and to complete a couple of side quests.

So where does that leave me? At the time of writing I have just beaten the final boss of the game and achieved the [spoiler]The Age of Stars[/spoiler] ending.

The Stat Spread at the end of my playthrough are as follows (these are with certain kinds of gear you will find throughout your playthrough):
[list]
[*]Level 136
[*]Vigor 55
[*]Mind 13
[*]Endurance 41
[*]Strength 65
[*]Dexterity 20
[*]Intelligence 10
[*]Faith 21
[*]Arcane 10
[/list]

So Elden Ring could be summarized as Dark Souls, but Open-World. The Lands Between had some extremely beautiful locations, challenging bosses, and [i]so[/i] many secrets to find that I wasn't able to find them all in my first playthrough.

I also generally played on High Settings, and only experienced stuttering in the late game areas and 2 bosses. Only had 1 game crash, 60hrs in.

I went with primarily a Strength, Dex, build in the early game; but late game I basically messed around with Strength, Dex, and Faith. I do like using summons, and did so for pretty much every important boss fight in the game, yet I did not equip a single spell or incantation. I didn't use an Ash of War until the 70hr mark (around level 80 for me) and the flask that gives buffs until basically 90hrs in (level 130). By base game standards and talking with peers, I was pretty overleveled for dealing with the final boss; ending at level 136. My starting class was the Wretched Class, so I started at level 1 and all of my stats were 10. No armor, and only a club. I figured this would give me an unbiased look at the game instead of gearing me to a specific playstyle as I had no idea how or when I could respec my stats.

I can say with confidence that I have a massive skill issue when it comes to recognizing enemy attack patterns, dodge rolling, and parrying. I basically fell for every single feint the bosses did and several of them took at least 10 attempts to complete. Yet through the power of perseverance, summons, and being over-leveled it is certainly possible to complete the base game. This is most certainly a game that is not for everyone, but I think one's ability to stick with it would provide an incredible experience.

I only really have 2 major issues with this game:
[list]
[*]Not being able to fast travel out of Catacomb/Cave system sucks. Generally, I had found myself dying in these, but I always had to walk out of them. Sometimes these underground areas are the closest Fast Travel Point to where I want to go; but this usually means that I had to wait for an elevator to come down, then ride it all the way back up only to then fast travel.

[*]The overworld map needed to have more layers to it. Several Fast Travel Points are technically underground or indoors despite being on the overworld map, and I had frequently gotten mixed up with which points I wanted to go. In general, I do wish the maps also showcased interiors; but I am sure that is just a me thing.
[/list]
If I had to give some tips for newcomers, it would be the following:
[list]
[*]Don't be afraid to run away from a fight
[*]Not every boss is required to beat the game
[*]Explore to your heart's content
[*]Don't be afraid to look up some things like item locations or dungeon navigations.
[*]Summons are cool to use and don't be discouraged by other people you call you bad for using them. This is a mainly single player experience, and you get to decide how to play it.
[/list]

Elden Ring is not just a game—it is a landmark achievement in modern game design, a culmination of decades of refinement in action RPG mechanics blended with an unparalleled sense of discovery. From the very first moment you step into the Lands Between, the game establishes a tone of mystery, scale, and quiet grandeur that few titles in gaming history have ever matched. It doesn’t hold your hand, it doesn’t bombard you with instructions, and it certainly doesn’t rush you. Instead, it trusts you—and that trust is what makes the experience so powerful.

At its core, Elden Ring succeeds because of its open-world design. Unlike many open-world games that feel bloated with repetitive tasks and markers, Elden Ring’s world is dense with meaning. Every ruin on the horizon, every strange structure tucked into a cliffside, every glowing item in the distance feels intentional. Exploration is not a checklist—it’s a genuine adventure. You are not guided by quest logs or GPS markers, but by curiosity. That sense of organic exploration brings back a feeling that many players haven’t experienced since childhood: the thrill of not knowing what lies ahead.

The combat system is another pillar of its greatness. It builds on the precise, punishing mechanics that FromSoftware has perfected over the years, but expands them with greater flexibility and creativity. Whether you prefer heavy melee weapons, agile dexterity builds, powerful sorceries, or hybrid playstyles, Elden Ring allows you to shape your character in meaningful ways. Every enemy encounter feels deliberate, and every victory feels earned. The difficulty is often discussed, but what truly defines it is fairness—when you fail, you understand why, and when you succeed, it’s because you adapted and improved.

Then there are the bosses—arguably some of the most memorable encounters in gaming. Each one feels like a test, not just of skill, but of patience and observation. They are visually stunning, mechanically diverse, and emotionally impactful. Some feel tragic, others terrifying, and a few even awe-inspiring. The game doesn’t just throw obstacles at you; it presents challenges that feel like legends within the world itself.

The atmosphere and world-building elevate Elden Ring even further. The Lands Between feel ancient, broken, and layered with history. There is a sense that everything you see has a story behind it, even if it’s not immediately explained. The game’s storytelling is subtle and environmental, encouraging players to piece together the lore through item descriptions, dialogue, and observation. This approach respects the player’s intelligence and rewards those who choose to dive deeper.

Visually, the game is breathtaking—not necessarily because of cutting-edge graphics, but because of its art direction. From golden fields bathed in sunlight to haunting underground cities lit by ghostly stars, every area feels distinct and memorable. The soundtrack complements this perfectly, shifting from quiet, ambient tones during exploration to intense, dramatic compositions during boss fights.

What truly sets Elden Ring apart, however, is how all of these elements come together into a cohesive experience. It is not just a collection of great systems—it is a world that feels alive, mysterious, and worth investing in. It respects the player’s time, intelligence, and curiosity in a way that few modern games do.

In an industry often driven by trends and formulas, Elden Ring stands as a bold reminder of what games can be when developers prioritize vision and craftsmanship. It doesn’t try to appeal to everyone in a conventional way; instead, it commits fully to its identity—and in doing so, it becomes something extraordinary.

Elden Ring is not just one of the best games of its generation—it is a defining moment in gaming history. A rare masterpiece that will be remembered, studied, and celebrated for years to come.

Probably because it seemed like such a tall order to talk about everything that makes this game good, so instead, I'll try to just hit the major beats. Elden Ring is Miyazaki/Fromsoft's Mangum Opus. This game is the absolute manifestation of perfection in gaming.

As a fairly new player to the souls-like genre, I was worried initially. Not that I wouldn't like the game, I was rather worried about mechanical confusion. I was worried about the fact that I couldn't understand the game. This primarily stems from the fact that the lack of guidance can be problematic. That doesn't mean I want the game to literally take me by my hand and lead me to the ending, but complete lack of guidance makes the game less enjoyable for me. Elden Ring balances this perfectly. Yes, there were some things that required research, mainly new mechanics, but the guidance is firm and telling enough to give me breathing space. The game clearly tells you "go in that direction, and you will progress in some way", and then hints at what is optional. Its not written anywhere clearly, like in a quest log, but there are subtle and simple ways of guiding you that do not spoil you the game.

Something that should also be noted is the method of storytelling. I had to learn this externally, but the game does not "tell a story" through collectibles, which is boring. The game tells a story by the environment. Almost everything in this game has a reason for its location, appearance, and behavior. Bosses tend resemble their personalities in the way they move, attack, speak, everything. The environment is shaped in such ways to tell a story. An NPC being concealed doesn't have to be just a visual decision, it can resemble something deeper and important. Not a lot of games take it to such a depth and often things looks the way "just because they were designed that way". A knight can have a very consistent pattern of attacking that does not change, because it literally "keeps calm". A teacher can test you, be consistent, and incredibly calm, but then once you fight his "real self", he throws away the composure, and becomes much more violent and desperate.

The game does not have a perfectly linear gameplay, but it does not fail at "telling where is the main progress" either. if a fight feels too hard, you should come back later once you are stronger. Or you can switch up your strategy and lure the enemy somewhere. Weapons are not perfectly universal, and tend to have specific uses for specific situations. So holding onto one single weapon is not very ideal here, because experimenting is rewarded.

A common complaint I see is the difficulty of this game. And I agree this game is difficult, but there is also a clear distinction between "difficult, because RNG", and "difficult, because of complex mechanics". there are games that are difficult only because of RNG, meaning you barely control the outcomes, the random elements do instead. These games tend to be much more frustrating, because you can learn only a very limited range of things, because there is so much outside of your control. But here? The game is not difficult, because of a ton of elements that you basically cannot control. The game is difficult, because of mechanical complexity. Bossfights, for example, are difficult, because you need to learn patterns. Learn patterns, recovery windows, read the enemy movement, tune your equipment,...  Each death that happens has a clear reason. If you happen to die, you always know why and what killed you. The visual clarity is strong enough that you notice it and physically see it. This is the type of difficulty that is much less random and actually is fair. A boss can be extreme hard, but still can be extremely fun, even if you repeatedly die over and over. You never have to deal with the boss being extremely random and unpredictable. This is the closes to a skill-based game you can ever get.

Yes, there are downsides. Especially in the engine. The game is obviously meant to be played with a controller, and on a console. That does not mean its unplayable on a keyboard, I would say the experience is pretty okay, but some keybinds can feel weird, and you may need to change them. The game is also permanently locked at 60fps, so your 1000hz monitor is useless here. And while unlocking it is possible, it can have some unpredictable outcomes, like some animations breaking, or acting weirdly. Not to mention that the engine is not really suited to hyper-optimize games. Foliage can be an issue, mainly around forests and trees. It can lower your fps on high settings, despite having capable hardware. I would also enjoy a bit better explanations of some systems. Not to necessarily add new explanations to gameplay mechanics, but to rather make the existing ones more clear and understandable.  


In the end I would say that the game is absolutely amazing. Its not often that I get so excited from games, and this one really made me enjoy gaming the same way when I was a young kid completely new to gaming. The price is a little high with small sales, but I would say its definitely worth it!

Overall, the combat lacks polish - enemies hit you through walls and pillars, there are no plunge attacks. It works well when it does, but enemy design quite often draws it back. On the bright side, there's a hand cannon. And crossbows are finally functional.

Quite a few things feel videogamey - every Ruin has exactly one(1) treasure chest. But then there's lore, and aesthetic, and all the actually good areas (though those start rather late).

An Absolute Beast: Fun! Die! Fun! Die! 

Elden Ring is an absolute beast of a game. Fun! Die! Fun! Die! That's the cycle, and I wouldn't have it any other way. There are literally 100 different ways to play this game. Whether you want to be a tanky strength bonk lord, a flashy mage raining death from afar, a dex bleed ninja, or some unhinged faith/incantation build — the game supports it all. The build variety and freedom keep it fresh even after dozens of hours.I killed way too many rats hunting for Rune Arcs (seriously, those little bastards became my personal nemesis), but other than that... no real grind. No tedious farming sessions that suck the soul out of you. You can just explore, fight, and level up naturally as you go. Some of the "easiest" moments were actually the hardest. And don't even get me started on gravity — that invisible boss has killed me more times than any actual enemy in the Souls series. Falling off cliffs, ledges, or just misjudging a jump in the middle of nowhere... classic. The world is massive and packed with secrets. Every new area feels like a discovery, and the boss fights range from "holy crap this is beautiful" to "I want to throw my controller." The open-world freedom means you can completely avoid (or come back way overleveled for) the things that frustrate you. If you're into challenging action RPGs with insane replayability, breathtaking exploration, and that sweet "I finally beat it" dopamine hit after dying 10 times, this is peak gaming. Just be ready to laugh at your own deaths — especially the ones caused by the environment. Highly Recommended. Twin Peaks thumbs Up.

Best game I've ever played. Not even close.

Miyazaki built something that doesn't feel like a game sometimes. The world is connected in a way that makes you feel like you're discovering something real. You walk into a new area and the atmosphere alone tells you what happened there before you read a single item description. The lore is scattered everywhere and when you finally piece it together it hits harder than any story that was just handed to you.

You start in Limgrave thinking this is the whole game. Then you beat Godrick and step into Liurnia and just stop. The scale hits you instantly. Then Raya Lucaria appears and somehow blends Harry Potter and Halloween and Bloodborne into one place and it works perfectly. Then you clear it and walk into Altus Plateau and a royal orchestra starts playing and you see the capital in the distance with the Erdtree towering over everything and you realize you haven't even scratched the surface.
And I didn't even mention Nokron, Eternal City, Nokstella, Eternal City, Siofra River, Ainsel River, Lake of Rot, Deeproot Depths,Mohgwyn Palace...

The exploration never stops doing that to you. Every time I wanted to quit I told myself just one more area just check that one spot and suddenly hours were gone. The dungeons the caves the open world are all designed in a way that makes discovery feel addictive. I spent 200+ hours on a single playthrough without NG+ leaving no corner unexplored no item behind. Not 100% completion. I did Something harder than that.

From the crumbling towers of Farum Azula to the rot-soaked beauty of Elphael every area has its own identity. You don't just travel through these places you feel them. And through all of it you're just a Tarnished with nothing slowly becoming something the entire world thought was impossible.

Then Messmer opened his mouth. "Those stripped of the grace of gold shall all meet death in the embrace of Messmer's flame." I sat there for a second just processing that.

The OST doesn't play fair. You reach Radagon the final boss of the base game and the music starts. Then it hits you. That theme is a reimagined version of the main menu track. FromSoftware told you how this story ends before you even started playing and you never noticed. There's no word for that feeling.

Promised Consort Radahn's theme in the DLC does the same thing differently. It hits like a war anthem and never lets go.

Combat is punishing but never cheap. You die because you made a mistake and deep down you know it. That's what separates it from everything else.

Every open world game feels hollow after this. Every RPG feels like it's missing something. Miyazaki figured out something that nobody else has and probably never will.

Nothing else comes close.

TL;DR:
A beautifully crafted open world with exceptional combat variety and style along with environments that are bound to leave you startstruck. However, obscure NPC questlines and lack of in-game tracking can make for a frustrating time without external tools if you are looking to explore all.

Detailed Review:

Pros:
- Boss fights feel like an intricate dance, with clear punish windows while still subverting expectations on subsequent attempts with their delayed or unpredictable attacks.
- Excellent build diversity, especially hybrid/quality builds like Faith-Arcane or Strength-Intelligence.
- Stunning, vast landscapes that encourage exploration due to the mystique they carry.
- Dungeons are generally well-designed, with occasional unique gimmicks that break monotony and keep it fresh.

Cons:
- NPC questlines are rather obscure and difficult to follow organically.
- No in-game checklist or tracking for collected items, making completionist runs unnecessarily reliant on external tools like MapGenie (Scadutree Fragments I'm looking at you).
- Just like any other FromSoftware game, ELDEN RING also doesn't explain much about its mechanics making it difficult to recommend to a lot of casual players. 

Shadow of the Erdtree DLC:
A very vertical and puzzle like map layout makes it very interesting but also frustrating to navigate the Land of Shadows. The performance is overall worse compared to the base game and a lot of bosses like to do attacks which are too long (almost like cutscenes). Despite all of that, the beautiful landscapes, more weapon variety and a good story made it quite engaging for me.

This is an excellent game for players of a particular sort: 
A. You like a game with a rich open world feel. The landscape is sumptuously rendered and can be interesting to explore.
B.  You do not want what fans call "hand holding" your way through the adventure. There is little intuitive about what the player is to do next other than a general cardinal direction.  ("Hand holding" also applies to understanding the interface of the game which is not especially intuitive unless you have played other Dark Souls games.)
C. You like pointlessly hacking and slashing your way through enemies for the only reward to level up" so you can defeat more challenging enemies until there are no more enemies to defeat.


As for A, Elden Ring is in the class with the very best games of the sort, Skyrim, BG3, Dragon Age, etc.

Regarding B, there can be much appeal to this philosophy.  However, unless one has countless hours to devote to exploration and experimentation, the feature can be frustrating. This is especially true regarding the interface and menu systems if one is new to the Dark Souls way of doing things. For example, multiple icons appear on the screen announcing some aspect of the gameplay, but with zero tutorials, there is no way of knowing what these mean or how to take advantage of them. HP, Mana, Stamina, are pretty commonly understood for anyone who has ever played a video game. Of the dozen or so other indicators, there is little intuitive about how to interpret them. In addition, Menu items and inventory control is vast.  That could be a good thing. Knowing how to manipulate and change items in your inventory, it will take you awhile.  Of course, the player always has the option to consult the various player guides and walkthroughs for help, but: 1. That defeats the purpose of no "hand holding: in the first place. 2. The interfaces are so complicated the guides are sometimes hard to follow even still.

As for C, my personal taste is that progress in the game only by killing virtually everything that moves is an unimaginative approach to game design. It lacks subtlety that better games employ to create an intriguing storyline. There is never any banter that gives the fights scenes emotional value - leveling up is pretty much the one and only point. There is never any negotiating with an adversary to obtain your reward without a fight.  95% of the living characters are out to kill you on sight. The other 5% only provide you information or an item of need, but rarely with any condition or side quest. There is virtually no subtlety here.  The closest to subtlety is that when you are underpowered, you can sometimes sneak past the bad guy to obtain the reward. For my preference, the Cardinal Sin of Elden Ring is it takes itself so seriously. There is a dearth of whimsy or humor. Out of thousands of NPCs with which I have interacted, only one made me laugh. 15 seconds out of 58 hours provides a really grim world and experience.

When it first came out, Skyrim was much like this. However, fans developed mods to add some entertaining NPCs and side-quests. Over the the years, Skyrim became a much better game. but Elden Ring makes modding cumbersome, as opposed to BG3 which incorporates modding into the interface, and Skyrim which incorporated fan mods into the later editions.

One final aspect of the game bears noting. Leveling up requires the player to collect "souls," hence all the killing. However, if you die in a battle, you lose the soul point you have collected.  On the plus side, this requires to player to plan strategically, especially since you cannot save before entering a fight as with so many other games.  It creates a unique challenge to gameplay. However, the downside is it promotes a "use it or lose it" approach to resource management and  an excess of passivity and reluctance to experiment in gameplay.  This appeal to some because it gives each battle higher stakes, but is also frustrating when player  has worked an hour to build up enough resources to level up and then loses it all.   Add to this, that the game is glitchy.  I have had it freeze up in the middle of a battle in which I was doing well to find on rebooting, I had "lost" the battle and my resource along with it.

BOTTOM LINE.  Very pretty game. The kinds of frustration it creates will appeal to some, but turn off others.  It lacks any motivation that appeals to human emotion other than self aggrandizement of killing others to get to the top. It engages no human emotion other than simplistic greed. In Elden Ring you'll have to trial and error what you can parry/block/roll/or jump over the game will not tell you. Which is fine, but most late game bosses have almost endless poise and stamina so they never really stop flailing. Hell, almost most endgame area basic enemies have infinite stamina it feels. 

The absolute death nail for this game being so frustrating is frame trap attacks. Now I think the most egregious frame traps have been fixed that are unfair by the devs standards. IE consort Radahn stuff, but most bosses just get so many damn free hits on you. They'll hit you somehow on the initial downswing of a sword or slam attack even though the attack is no where near you. Any weapons based enemy or boss has parry and dodge timings are all over the map. Sometime its the start of the swing or it could be the very end of it. You just don't know and there are so many areas and enemies that as a normal person you never get good naturally at this combat system. 

Bosses move so damn much in this game it makes The Dancer from DS3 look like its in slow mo. I think I spent more time getting rolled around and chasing the boss in this game than I did fighting and enjoying the dodging and learning attacks. I remember hearing about Elden Ring for the first time in 2022. A lot of my friends hyped the game up as one of the greatest of all time. and ranted and raved about how innovative it was.  I had never played a "souls-like" game in my life and thus wasn't very interested. Fast forward to ~2024, I started to dip my toes in the genre. My first was a game called Mortal Shell. I liked it. Then I played through Sekiro (also from fromsoft) in 2025 but got hard-stuck on the final boss. 

In 2026, I decided to try Elden Ring for the first time. I bought it on sale for I think around 30 dollars. From the first couple hours, I was totally entranced by this game. My friends were not kidding - this game is legitimately a modern masterpiece.

The Pros:
The map is absolutely shockingly massive. The overworld map alone feels much larger than any other game I have ever played. And then you find out about the wells, and realize "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, It gets even bigger." Most games that have large maps have long stretches of barren, lifeless areas that artificially increase the size. Not Elden Ring. Not at all. EVERY area of the game is not only breath-takingly beautiful, but also filled to the brim with unique structures that even transform and change as you reach milestones in the game's story.

There are hundreds of unique enemies, mini-bosses, and bosses to fill in the aforementioned map. Exciting, challenging encounters lay waiting around every corner to be discovered by the player. You'll be walking through a dungeon, and all of a sudden - "WHOA WHAT THE F**K IS THAT THING" - you'll be attacked by an abomination. Skeletons. Lizards. Dragons, Worm people. Dogs. Crazy villagers. etc. Each enemy and boss has their own unique attacks and animations and it absolutely never gets old. It is a very refreshing change from most modern video games, that largely reuse the same "pool" of attacks and animations without really caring about the gameplay becoming boring.

What's the point of enemies without weapons, right? Good news - Elden Ring has hundreds of unique ones to choose from, most of which can be further modified with "ashes of war" found throughout the game. You want to wield a battle-axe that makes people bleed? Done. What about a sword that freezes enemies? Done. What about a giant hammer that poisons? Done. The customization is borderline limitless. And the armor in this game is largely the same way. There are tons of different sets to choose from or mix and match, that raise certain attributes to fit your particular playstyle. No matter how you want to play, this game has options for YOU which is awesome and shows they really deeply thought about the combat from an early stage of development.

The voice acting in this game is another thing I'd like to highlight. It is absolutely perfect. Every enemy. Every boss. Every NPC. There were many times during this game that the voice acting gave me chills - which is very rare  for me and especially in video games- such as mohg's "NIHIL! NIHIL! NIHIL!" or Godrick's "Forefathers one and all, bear witness!" This game FEELS like you as the player are actually living in this huge fantasy landscape. It's amazing.



The cons:
It pains me to really say anything negative about this game because I, like many others, consider it a legitimate modern masterpiece to gaming. However, with that being said, there are a few things I must critique.

The storyline, while there, certainly feels a little bit lacking to me. The developers absolutely give you bits and pieces of a story throughout the game but it is largely through experiencing the world and going to different areas. It feels a little bit disjointed and confusing at times.

Some particular bosses in this game have legitimate "Guaranteed hit" moves. It's a souls-like game, so of course there's going to be stuff like that and what I'm about to say isn't a "major" critique but remains true to me. I feel like a lot of bosses (particularly late game bosses) should be a little more choreographed than what they are. Some bosses are programmed to essentially do "random mix ups" meaning they can chain an attack with another attack or this other attack or this other attack. They essentially randomly pick from a set of moves. In theory this is cool, until you encounter a boss like Mohg, lord of blood or Malenia and then you want to smash your controller into bits and pieces. You are going to be hit by a lot of attacks that will have you going "wait a second, that wasn't even close to me wtf" and you aren't tripping. Some attacks really, literally, can look or feel as though they are clearly dodged and just.... aren't. On the flip-side, some attacks are virtually guaranteed regardless of how you want to dodge/roll. Malenia's "waterfowl dance" is a perfect example of this. Although *technically* dodge-able, if you are close to her when she does it? Son... It's over. There are memes online that say the best thing you can do when she does waterfowl close range is to just exit and try the run again until you get a tamer mix-up and lowkey?....... they're accurate LMFAO. I just really wish that wasn't the case. Your success, particularly in late-game bosses, often feels like you're just waiting for a fight where they don't do X attack or don't have such punishing mix-ups. The fight that I finally killed Malenia she only did waterfowl once in phase 2. There were other fights where she'd do it 4-5 times and again, if you get a fight like that (which mind you is rng) it is ACTUALLY just over unless you're a perfect god with thousands of hours on these types of games. Again, not a major critique because it's a souls-like game - just a personal preference. I like bosses that have more choreographed attacks. If this part is putting you off from trying this game - Don't worry! This game has lots of fights that are fairly choreographed and very fun!! There are only really 3-5 bosses in the whole game that I would consider just outright unfair in the sense that your success is literally just waiting for good rng. And believe me, when you run into them in your journey... you'll know. (lol)

My only other gripe with this game is how it does quests. I considered tying this part in with the storyline critique but my issue is with characters that aren't necessarily "needed" for the story and thus I feel it deserves it's own section. A lot of the quests in this game are - and I am not exaggerating in the slightest - Find X character here at random location on the map. Then talk to them and find them here in totally different area opposite side of the map. Then talk to them and find them here in this totally unrelated area of the map opposite to that. If you want to do a particular ending or just help particular npcs - you will 100% without a doubt need to search up how to do some things. I personally wanted to save Melina from her death and so I did Hyetta's questline. It was horrifically painful to experience before I succumbed to using google for help. Her questline in particular is absolute, total dogs*it so much so that it's actually unbelievable. Her questline involves an invisible door that you open with a pressure plate some place in a random dungeon on the map. For real. I am not exaggerating.(LMFAO) Remember how I said that you will need google for certain parts? I really mean that. I don't think it is actually possible as a solo player to find certain things without it. And I got to say - that right there is my biggest critique about this game. Even if the developers included vague dialogue like  "I'm going to the mountains of ____" or something just to give the player a general idea of where to look for them to advance their quest would be all they would need to do to fix this. 

All in all, Elden Ring is an absolutely INCREDIBLE game. Despite having a few cons, I believe the pros vastly outweigh them. It is one of the best games of all time, and I would have paid double full price if I had known.

Nothing to love. From the fist King's Field From games were complete, whole: with philosophy, questions, logic. This game has only content, no author's questions, it's just a product, it's not art. This game has no soul. Because of that there is no reason to explore it. There is nobody to talk to (I mean author's voice, author is mute!), no statement, no argument, no mystery. Nothing. Just endless Santa Barbara. Who are all these characters? Who cares? From was making adult non-indy games until now. They were like the only one who were doing that. And now, it's gone.
