My journey with soulslikes started right here with Elden Ring. The world is masterfully crafted brutal, harsh, mysterious, and filled with stunning locations. Unlike many other titles, this game doesnt treat the player like an idiot. The obscure side quests add a lot of flavor, theres zero chance you wont miss something during your first playthrough. The combat system is excellent, with beautiful animations and spectacular effects for spells and incantations. While the difficulty especially the overused delayed attacks can be off putting at first, the game becomes even more enjoyable once you master the mechanics. As an RPG fan, the open world really spoke to me, though I understand its not for everyone. Personally I think it gives the game much higher replayability than the linear Dark Souls titles, as every new run can feel completely different.

Now, what you really need to look out for is the lack of a save anywhere feature... just kidding! Honestly, one of the main issues is those previously mentioned delayed attacks practically every single enemy has them! Another downside is the heavy boss recycling. I would also point out that the rewards for clearing catacombs are often unsatisfying, usually just being spirit summons. And finally, optimization issues? Im not sure what to call it exactly, but there are micro stutters that can ruin a fight. I dont think its a hardware issue, even after upgrading from an RTX 2060 to a 5060 Ti 16GB and from an i5-10400F to an i7-11700K, absolutely nothing changed in that regard. Interestingly, these stutters dont occur at all on a handheld like the Lenovo Legion Go.

Overall, I highly recommend it, a game easily worth hundreds of hours. Definitely in my top 10.

When I first played Elden Ring, I thought it was great, but not necessarily one of my favorite games. A big part of that is that I have a ton of respect for the world design of the original Dark Souls, and I feel like Elden Ring's Open World can lose a lot of the marvelously layered world design that makes Dark Souls legendarily fun to explore. The fact of the matter is that this is partially the case, but it is part of what makes Elden Ring legendary. 

Elden Ring is one of the greatest Dungeon Crawlers of all time. Most people do not think of it as one, but it is. Sure, the open world is gorgeous and well-designed, but I actually find its endless vaults and tombs to be marvelously compelling. The better designed "Legacy Dungeons" are obviously great, but this game is a fantastically fun one to play through when you delve below the earth to see what's hidden in the old and forgotten places. I imagine that it's only better with some sort of randomizer and I cannot wait for the days when I've forgotten enough about Elden Ring to by surprised by it once again.

From the creators of Bloodyborne and Dark Souls, you essentially get a glorified dating sim that is confusedly also an open world RPG. The areas are vast and beautiful yet the main attractions remain the women in this game. You have Ranni the Witch. I don't need to tell you how popular she is. Let's just say 4373 is a large number for people dedicating "art posts" to her. Then you have Melina, your first maiden. That childhood friend/neighbor girl character who has been helping you along the way throughout out your quests and just waiting for you to notice her. Soft spoken yet meaningful in her words and easy on the eyes. Just don't show her the three fingers, she's not into that...Then you have Fia. The deathbed companion. The character you go to after dying to the boss over and over again. Why? Because if you can't feel the warmth of a woman's body in real life, might as well pretend to feel it in a triple AAA game from Miyazaki. And to maintain realism, whenever you hug her you get debuffed, just like how it feels to hug women in real life; it doesn't last long, its lackluster, and you keep coming back for more while losing your grip on reality. Then you have Hyetta. She's the gal with an appetite. Feed her some grapes and she'll be over the moon. Feed her enough, and she will show you her three fingers (pun intended). You also have the amazon goddess of snoo snoo herself, Nepheli...the one with daddy issues. I know Gideon said he "adopted her" but...cmon. The guy who is all knowing wouldn't know how to court a barbarian women? Really?. That aside, the cutest one...the tsundere that sets your heart on fire...Dung Eater-chan. I swear...his eyes are as brown as the left over basketball sized chocolate mud babies I leave in my toilet after a hearty Taco Bell breakfast. A character of rigour and personality. 

The characters are as diverse as the regions you play in. The weapons are unique and all usable up to end game. The only regret I have with this game is not being able to continually fight bosses like you could in Sekiro for example. That was a huge missed opportunity. 

TLDR: You either get frame Moghed or you mew hard enough to be Elden Lord. In essence, a game I will never put down and the true successor to Dark Souls.

I don't understand why people say souls games aren't hard. They are definitely hard when you are underprepared, which happens alot if you haven't played these games before. But they can extremely easy if you are overprepared without limiting yourself (farming, memorization, etc). Honestly, play how you want to play, don't dwell too much on the challenge from these types games because it differs from player to player (personally i hate the enemies that don't stop attacking). Don't compare difficulties of other games to this. Nor is this game too hard because its bearable. In the end, its an adapt to game or suffer. 

That being said, this is far from my ideal type of game due to lack of creativity for the player near the end of the game when they max out their stats. The atmosphere really good but I started to get tired of fighting similar bosses. Using the Serpent Spear on Rykard was so amazing (maybe I like whacking large bosses) but not having any of that feeling at the end of the game felt underwhelming (chasing the final boss feels annoying than hard)? At some point I started to spam either Carian slicer or Zamor Ice Storm and its hard to change the build because the other spells are kinda butt tbh (and changing builds requires an investment which is kinda weird to me). And no, Horseback battles with Torrent is cool only for a few fights.

Lastly, how do people play this game blind sometimes? there is so many missable items, quests, events, etc (YES THAT INCLUDES THE STORY ITSELF), and be able to lock yourself out of. It might be little obvious sometimes but finding that one random npc to start the quest or learning that event that locks you out of ending isn't fun (atleast to me). Some say that gameplay should come first before the story but I find it best when they come hand to hand. They just feed you bosses but its up to the player to come across and piece together the story, but I struggle to fill in the cracks for the story sometimes. So don't think I could talk about the story itself.

Its a 8/10, had a pretty fun time, reading player messages, watching cutscenes, exploring the world (the best part of the game), listening to the godlike ost, etc. Idk if this is a hot take but I wish the game was shorter (more areas for using Torrent and less areas with elevators or ladders).

Elden Ring is a disappointing experience. I recently completed both Dark Souls 1 and 3 (I'm not an expert by any means) and went on excitedly to play Elden Ring but it ended up being a huge mistake. This game is pretty and the story is at least interesting and I understand why the masses would like this game but having played it myself I think it's not a bad game per say but it is not a good Souls game. The open world structure actually feels detrimental to the game and sometimes the exploration can be very confusing (especially the Rauh Ruins in the dlc that are easily the worst offender in that regard). The enemies drop very little runes which ended up being a problem as it meant this game was the first Souls where I ended up having to farm levels to progress. The difficulty feels very artificial as well, from the midgame onward the enemies feel very spongy, have a ton of poise and deal a huge amount of damage, so much so that it's common to get two shotted in the end game. As for the bosses, they usually have a very cheap attack pattern where they attack a lot very fast and deal a truckload of damage, so it's not really a matter of skill issue and more a matter of luck in the latter bosses. There's also a lot of things that feel re-used and areas that feel samey wich is a shame because Dark Souls 1 for instance had some pretty nice diversity in areas in my opinion (granted not all of them). In the end, in my opinion, I feel like you should pass up on this game. It is simply not a good Souls game and the difficulty is way too high for very little reward; in the end, the only real regret I have is that I played too much of this game and I can't get a refund anymore.

the way Souls games chooses to make you build has always been amazing. every combo can be good with the right set up, the longer you play... the stronger and more skilled you will get with that gear.

Elden Ring is a massive achievement, but the difficulty sometimes feels like its coming from the wrong place. After putting in over 100 hours, I have a few thoughts.


The Good: World & Play

The level design is genuinely amazing. The way the world is built is top-tier; these levels are expansive, twisting, and turning into each other in ways that are actually hard to wrap your head around. It’s beautiful to look at, and the enemy variety is awesome. The 'come up' of getting stronger is where it really shines.


The Bad: Controls & "Artificial" Difficulty

I found the controls to be ridiculous, I don't think making a game harder with cumbersome controls is good design. The queue up system for inputs acts so strange that I found myself still making mistakes even after 100+ hours. The amount of times I have accidently dismounted from my horse its unbelievable, call me bad, but this is my experience.

Bad physics isn't a puzzle, it's just frustrating. Same goes for some of the site of grace layouts; tedious for no real gain.


The Ugly: Narrative & Inventory

The story makes very little sense. Call me a smooth brain, but FromSoft just doesn't tell a good story I almost never knew what I was actually doing.. The lack of explanation carries over to items, I have a million things in my inventory, most of which where useless, or that I had no idea how to use. Managing it all was a chore; when the expansion started I had to look up what the first item did. Why?


Multiplayer: PVP & Coop

The PVP was mostly try hards wasting my time, the native coop is quite clucky and I highly recommend Seamless Co-op mod, it made the experience a lot better for me. It removes a ton of the friction from cooperative play.


Performance:

My PC is a literal god computer, and I’m still seeing 40 FPS at times. Lul.


Final Take:

Its a gorgeous, expansive world with fun boss fights, and great multiplayer held back by clunky UI and controls. I still recommend it, its a fun game, but its probably going to piss you off at times.

I will add this preface to my review, now that I have played for sixty hours: 
Everything I wrote below is still true, but the game is absolutely beautyful, and riding around in the world is fantastic. The mounted combat is also quite fun at times, something I don't think any other game has done well.
I will also say that I now believe that some of the problems I mentioned below stem from weird hitboxes, especially on the player character.

I loved Dark Souls 1, and think Dark Souls 2 is a fine but flawed game. Elden Ring is beautiful, but it sucks! Mechanical Death contraptions clip so badly, that you can't solve the puzzle without dying first. Quite a few attacks bypass your shield, without animating the shield actually being pushed aside, and your stamina isn't touched, your hp is just suddenly drained even though your shield should have protected you.

I can't believe From Software released such an unfinished game, and three years later they haven't fixed anything!
Within two hours of playing the game, I lost all desire to ever play a From Software title ever again, and I was really exited to finally try this game.

I have now played three additional hours, and I can say that dodging slow moving ranged attacks apparantly doesn't work for a certain miniboss near the beginning of the game. Did From Software forget to implement quality assurance because they got high?

Many hours later, this game is so full of Bed of Chaos moments, that I'm not sure I will actually want to finish the game.

Also it is absolutely insane that the game is so easy to play as a sorcerer. My two main beginning chararacters are a faith based melee fighter, and a ranged int based magic-user.

I think one of my main complaints with this game, is the lack of visual feedback. In Dark Souls 1 I could visually see why something failed and why my character got hit, that is not the case in this game.

Addendum after having played a lot more. I'm really not sure wether I actually enjoy the game or if I'm continuing because of some weird stubborness.
The clipping in this game is really inexcusable, there are such glaring faults, like when giant creatures clip through entire buildings in the combat arena. Elden Ring is a masterpiece and easily earns a solid 10/10. It takes everything great about FromSoftware’s previous games and expands it into a massive, open-world experience.

The world design is one of its biggest strengths. The Lands Between are vast, mysterious, and full of secrets. Exploration feels rewarding, with hidden areas, bosses, and items around every corner. The sense of discovery is unmatched.

Combat is excellent, offering a wide variety of weapons, builds, and playstyles. Whether you prefer magic, melee, or a mix of both, the game gives you the freedom to play how you want. Boss fights are challenging and memorable, pushing players to improve and adapt.

The atmosphere, music, and art direction are all top-tier, creating a dark and immersive world. The lore is deep and intriguing, even if it’s not always directly explained.

While the game can be difficult and occasionally frustrating, that challenge is part of what makes it so rewarding.

Overall, Elden Ring is an outstanding game with incredible world-building, gameplay, and depth. It stands as one of the best RPGs in recent years.

This game is 4 years old and has made how many millions, yet it has this horrible stuttering issue on my relatively decent rig (RTX 5070/R7 9700X) that made it unplayable. Totally unacceptable. You're better off playing on consoles.

Edit: Ok, I finally managed to fix the stuttering issue. Turning off variable refresh rate in windows graphics settings, and hardware accelerated GPU scheduling for good measure did it for me. So here is my final review.

I enjoyed Elden Ring much more this time around than during my first playthrough. I went in with a few specific protocols because Elden Ring is a game that breaks if you do not cooperate with it.

If you are a thorough explorer, it is easy to trivialize the challenge by over-leveling. To counter this, I spent my accumulated runes on purchasing in-game items instead of levels, by the midpoint of the game, I stopped leveling altogether. Furthermore, your horse, exacerbates an age-old problem in these games by making it easier than ever to run past enemies. To stay engaged, I made a point of fighting any enemies that aggroed toward me.

Because the combat can feel like a stagnant, simplistic system that turns monotonous after a few hours, I constantly respec'd my character to try different builds. Incorporating various Ashes of War and elemental damage types brought much-needed variety to the gameplay. Finally, I found that the 2D map is far too detailed, it spoils the sense of discovery and can turn the game into a Ubisoft-style checklist affair. I ignored the map throughout the entire playthrough, relying on it only for fast travel when resting at a Site of Grace.

With these self-imposed rules in place, Elden Ring is a much more enjoyable experience, making it easier to appreciate the impressive work that went into the open-world design. The world is highly vertical, with constant elevation changes that make the act of navigation inherently interesting. You will rarely traverse a flat, empty expanse for long, instead, there are cliffsides, ravines, and hills everywhere that force decisions and encourage attentiveness. A seemingly flat horizon might suddenly give way to a cliff, and if you are mindlessly galloping on your horse, you will fall to your death.

This same feeling of handcraftedness extends to the visual design. In my Bloodborne review, I commended Fromsoft for creating these cinematic framings while the player maintains total control, whereas other developers resort to wrestling control away from the player and restricting their abilities to achieve a similar end. Fromsoft managed to one-up themselves by replicating this accomplishment in an open-world format. It is incredible how the game can look like a painting from every angle while control of the camera remains entirely in the player's hands.

On top of that, the density of content in the open world is unprecedented, there is simply something to do in every square inch of the map. In the first region alone, you can spend upwards of 30 hours exploring every nook and cranny. If you get tired of the monotony of running around in the open world, there are a number of caves and catacombs you can find through natural discovery. These give you a short burst of that classic, structured Dark Souls experience, complete with traps and ambushes in tight spaces and a boss at the end. This turned out to be an addictive loop to cycle between.

One thing you wouldn't expect to survive the transition to an open world is the impressive enemy variety the Souls series is known for. Elden Ring surprises by filling virtually every sub-region with unique enemy types. Although understandable compromises have been made, even the repeated enemies tend to have unique movesets to make them feel distinct.

While all of that is happening in the open fields, Elden Ring also features these imposing structures that you can view from a distance, which then seamlessly transition into expansive multi-layered dungeons when you get up close. These areas are fully explorable and packed with shortcuts, interesting enemy encounters, secrets to find, and bosses with high-level presentation. Although there are a bit too many sites of grace in these areas for my liking.

Fromsoft wasn't content with this, however, so they hid entire underground regions below this vast surface that already possesses a daunting size. These underground areas themselves contain even more secrets worth dozens of hours of content. This is an insane escalation of what I praised Dark Souls 1 for.

There is so much more to be said about this gargantuan game, which took me a little more than 200 hours to finish. If nothing else, Elden Ring is a monumental achievement due to its sheer scale and its ambition to make the experience feel as curated as a linear game, in spite of its size. For the most part, they accomplished that, but it requires that you negotiate with the game.

Still unforgivable that the game doesn't work perfectly straight out of the box though so be mindful of the technical issues.

[h1] The TL;DR  [/h1]
Elden Ring is what happens when you take the tight, punishing combat of Dark Souls and set it loose in a world that actually rewards your curiosity. It is massive, beautiful, and occasionally makes you want to throw your controller into the sun—and yet, you’ll keep coming back for more.
[hr][/hr]
[h1]The Breakdown[/h1]
[b] 1. Exploration (10/10)[/b] 
Unlike most modern open-world games, there are no "towers" to climb to reveal map icons. You see a weird building on the horizon? You can go there. You see a massive well in the middle of a forest? It probably leads to a literal underground galaxy. The sense of discovery is the best in the industry.
[b] 2. Gameplay & Combat (9/10)[/b] 
Variety: Whether you want to be a colossal-sword-swinging tank, a sneaky assassin, or a wizard nuking bosses from afar, the build variety is staggering.
Difficulty: It is hard. Really hard. However, it’s the most "accessible" Souls game. If a boss is beating you senseless, you can just leave, level up elsewhere, and come back later.
Spirit Summons: A new mechanic that lets you summon AI ghosts to help in fights. It’s a literal godsend for solo players.
[b] 3. Visuals & Atmosphere (10/10)[/b] 
The art direction is carrying the heavy lifting here. Every "Legacy Dungeon" (like Stormveil Castle or Raya Lucaria) feels like a masterpiece of gothic architecture. The scale of the world is genuinely intimidating.
[b] 4. Performance & Technical (7/10)[/b] 
This is the only real "tarnish" on the experience.
PC Port: Still capped at 60 FPS.
Stuttering: Even on high-end rigs, you might see occasional frame drops in specific areas.
Ultrawide: No native support without mods (which disables online play).
[hr][/hr]
[h1]Pros & Cons[/h1]
✅ [b] Pros:[/b] 
Absolute freedom to go anywhere.
The "Horse" (Torrent) feels great to control.
Incredible boss designs (mostly).
Hundreds of hours of content for a single purchase.
❌ [b] Cons:[/b] 
The UI is still a bit clunky (standard for FromSoftware).
Some late-game bosses feel slightly "unfair" with infinite stamina.
The story is told through item descriptions—don't expect a cinematic movie plot.
[hr][/hr]
[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
If you have any interest in RPGs, you owe it to yourself to play this. It doesn't hold your hand, but that’s exactly why winning feels so good.

[h3]Final Score: 10/10 (Masterpiece)[/h3]

I want to preface this review by saying that I have not played Dark Souls or any similar boss-focused fight games, and I am guessing this genre is just not for me, which may color my strong dislike of this game.  I played for 45 minutes before requesting a refund (which I have never done before on a game).

Positives: This game is very beautiful in its environmental production with some stellar fight mechanics.  I can also see how people would get an adrenaline-boost when faced with battling the monster bosses as well as the intellectual challenge of finding ways to overcome their overwhelming power over you.

Negatives: The story is basically Lord of the Rings (which I love) but void of any heart or soul or character ambitions.  The playable character lacks motivation and I do not know what I am trying to accomplish by seeking the Elden Ring.  The game is also extremely difficult, which is fine except that it forces the player to grind hours trying to beat a boss who I don't even understand why I should be trying to defeat.  I could see a scenario where I dedicated hundreds of hours into this game only to achieve nothing, which is why I decided not to waste my time with it.  It is basically fan-fiction for Lord of the Rings where you play as a nameless Easterling (evil man) fighting in Sauron's army and have to defeat all the big-bads of the franchise without even knowing who they are besides their names or what the One Ring does or why you are trying to wield power over it in the first place.

The gameplay is also very repetitive: basically you go and attack something, try to kill it, and then go onto something else to kill, then heal, then often re-kill all of these monsters again and again and again.  And your reward for these battles?  Some random loot that is so difficult to understand it is like getting paid for farm work with NFTs.

If you like hack and slash games without story or purpose, this may be a great time suck for you.  Otherwise, it is truly a waste of your life.

[h1] Elden Ring is one of those games of games. [/h1] 
[h2] Intro [/h2]
Took 150 Hours for me to 100% (and do the DLC). It's about 4 playtrough. I love this game and it is truly one of the games you have to play if you are into souls-like. The first playthrough is a bit rough. It takes a while and you die... a lot. Slowly you understand how the game works and how much exploration there is to do and you begin to lose yourself in the world. I'm 100% sure that i missed a bunch of things in the main game and DLC.

[h2] The Good ! [/h2]
[h3] The Exploration and environment [/h3]
The exploration in this game is truly incredible. HIDDEN STUFF EVERYWHERE. Invisible walls, hidden platforms, Invisible floors, deadly traps, enemy ambush, dragon ambush, ball ambush (yes ball ambush, don't ask). There is so much to see and to do that it might be overwhelming. The game never take you by the hands and pushes you to take your time and to explore every nook and cranny of this Grand world. yes i used Grand with a big G because everything looks massive. The environment, from afar (we'll speak about that further down) is magnificent and beautifully handcrafted. The environment also contribute a lot to the storytelling of the game.

[h3] Storytelling and Design [/h3]
The storytelling and design of the game are a bit weird, but not in a bad way. If you are familiar with Darksouls you already know that but the story is told via item description and enemy design. If you want to read then oh boi, you are going to have fun with the descriptions. Every item has his own description which ground it in the lore. It's even better for the items which comes from bosses. Every enemy also contributes to the storytelling just via their designs. Some are really disgusting though so don't stare too heavily :)

[h2] The Bad ! [/h2]
There is not much bad to say but there is still some problems that me or others i know encounters. So.. what is it??  So, still in 2026, the game is locked in 60 fps. It also doesn't support widescreen. There is still some hiccup with the perfomances too. 

Other than that, no guidance from the start may be detrimental to your experience because you may miss actual features and plots. You see for yourself if you see it as a negative or a positive. Most People won't interact with the story of the game other than via the cinematics because the game doesn't show you that the items can be interacted with in another way than equipping it. 

[h2] Tips ! [/h2]
If you have a hard time against a boss, go explore, get new gear, level up. Your best friend is reading and talking to npcs. Quests are not written in a journal so you may want to take note of what npcs tells you.

[h2] The End! [/h2]
[h2] Thanks for reading! [/h2]

Review & Genre Analysis: Elden Ring
Elden Ring is an action RPG created by FromSoftwareAG, and falls under the categorie called “Soulslike”. Essentially, it means it’s a difficult game where the player can choose a lot by themself and don’t realy get a direction set. But it’s also what makes it so interesting.
In Elden Ring, you get to explore a huge open world called the Lands Between. The catch tho is that, it does’ t tell you what to do. Essentially, you are left to explore and fight enemies on your own. At first, it can get quite confusing, but it is also quite nice to be free to choose your own path. The combat is possibly the most important part of Elden Ring. You cann’t just press buttons and expect to win. You have to get to know your enemies and be quite patient. On top, you will lose many times, but it’s part of the experience. Each time you lose, you will also learn something new, making it quite satisfying when you finally beat an enemy. 
A big difference between Elden Ring and older games like Dark Souls (1-3) is, that it is an open world designed game. This means that if you are unable to beat a boss, you can leave and come back later when you are stronger. This is possibly why it is a bit easier to play. Compared to the other “soulslike”-games it’s completely up to you where to go and who to fight in which order. 
The graphics are also a prompt where elden ring got a lot of compliments from players as well as form judges. The game has a lot of variety in the world, such as castles, forests, dark caves, and it all looks detailed and realistic. The enemies are also creative and, in some cases, a bit creepy. The music is good, but it’s not too distracting. Sometimes it can get a bit overwhelming tho because when there are bosfights or special enemies the muisc get catchy and pushy. 
However, the game is not perfect. There is no real quest log, and it’s not clear what you're supposed to do at some points, which can get a bit frustrating. It’s also worth mentioning that, if you have not played a Soulslike game before, this might not be the best game to start with. There are often too many questions for the player if you aren’t used to soulslike games. Therefore it might be better to start with a game which has more guidelines and quests to follow along. 
Considering the game genre, it’s clear that Elden Ring is a good game in the Soulslike genre because it improves the genre and shows the direction in which it can be taken. It does this by including the original elements of the Soulslike genre, such as difficulty and abstract storytelling, but it also includes an open-world element, which makes the game more accessible and makes it one of the best in recent years.

There’s a point where praise starts to sound exaggerated, but Elden Ring somehow pushes past that and still earns it.

This isn’t just another great RPG. This is FromSoftware’s opus magnum. The kind of game that makes you wonder how anything is supposed to top it.

In an era where nearly every developer is chasing the open-world formula (especially after The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild) Elden Ring doesn’t just follow the trend, It perfects it.

The world isn’t just big for the sake of being big, it’s ALIVE. Every direction you move in, there’s something waiting; whether it’s a hidden dungeon, a terrifying boss, a new weapon, or some quiet detail that pulls you deeper into the world.
Every bridge, every ruin, every mountain, every empty-looking field somehow has purpose. Exploration doesn’t feel like a checklist, it feels like curiosity that is constantly being rewarded.
And at its core, this is what makes Elden Ring such a perfect RPG.

You don’t need to have played any previous FromSoftware titles. You don’t even need to fully understand the story. You could skip every line of dialogue and still walk away with an unforgettable experience.
But if you do choose to engage with it? That’s when the game opens up even more.

The lore, the characters, the side quests, they’re all layered in a way that rewards attention without demanding it. You’ll find yourself actually caring about what happens next, listening more closely, exploring more thoroughly, and getting invested in a world that never forces you to care, but makes you want to.

Combat is where the game truly tests you. Bosses are brutal, sometimes frustrating to the point of disbelief and broken controllers/keyboards, but beating them? That feeling never gets old. Every victory feels earned. Every new encounter makes you wonder not just how you’ll win, but what kind of fight it’s going to be.
And the tools you’re given to face those challenges are just as impressive.

Weapons, armor, spells, abilities, EVERYTHING feels handcrafted and meaningful. Whether you’re running a raw strength build, a dexterity bleed setup, or diving into magic, faith, or even dragon-based abilities, the variety is insane. Every build feels viable, and more importantly, fun.

Visually, the game is just as powerful. The landscapes are massive and hauntingly beautiful. The lighting, the textures, the atmosphere, it all works together to create moments where you genuinely have to stop and just take it in. Everyone’s first screenshot is the Erd Tree after the elevator for a reason. The music elevates everything even further, turning already intense encounters into something unforgettable.

This is the kind of game that doesn’t just pull you in, it CONSUMES your time without you realizing it.

You’ll want to explore everything. Collect everything. Understand everything. And somehow, even after hundreds of hours, it still doesn’t feel like enough.

With over 400 hours put into the game, most of that in pure, unmodded gameplay, it never once felt boring. And if you decide to go beyond that into the modding scene, you’re looking at hundreds of additional hours of fresh experiences layered on top of an already massive game.

At full price, Elden Ring is more than worth it. The amount of content, the level of detail, and the sheer quality of the experience make it one of the best value games out there.

So honestly?
Stop reading the endless reviews.
Stop scrolling through the million opinions.
And just go play Elden Ring.
Because this isn’t just one of the best games ever made.

It might be the one everything else gets compared to from now on.

Maybe this is where I officially become the old guy yelling at games. Because somewhere along the way, “bigger” replaced “better,” and nobody seems to question it anymore. Elden Ring is what happens when you take every questionable idea during development and decide not only to keep it but double down on it. The real difficulty is genuinely in your effort to remember that you’re playing something critically acclaimed, because so much of the experience feels confused, stretched thin, or undercooked.

I forced over 40 hours into this. Having played every mainline Souls game, I had to see it through. I wanted to know what the “final form” of this formula looked like.

Now I know.

The disappointment is as vast as the empty landscape, and the confusion is immeasurable. This isn’t a case of “you need a break from the game.” This is a case of needing a break because of the game because of its design, its systems, its world, and the constant feeling of randomness pretending to be depth. It’s not challenging in a meaningful way, it’s not rewarding in a satisfying way it just slowly drains you. Not from difficulty, but from repetition, confusion, and the sense that everything is just slightly off. You’re not playing a game anymore, you’re enduring one. And my patience ran out around the 40-hour mark.

To put it front and center:

The big selling point here is the open world. And like most open worlds, it proves a simple rule: scale does not equal quality. What you get isn’t a carefully crafted experience, but something closer to an “MMO from 2008 but with better lighting.” Vast, empty landscapes filled with enemies awkwardly standing around like they’re waiting for their shift to start. Half of them look like they spawned in five seconds ago, the other half like they forgot to despawn.

Instead of the tight, interconnected level design that made earlier Souls games work, you now roam what feels like the Scottish highlands populated by idle mobs, copy-pasted assets, and the occasional enemy placed on a hill or in a ditch for dramatic effect. Not because it makes sense, just because.

I can sense the confusion in the mobs themselves. Hollow soldiers guarding a broken cart. Patrols defending a handful of rocks in the middle of nowhere. Entire camps built around absolutely nothing of value. It feels less like worldbuilding and more like someone forgot to remove placeholder assets. Whatever themes were intended are completely lost, overwritten by sheer randomness. At times it feels less like exploring a world and more like wandering through a very expensive early-onset dementia simulator.

To make this scale even remotely playable, the game introduces a mount. And this is where the domino effect really kicks in. The world is too big → you get a mount → encounters lose structure → enemies become filler → combat turns into drive-by hits or stamina management on horseback. What used to be deliberate level design is now replaced with wide open killing fields and loosely scattered content.

Combat has also gone in a direction I personally can’t stand. After Dark Souls II, things have been getting faster and more “spectacle-driven,” but here it hits rock bottom. What used to be methodical combat is now closer to button mashing with extra steps. Most fights boil down to abusing dodge invincibility frames and hammering heavy attacks until something breaks (guard or poise). Repeat from start to finish.

If that’s “skill,” then sure. To me, it feels more like exploiting a system than mastering one.

Then there’s crafting, which might be the most pointless system in the game. Enemies rarely drop anything meaningful, materials are scattered everywhere with little thought for what, where, or why, and the whole system feels like it exists just to justify itself. You end up running around committing wildlife genocide deers, turtles, birds, rabbits just to craft items that could have easily been sold by a vendor. It adds nothing but menu clutter and busywork.

And even when the game does give you loot, it quietly undercuts it somewhere else. Rune (souls) gain from regular enemies is so low that it might as well not exist. Your actual income comes almost entirely from bosses. Everything else either gives too little or takes too long to be worth the effort.

So the usual gameplay loop “farm a bit, get stronger, try again” barely functions. There’s no real incentive to clear areas, no satisfying buildup of progress. If you’re underleveled, you’re not grinding your way up you’re waiting for the next boss payout. At times it feels like you’re more likely to grow bored than actually progress through effort.

The core issue with the game: it constantly adds systems without improving the experience. More space, more mechanics, more items but less purpose.

There are moments where you can see what the game could have been. But its dead and buried under repetition, filler, and design decisions that work against each other. Honestly, it’s almost worth playing just to witness how all these pieces somehow fit together into something so mediocre, so confused, so boring.

om min recension av dark souls 1 inte gjorde det tillräckligt tydligt så är detta inte längre mitt favoritspel genom tiderna. jag har med tiden lärt mig att uppskatta den äldre souls-formeln betydligt mer. världssammanlänkningen i dark souls 1 gör ett mycket bättre jobb med att få världen att kännas levande, jämfört med en stor karta som tyvärr saknar vertikalitet, nyans och inlevelse. det kanske låter som en kontroversiell åsikt, men i jämförelse med tidigare spel kan jag inte låta bli att känna att elden rings tillvägagångssätt är något av en besvikelse. det betyder dock inte att jag tycker mindre om spelet, jag står fortfarande fast vid att open world-konceptet fungerar bra inom souls-formeln. men bias, erfarenhet och personliga preferenser påverkar min uppfattning, vare sig jag vill eller inte

som jag nämnt i mina recensioner av dark souls 1 och 3 uppskattar jag verkligen fromsofts sätt att designa bossar i dark souls 3... jag skulle till och med kunna kalla det nästintill perfekt. det finns en otroligty fin balans mellan variation (både inom enskilda bossar och bossarna i sig), tempo, positionering och inlevelse. här upplever jag däremot att bossarna, trots visuella och mekaniska skillnader, känns ganska lika i hur de spelas. tillvägagångssättet i striderna blir ofta detsamma: lära sig när man ska ducka och utnyttja de långa öppningarna för att slå tillbaka. spelet uppmuntrar dessutom användning av externa hjälpmedel, vilket jag personligen undviker, och det bidrar till att striderna känns mer ensidiga. den högre hastigheten hos bossarna verkar ha lett till att man istället för variation lutar sig mot svårundvikliga attacker eller ganska enkla AOE-lösningar. med det sagt vill jag ändå understryka att jag tycker om bossarna -- jag hade bara önskat att ett så pass polerat spel vågade variera sig mer även i hur striderna faktiskt spelas, inte bara i det visuella

avslutningsvis kan jag verkligen uppskatta hur genomarbetat spelet är som helhet. samtidigt tycker jag att det saknar en viss charm. upplevelsen är imponerande, men annorlunda. jag har svårare att känna samma driv och motivation som i de tidigare spelen, vilket också är anledningen till att jag lagt det åt sidan flera gånger. när man väl tar sig igenom det inser man dessutom hur relativt begränsad den "huvudsakliga" vägen faktiskt är. sidoinnehållet följer en ganska typisk open world-struktur, vilket inte riktigt tilltalar mig. de många nådepunkterna bidrar visserligen till en smidigare upplevelse, men jag upplever det också som ett något bekvämt designval. jag föredrar den mer krävande strukturen i dark souls 1, där man utgår från en enstaka bonfire och tvingas ta sig tillbaka genom området -- något som gör att man lär sig av sina misstag och förblir engagerad genom hela processen, snarare än att stänga av hjärnan och bara ta sig igenom nivåer som ibland saknar samma genomtänkta design

hursomhelst rekommenderar jag verkligen detta spel. allt som sagts är mina personliga åsikter, men jag kan inte bortse från att det i grunden är den mest tillgängliga (och enklaste) souls-upplevelsen -- och ett utmärkt sätt att komma in i de andra spelen

There are great games. There are masterpieces.
And then there’s Elden Ring - a game that feels like a once-in-a-generation moment. And apparently not even Miyazaki's true ideal of a game. We do not deserve what this man and FromSoftware have for us.

[h1] TL;DR [/h1]
[h3]Pros:[/h3]
-Massive open world: Seamless exploration with secrets everywhere
-Freedom: Build, playstyle, and path choices are very flexible
-Combat depth: Challenging, skill-based, and satisfying
-Lore & atmosphere: Rich, mysterious world co-created by George R.R. Martin
-Replayability: Multiple endings, bosses, and builds
-Fantastic mods

[h3]Cons:[/h3]
-Difficulty spikes: Can be punishing for newcomers
-Opaque mechanics: Some systems (stats, crafting, progression) aren’t well explained
-Navigation: Open world can feel confusing without guidance
-Sparse story clarity: Narrative is subtle; some may find it hard to follow
-Extremely sparse sidequest story: Extremely difficult to follow side quests as a new player - narrative is extremely subtle, and NPCs randomly cark it if you don't meet their needs...
-Terrible online/co-op play (the typical FromSoftware co-op experience)

From the first step into the Lands Between, you realize something is different. There’s no rush, no pressure like the other installments from FromSoftware - just a vast, mysterious world stretching endlessly in every direction, quietly daring you to explore it with music in-hand blessing your ears. And when you do? It rewards you in ways few games ever have.

Every hill hides a secret. Every ruin tells a story. Every unexpected encounter - whether it’s a wandering boss, a hidden dungeon, or a breathtaking new region - feels like it was placed there just for you to discover.

This is freedom done right. Combat is the culmination of everything FromSoftware has learned over the years. It’s tight, punishing, and deeply satisfying. Whether you’re a spellcaster raining destruction from afar, a heavily armored juggernaut trading blows, or a nimble rogue dancing around enemies - every playstyle feels powerful when mastered.

And yes - it’s difficult. It will knock you down without hesitation. But unlike anything before it, it also gives you the tools to rise again. You can go somewhere different. Farm runes and level yourself to become unstoppable. Or you can do it the old fashion way - spawn, die, spawn, die, spawn, die... Explore somewhere else. Get stronger. Come back wiser. Victory is never handed to you, but it’s always within reach. The boss has to defeat you forever, but you only have to defeat it once.

The world design is nothing short of breathtaking. Not just in scale, but in intention. The Lands Between feel alive, ancient, and deeply interconnected in ways that constantly surprise you. And the moments… the bosses… the music…

Standing before something that seems impossible, failing, learning, adapting - and then finally overcoming it. That feeling? Elden Ring perfects it.

Flaws? Minor ones exist - but they fade into irrelevance compared to what this game achieves as a whole.

And just when you thought Elden Ring had already said everything it needed to say… the DLC arrives and somehow raises the bar again.

Shadow of the Erdtree isn’t just an expansion - it’s a statement.

It’s almost absurd to say this, but the DLC alone sparked “Game of the Year” conversations… again. Not for a new title. Not for a sequel. For an expansion. That’s the level we’re dealing with here. It feels less like extra content and more like a second masterpiece layered on top of the first. 
And then there’s the difficulty.

This is where it hits. If the base game gave players more freedom and flexibility to overcome challenges, the DLC reminds you - very quickly - where this series comes from. The enemies are relentless. The bosses? Absolutely ferocious. Every fight feels like it demands your full attention, your best build, and your willingness to adapt or be crushed. Let's not give people flashbacks of pre-nerf Consort Radahn.

That old feeling is back. That “I don’t know if I can do this” moment. Followed by the attempt. The failure. The adjustment. And eventually… the triumph.

The world itself is darker, denser, and even more haunting. There’s a weight to everything here. A sense that you’re stepping into something forgotten and dangerous. Exploration feels tense again. Every corner could be your next mistake… or your next breakthrough. And somehow, even after hundreds of hours in the base game, it makes you feel small all over again.

That’s not easy to do. Most DLCs add content. This one redefines the experience. It reminds you why you fell in love with Elden Ring in the first place, then pushes you further than you expected to go.

I was disappointed with the character creation because the visuals look dated, and ugly.
I spent an hour trying to get a likeable face, but that hour was not an enjoyable one because it felt like a battle to see meaningful changes.

After starting the actual game, the cutscenes were stills not even animated stills or in-game video. A minor gripe, but it undeniably conveys the feel of an indie production, not a AAA title—which is not OK if the goal is to achieve AAA standards.

The interface looks and feels like it was made circa 1998, you know, that era where developers hadn't really had time or experience to figure out what works well for an interface system.

The tutorial was frustrating because explanation text boxes kept popping up, not centered properly with quickly written text, child-like, noob indie feel. Incomprehensible clickable "messages" scattered about the environment, and some kind of ridiculous voting system for those messages popping up in this horrible interface, was torture.

The combat system while probably not terrible, does not have a fluid feel such as can be experienced in games like Oblivion, Skyrim, Ghost of Tsushima, or Guild Wars 2 among others. It felt very slow, clunky and out of sync. Enemy combat behavior was too simple, the animations merely rudimentary, and their death sequences uninteresting.

I didn't get past two hours, but, after checking with Gemini AI, apparently there are no populated towns or "complex" NPCs--the likes of which can be found in the aforementioned games.

From the outset, with a story that felt dull and barely existent along with an indie-feel to most other elements: interface, visuals and combat, I could not find a reason to continue, and so I requested—and received—a refund. Thank you.

For a game that has received such high praise I did not expect to become so dissapointed. The game is praised for breaking the curse of bloated open world games, yet falls into the same pitfalls. Every hour feels more boring than the last.

Open world and progression
The first hours of this game feels fresh and exciting. There is lots to explore and the scenery is stunning, yet this feels like the most the game has to offer. Past a certain point the world loses its appeal, due to the insane amount of repeat bosses, dungeons and ruins. This is a shame, because there is a good amount of unique and fun bosses and dungeons, but the amount of trash I have to wade through the get there is painful. This is made worse by the fact that bosses who feel unique and powerful are casually thrown back into the game when the devs feel the need to fill their massive open world. Not only does the game bore me with repeat dungeons, but they actively ♥♥♥♥ on any good experience I just had. 

The progression system in this game seems to actively contradict what it means to be an "open world". In Dark Souls 3 the progression was pretty straight forward. You complete an area, you get stronger, you get to the next area and the enemies have also gotten stronger. It is a linear game, so thats what you would expect. Yet elden ring copies this formula with little concern for how this would affect the open world experience. Early on it is established that the player has to explore the world. Both the Iron Sentinel and Margitt teaches this to the player as if you go fight them as early as possible you'll be massively underleveled. This does not reward exploration, this punishes the player for not doing so. Whatever I'll level up. I explore some stuff, get stronger, complete stormveil castle. After this the game takes a weird turn for me. I go to  Liurna of the lakes, but by doing so Caelid becomes massively underleved. Atleast games like the witcher 3 tell the player what the recomended level is when such an artifical barrier is set up.

There is fun to be had in the world, yet that is only when the game feels like dark souls 3. The so called legacy dungeons are fun, precisely because they took what fromsoftware had mastered from previous releases. It is almost like this is because the game becomes more linear, the enemies are more tighly packed, healing becomes restricted creating tension and consequences, and because the map becomes both interesting to traverse and look at. Oh wait, that is what every other fromsoft game is known for. 

Combat
This franchise has become synonymous with difficulty. It is dissapointing to see fromsoftware forget why that difficulty was interesting in games like ds3. The whole reason is that the difficulty felt fair and that the player could overcome it by reasonable means. Fundamentally this game still feels like ds3. The same core mechanics are still here yet the bosses have become more agile, more dyanmic, they have more delayed attacks, more aoe attacks and overall more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The whole point of the game is that I can take all that to the face and learn something, yet on every new run the boss decides that it can chain another combo in a series of absolute tomfoolery, where if I even dare try to get a light attack in, I get a stick shoved straight up my ass. The fact that the AI can chain up attacks like this promotes a passive style of play, where I am left up eating scraps when the boss eats a 9 course dinner. 

Then there are attacks that are just completely ridicuouls. Rykard's earthquake, Malenia's waterfowl and tons of other aoes or grab attacks. Their timings range from delayed, arbitrary or non existant. This game is incredibly insistent upon difficulty for difficulty's sake. 

The game has tons of gimmicky ways to offset difficulty, but I find them to be just that, a gimmick. Summons are at the core of this, yet the game fails to convince me that it was balanced around them. Bosses becomme laughably easy when using them, since they can usually only target one at a time.  Gimmicks only push the problem back. Why are they needed? Are fights too hard or just not rewarding enough when using the core mechanics? 

Story and narrative
Despite the harsh words above, this has to be weakest part of the game. There are some fun moments to be had exploring and there are fun bosses to be fought, however the answer as to why the player is doing this seems non existant. This game borrows the same principles from soft have worked with. That is to tell a vague story with item descriptions. In elden ring it works less than ever. In dark souls 3 the vague story could be tied to the very themes themselves. The world felt hollow, because it literally was. Humanity was fading away and that was the motivation for the whole journey. Elden Ring shares this same broken world premise, yet struggles to captivate me. Why does the player blindly follow the path to become elden lord when no one else does? Even when this game wants to pretend that it is a good rpg, every quest follows the same trends: blindly gain persons trust, go fetch item, npc dies or you kill them. This is made worse by the fact that I need a wiki glued to my ass to find the npcs in this vast world. Every quest feels impersonal, becuase they are. Joining volcano manor and killing other tarnished holds no weight. Killing demigod after demigod changes nothing, nothing happens to the world and no one acknowledges my effort. There is no change troughout the plot, the story is still the same. Kill boss, collect the rune. If I had not played the first half and was put into the game, there wouldn't be much I missed in terms of the main story. 

People often state that this game isn't trying to tell a regular story. It wants to be vague and doesn't want to "handhold" you throughout. This feels strange when in the first 10 minutes I meet 4-5 npcs, who i will continue to see throughout their sidequests. The game wants to tell a obscure story, yet still wants to use npcs and dialogue in a traditional sense. This ends up being boring, because of the aforementioned tropes. The ingenuity of fromsoft storytelling, seems to lie in the item descriptions. They tell the lore of various parts of the world, but I couldn't bother. 1 Why should I care when the lore so often depicts random "fun facts"; Why should I care about the backstory of some random enemies when the narrative is still the same? Kill, loot and move on. 2 The act of stopping to read is a lazy way to utilize the video game medium. If read dead 2 and the like get critique for being too much like a movie, then elden ring wants to be too much like a book. I feel like just observing the community is a great affirmation of item descriptions being bad: Why do people watch lore videos, when you can play the game?

A game that supposedly fixed open world gaming still commits the same mistakes. A game that wanted a rawer experience with less map markers outsourced the problem to the wikis. A game that was supposed to be the newest iteration of souls combat feels derivative and cheap. In the end this game struggles from wanting to cater to as many as possible: Being open world to challenge the AAA market and being more difficult to cater to the loudest fromsoft fans, but to make the game feel fair it is offset with gimmick summons.

I would not recommend this game simply because there are better fromsoft games.

If I could give this game a "mixed" I absolutely would. This game is utterly fantastic. It has incredible environments and exploration, so good that that aspect alone carried me through 3 playthroughs. The boss fights, when done well, are extremely rewarding and feel like a hard yet fair challenge.

It's everything else that drags it down for me. The terrible boss fights are *really* terrible. So much so that they drag down the experience for a while. Also, the quest design in this game is bafflingly bad. They tried to keep the vague, cryptic quests of the original Souls games and put them in an open world format where 90% of players will likely never return to the specific area the NPC decided to move to. Of course there are hints to where they've gone, but unless you've got a notebook keeping track of it there's no way to follow all 10-20 questlines organically. That said I don't think the quests even add much to the game and you can beat the game without progressing any of them.

There's a lot to love about this game, and even more to learn to love. Yet the downsides can't be ignored. This game is a trailblazer yet suffers from some obvious flaws that just kinda carried over from past games. I guess whether or not you should buy this game is how much you're able to tolerate and if the highs of this game resonate with you, which it definitely did for me.

If you are a fan of SoulsBorne games and you’re wondering if this is worth it—stop wondering. Get this game.

True Freedom: The game gives you a little nudge at the start, but then the leash is off. You are free to roam a breathtaking open world filled with more items, gear, spells, and secrets than you’ll know what to do with.

A Quick Note for the Co-Op Travelers:
If you want to experience this journey with friends without the constant threat of invasions, do yourself a favor: search for the "Seamless Co-op" mod and play your way: It deactivates the standard Easy Anti-Cheat (which, let’s be honest, you don't really want on your system anyway) and puts you on a private "server." Bottom line: This is an incredible journey. Play it how you want, enjoy the world, and be happy. See you in the Lands Between!

Elden Ring was my first FromSoft game. I play very few 3rd-person action games, and very few open-world RPGs, so I was way out of my element. However, by the end of my 225-hour playthrough, I loved it! Elden Ring was an epic adventure unlike any other I have played.

I played without using the wiki or any external guide other than seeking occasional hints from a trusted friend.

My favorite aspect of Elden Ring was the world and level design. The towering verticality, the epic scale of it, the huge vistas. I loved how the world was designed to showcase views of faraway castles and mountaintops, enticing me to discover and explore them. I loved the way the dungeons and sub-areas twist and wind on themselves, making clever use of vertical space. Exploration is one of my favorite activities in video games, and Elden Ring was a dark wonderland of discovery. There were constant surprises waiting in every tunnel, behind every castle wall, atop every rugged peak.

The 3rd-person melee combat was very unfamiliar to me. It was brutally difficult initially, but I used loading screens tips to gradually learn some mechanics. I lacked the dexterity and experience to properly time melee attacks, dodge-rolls, and blocks, so I brute-forced my way through much of the game by attacking with ranged spells and running away.

Even if I never got very good at the combat, I was glad that levelling up my character had a meaningful impact on my success. Whenever I was not able to progress in a certain area because the enemies were too hard, I could always go somewhere else to make progress, then come back later with better stats and gear. This was a huge upside to the open-world design.

Ultimately, the game felt tough but (mostly) fair. It did provide many conveniences to the player -- for example, never losing my loot, and using the same currency for levelling up as for purchasing at merchants. The generous abundance of instant-travel points and the tireless double-jumping super-horse made map traversal easy.

My least favorite aspect of Elden Ring was the unwieldy feeling of having to manage character animations constantly. Getting smacked by an enemy while my character slowly did his "stand up" animation. Some animations queued; some didn't. Some animations could be cancelled, some couldn’t. Not being able to block because I'm still doing a spell cast animation. Going off a cliff because my horse had to do its "turning around" animation. And most fatal of all, the unstoppable "I'm out of mana potions" animation.

Elden Ring features a quest system which is very obscured to the player (i.e. no quest log, no quest markers) but is also very conditional (i.e. there are unseen conditions determining whether a quest can even be started, progressed, or completed). Unfortunately, this is a very player-unfriendly combination. I appreciate games which don't hold the player's hand, and as such I kept a very large and thorough document about leads and mysteries I wanted to pursue. However, I found instances where a quest character did not appear where they were supposed to, because I hadn't reached some other unrelated checkpoint yet. Or reaching some unrelated checkpoint caused the quest character to not appear, despite the insistence to the contrary of some clue or dialogue I had found. There were also instances where reaching a destination was not tied to any intuitive geographical progression or clues, but by finding a teleport from one arbitrary location to another.

Anyway, those gripes aside, Elden Ring was an incredible journey, full of struggles and triumphs. Exploring and discovering this dark and mysterious world was fully absorbing, and I felt incredibly accomplished when I finally reached the end.

After a thorough 230 hour playthrough, I find it dishonest not to give this game the tagline it deserves. MASTERPIECE. Objectively and subjectively. Don't let the soulslike snobs discourage you. This game is HARD, no question about it. But for that same reason is so rewarding. No run is the same, not even close. The world is massive and dense. There is so much to explore and to do. The gameplay is smooth and addictive in the best way possible. So many build possibilities, so many cool weapons. There are only two things that keep it in third place for me. One is the fixed frame rate. 60 is enough on paper, but only if it's guaranteed. And in my experience it wasn't. I know they do it for stability reasons, but uncapped frame rate in 2026 seems like a no brainer to me. The second reason is the story. I'm a kind of guy that appreciates a non-linear story that doesn't necessarily spoon-feed you the details. But I barely cared about the story here unfortunately. I just wanted to play the game, which is of course a good thing because it's a GAME at the end of the day. However, that's why Cyberpunk 2077 takes second place for me, because it's equally fantastic on the gameplay front, but the story is way more human and relatable. The first place is held by Sekiro, which aside from the perfect gameplay, in my opinion has the best balance between mystical and human elements. Nonetheless, Elden Ring deserves its 2022 GOTY title and much more, because it has achieved something incredible. As a 25 year old man, I rarely find a game that I cannot put down. I'm happy to say that this is one of those cases. I totally recommend it for every video game enthusiast, even the more casual ones. I say give it a shot.

I originally planned to write this review after my first playthrough, which took me about 100 hours. I took my time exploring every corner of the Lands Between, doing side quests, hunting for items, and soaking in the world. But the game hooked me so hard that I kept coming back for more runs, waited for the Shadow of the Erdtree DLC, crushed its bosses, grabbed every achievement, and now I’m sitting at over 1000 hours.
This is easily one of the best games ever made—perfect for both newcomers dipping their toes into FromSoftware titles and veteran Souls players looking for something fresh.
What stands out most is the incredible freedom and flexibility. The open world lets you go almost anywhere from the start, tackle challenges in whatever order you want, and experiment with literally hundreds of build possibilities. Weapons, spells, ashes of war, talismans—everything combines in ways that keep the game feeling new even after hundreds of hours.
After hitting around 700 hours on vanilla runs, I dove into mods. Adding new weapons, quality-of-life tweaks, and especially the Seamless Co-op mod completely transformed the experience. It makes co-op smooth and unrestricted—no more summoning limits or session drops. I got my friend back into the game, and now we’re running modded playthroughs together, exploring, fighting bosses, and having a blast. The modding scene is super accessible, and co-op has never been easier or more fun.
Whether you’re playing solo, grinding for that perfect build, or teaming up with friends, Elden Ring delivers an unmatched sense of discovery, challenge, and beauty. The world is breathtaking, the combat is deep and rewarding, and the sense of accomplishment when you finally take down a tough boss is unbeatable.
If you’re on the fence, just buy it. 1000+ hours later, I’m still finding new things to love. Masterpiece. 10/10, would get invaded by again.

Can't believe I'm saying this...but it's finally over.

It's taken me well over a year, well over 100 hours, multiple lengthy hiatuses, and lots of outside help to finish my first playthrough, but I finally did it.  And it was worth it.

The high you get from beating really difficult boss after several or even dozens of attempts simply cannot be easily replicated.

First off, I had never and still have never played any traditional "Dark Souls" games as of this writing, so your mileage may vary if you're already familiar with that game series and genre.

Imagine, if you will, an impossibly large open world that's bigger than Breath of the Wild, with way more darkness and depression than Twilight Princess and Majora's Mask combined.  

Unlike most RPG's you may have played, there's no journal, no quest log, nor dialog history.  So that makes keeping track of quests and storylines difficult if not impossible unless you have an eidetic memory or use pen and paper to keep your own notes, or like me just used the Elden Ring wiki when all else fails.  And compared to how vast this game is, there's comparatively few NPC's to interact with, and very few "quests" in the traditional sense.  You may not even notice you're in the middle of a quest.

To add to the difficulty, there's no save scumming or reloading here; you're stuck with every choice you make, no matter how mundane or incidental.  There's also arguably no pausing in this game either, certainly not when you're in combat, so plan accordingly.  And the game explains very little to you, including some mechanics that people only figured out much later after the fact through data mining.

I was advised to look up a character build that I wanted to target in advance, otherwise this game could have been too difficult if not impossible to complete.  While doing so takes some of the mystery out of the game when it comes to truly customizing your own character, I learned upfront that some stats are completely wasted depending on the weapon and playstyle you want to use.  In my case, "strength", despite what the name suggests, was not needed as much as stats like dexterity for increasing damage with the weapons I wanted to use.  Thankfully, there's a mechanic later on to re-spec your character so you can theoretically re-spec into a completely new character build mid-playthrough if you want to change things up.  I took advantage of this late game once I unlocked some particular weapons.

Admittedly, the "blink and you miss it" part of this game gets really obtuse sometimes.  One quest I was doing requires you to pay attention to options available at a very specific grace (basically a save point), and another quest I was only able to continue after paying attention to a very casual reference in an NPC's dialogue.

So don't be ashamed to look up where NPC's can be found during their questline, as this world is so vast it is quite probable that you completely miss them otherwise, unless for some crazy reason you desire to do playthrough after playthrough in this game all on your own.  At least the New Game+ is an option once you finish your first playthrough and I believe ever subsequent playthrough afterwards.

Make sure you have some sort of ergonomic way of playing this game, otherwise you'll wreck your finger joints.  I used a HORI PS4 first person shooter controller.

There's enough replay value to this game to warrant more playthroughs...one day.  Maybe I'll even get the DLC for this game as well.  But after experiencing what this game had to offer, I just need a really long nap.

I played Demon’s Souls years ago and came to Elden Ring after finishing Tainted Grail. I was expecting a challenging 3rd person Action-RPG but spent my first 20+ hours feeling like I just wasn’t connecting with it before I realized that in spite of its massive open world, skill leveling, and item looting, it’s really more comparable to a NES game than something like Skyrim.

Sure, it gets compared to Zelda but it’s more like Zelda II than the newer releases. However, I’ve come to think of it more like Super Mario Bros. (meets Ninja Gaiden). You’re going to die. A lot. While there’s an overarching story, it’s secondary to the gameplay and there’s not one way to play, so whether you want to try and collect every “coin”, find all the secrets, or just race to the end - it’s your game to play however you’d like. Also, don’t overthink the characters and creatures you encounter. Some are there to advance the story but everything else is an extension of the game’s mechanics and exist to be a challenge and/or exploited (rune farming is basically bouncing on the last turtle in 3-1 to get all the lives).

I’m now 60’ish hours in and although it wasn’t what I thought I was getting into, I’m glad that I stuck with it. While they’re both dark fantasy games set in a broken world, it’s basically the inverse of Tainted Grail which was a very immersive story driven experience with decent gameplay. Elden Ring is a gameplay driven experience with a decent story. It may look like a modern game but it has the heart of a retro experience. Or at least that’s my 40 years of gaming impression.

Writing a review for such a generational game is really hard, especially because I don't share the common sentiment that Elden Ring is one of the best games of all time.

The gameplay is fine, it manages to be as polished as Bloodborne's or Sekiro's while keeping (and surpassing by far) the build and weapon variety of the Dark Souls trilogy. However, I quickly grew tired of the countless ganks, infinite combos, delayed attacks and insane tracking that the game likes to throw at you at every corner.

Another thing I'm not a huge fan of is the open world. While it's far from a generic empty AAA slop open world, it still introduces a lot of "padding" to the experience. Most of the items you find on the ground are just boring crafting materials, most of the dungeons have the same generic copypasted bosses, etc. The open world also makes following NPC quests basically impossible without looking up their locations (because they often move to places you have already explored before starting their quest and have no reason to come back to). In general ER feels like a less tight and cohesive experience compared to DS or Bloodborne and has much more unnecessary bloat.

The graphics and art direction department is probably the only one I can't complain about, most areas in the game are genuinely stunning and the colorful, saturated world of Elden Ring felt like a breath of fresh air after the desolate greyness of DS3. The music is not as good as previous FromSoftware titles imo, but that's a really high standard.

Overall, Elden Ring was a mostly enjoyable experience with some highs and lows, and while it didn't resonate with me as much as the other FromSoft titles I've played, it was still definitely a net positive.

This is one of those games that will never make you regret buying it. Elden Ring offers incredible replayability, countless build possibilities, a massive open world, and hundreds of bosses and enemies to encounter. The diversity in this game completely blew my mind. There is an unbelievable amount of content packed into it, and every playthrough can feel different depending on how you approach the game.

The boss fights are one of the strongest aspects of the game. The cutscenes, atmosphere, and voice acting during boss encounters make them feel truly epic and memorable. Every major boss feels unique, both in design and mechanics, which keeps the combat exciting throughout the journey.

The difficulty scaling is also handled very well. Like other games developed by FromSoftware, the game can be challenging, but it gives you many tools to make things easier if you want. Using spirit summons such as Mimic Tear or Tiche can make difficult bosses much more manageable. The co-op system is also fantastic—many players in the community are very supportive and are willing to help others defeat bosses if they are struggling.

One of the best parts of the game is exploration. The world of The Lands Between constantly rewards curiosity. When I first started playing, I thought only Limgrave, Weeping Peninsula, and Stormveil Castle were the main areas of the game. But after defeating Godrick and stepping into Liurnia, and later reaching Altus Plateau, I was shocked. I realized I hadn’t even explored 10% of the entire map.

Besides the massive overworld, there is also a huge underground world with hidden places and mysterious locations. Exploring these areas feels magical and often leads to powerful items, secret bosses, and beautiful environments. Every cave, ruin, and catacomb usually contains something valuable that you can only discover by exploring.

Another thing that makes the game special is the freedom it gives to the player. You can approach fights in many different ways—melee builds, magic builds, hybrid builds, or even your own creative builds like becoming an assassin or samurai. This flexibility is one of the main reasons the game has such strong replay value.

If you ask me about the cons of the game, honestly there are almost none. Some players might say the story is not presented directly, but that is very subjective. The lore is actually incredibly deep and fascinating if you take time to understand it. In fact, the story and world-building feel so rich that they could easily inspire a movie or series. The only minor issue I faced was fall damage, which can sometimes be frustrating, but it’s manageable once you learn the map better.

In my opinion, this game has top-notch graphics, music, characters, and gameplay. The soundtrack during boss fights is phenomenal and adds a lot to the tension and excitement. The game is also fairly well optimized, although it is locked at 60 FPS.

Overall, Elden Ring feels like a once-in-a-generation gaming experience. Few games manage to create such a vast world while still keeping exploration meaningful and rewarding. It constantly surprises you with new locations, enemies, and secrets even after dozens of hours of gameplay.

Back in 2011 my friend got me to play Dark Souls. I loathed it. I had no comprehension of the game's stats, general level layout, or mechanics. I let myself be lead around by the nose and more or less gifted an electric zweihänder that I could barely lift to carry me along.

Fast forward to 2022, this new Elden Ring game is being lauded as the greatest thing since sliced bread. And I was skeptical. It wasn't until a coworker, a silly man in his late 50s proudly declared that he was 'the Elden Lord', if he could beat it so could I. So I bought the game.

I decided I wanted a faith/strength build as I quite adore the paladin archetype. So I picked that class- But I could not understand in the slightest what I was doing. I ran along and somehow ended up in Liurnia before I'd even seen a boss. One lobster chase later I was ready to put the game down and get back my money.

Then my friend stepped in. He gave me simple instructions; "Pick wretch so that you are introduced to the game's mechanics slowly over time. Then, pick any direction and follow it in a straight line and see where your adventure takes you- It is after all an open world game."

A game that expertly combines gameplay, narrative, visuals, and world building, making for an unforgettable experience overall.

Whether you want to unravel the mysteries of a brutal fantasy world, have your skills tested in challenging yet fair combat, or escape to a place like no other, this game has you covered.

Personally speaking, the main highlight of this game for me is its narrative and world building combined. You have your basic plots and characters, which are compelling and enjoyable in their own respects, but I love how a majority of this game’s stories are told through character dialogue, environmental storytelling, and item descriptions. Like one giant puzzle that can be completed and interpreted in a number of ways, with there being no “right” option to most in-game quandaries. Allowing for the game to have increased longevity, since the appeal of debating this games lore is likely to be the main appeal to this game. Decades down the line, at least. Along with making the world as a whole more interesting, as everyone who explores it gets to enjoy and see it in their own unique way.

The only problem I have with this game is its multiplayer. It works great when you want to play with strangers and don't have to worry about the progress of others, but it can be a slog when trying to do a whole playthrough with friends and/or family. The way the in-game cooperative play currently works has tow major flaws, in my opinion.

Firstly, the player who is summoned doesn't get any of the benefits and rewards (besides Runes, maybe, the duo main in-game currency and levelling up resource) when completing the host players boss or dungeon. Making it so that if both players want to progress at the same pace, they will effectively have to do each segment of the game twice or thrice, depending on how many people are playing together. Which, can make each part of the game played together feel more tedious and annoying for all players involved.

Secondly, since you can only summon players for the specific parts of the game mentioned above, it effectively makes it impossible to play any open world parts of the game together. Though, given the loopholes some players have found, it would be more accurate to say unnecessarily convoluted. And, given how one of the main appeals to this game to most players, including myself, is its open world nature, you are heavily incentivized to not partake in a good percentage of this games content. At least, if you wish to play the whole game with your friends/family, that is. Which, be it intentional or not, is a pretty strange and poor decision in my opinion.

The popular Seamless Co-Op mod does fix both of these issues, so I would highly recommend installing and using that if you wish to play this game with others.

Besides the multiplayer, this game is a masterpiece, and is easily in my top three favourite games of all time currently. Thus, I would highly recommend all of those interested in buying and playing it to do so. It is well worth the price in my opinion.
