[h1]Elden Ring is not hard. It is annoying.[/h1]

There is a difference.

A hard game tests timing, judgment, adaptation, and consistency. Elden Ring often tests patience instead. Too many fights are built around bosses flying to the other end of the arena, chaining disengages, or forcing long chases that add nothing except downtime. That is not difficulty. That is irritation.

Even Miyazaki has described Elden Ring as being designed to reduce hard progress walls by letting players leave bosses for later and by making it easier to get help in multiplayer, and he has also said FromSoftware “expect” players to use outside help like guides and community knowledge. In other words, even the design philosophy seems to assume players will route around build problems instead of solving them strictly within their own build.

That becomes a problem when the game counter-picks you.

Want to play a Holy paladin? Fine, until the late game starts stacking major holy resistance on the exact bosses that matter most. Community strategy references for Radagon and Elden Beast routinely note heavy holy resistance, broad status immunity, and a practical push toward physical damage over many themed setups.

And that gets to one of Elden Ring’s biggest issues: build fantasy is not evenly respected. Bleed and frost are allowed to feel explosive and rewarding, while poison often feels undertuned by comparison unless you build around very specific synergies. By the end, a lot of players are not expressing a build so much as learning which builds the game still permits. That imbalance is one reason so many discussions keep converging on bleed and frost as the stronger status options.

The boss design has similar problems.

People love to brag about the boss count, but the raw number is inflated by repetition. A huge number of “bosses” are reused, remixed, doubled up, renamed, downgraded into normal enemies, or upgraded from normal enemies into bosses. So yes, Elden Ring has a lot of bosses on paper, but in terms of truly memorable, one-off headliners, the number feels dramatically smaller. There is a reason one recurring criticism of the game is that the open world is stuffed with repeated encounters rather than consistently new ones.

That repetition undercuts the game’s sense of wonder. When a “boss” is just something I already killed three times in a mine, a catacomb, and then later saw wandering around as a regular enemy, it stops feeling like a boss and starts feeling like recycled content with a health bar.

The camera does not help. Large or hyper-mobile bosses have been a complaint since launch, and Elden Ring still has encounters where the camera is a bigger enemy than the moveset. Fire Giant, Elden Beast, and Maliketh are the obvious examples. If the boss is too large to read cleanly up close, or too erratic to track cleanly at medium range, then target lock becomes part of the problem instead of part of the solution. That is not a satisfying skill check.

Then there is the final stretch.

Radagon and Elden Beast do not feel like a final exam for the game’s build variety. They feel like a rejection of it. Radagon shrugs off or resists a wide range of things, and Elden Beast is notorious for broad status immunity and strong elemental resistance, especially to holy. The result is that many builds arrive at the finish line only to discover they are effectively nerfed for reasons that have less to do with player execution than with the damage types the game decided to invalidate.

So what happens? A lot of players converge on the same practical answer: simplify the damage profile, lean physical, survive the chase, and work around the arena-wide movement. That is not build expression. That is funneling.

Elden Ring is still a very good game. The world is striking, the art direction is exceptional, and when the combat clicks, it really clicks. But I am tired of people describing every frustration in this game as proof of brilliance.

A boss sprinting away for the fifth time is not genius.
A giant enemy breaking the camera is not genius.
Copy-pasting bosses into caves and later turning them into normal mobs is not genius.
Making entire archetypes feel invalid in the late game is not genius.

That is not “hard.”
That is annoying.

Quite good overall, though being open world both adds and detracts from it in huge ways. You get a huge world and beautiful sights and many environments, but very poor interconnectivity and all the usual open world problems.

Even though it's Fromsoft and they're usually quite independent in how they design stuff, there are numerous things in ER which feel like they're only there because every other open world game does it. The pointless crafting, easy fast travel from anywhere, copy and paste caves/catcombs, fast movement on a mount, etc. Doesn't feel tightly designed at all. Thankfully they did avoid losing all identity and the map isn't littered with question marks.

The world feels huge. But after a while it starts to compress because you wind up teleporting everywhere and never actually travel to places anymore. It's a conceptually flat, there is little of the intricate interconnectivity which Fromsoft is known for. Because of this there's little reason to revisit places. You don't need to and you don't really have time. I feel like the world should've been more creatively shaped at a fundamental level, like maybe some crazy spiral around the Erdtree.

Being able to teleport anywhere when not in combat, being able to escape instantly with the horse, and the very high frequency of the teleport spots really takes away a lot of the danger from the game's open world. With little friction in moving from place to place, there is no real planning/survival aspect like Dark Souls has. Engaging with it is a bit dull aside from the pure exploration and beauty of it. It's shallow, like most open worlds.  "Why is it always mushroom...?"

And speaking of the horse... Torrent has no personality at all because it has no interactivity or world presence. You just teleport onto it instantly and then it disappears when you get off. A far cry from something like Shadow of the Colossus and Agro. Torrent isn't a companion but a movement mode. This looser integration of gameplay/world/narrative is pretty noticable compared with DS. ER feels more generic, with nothing like Humanity or hollowing or whatnot.

The game is at its strongest when you're in an actual level. A castle, a city, a swamp, etc. Classic Souls stuff. The bosses are also great fun and a huge spectacle, though the difficulty can be a bit extreme at times because they do crazy high damage. There's plenty of praises to sing but I'm not going to bother lol

[h1] Very high high's and some pretty low low's [/h1]

[h2] The good: [/h2]

- Fun combat with multiple playstyles and lots of replay value
- Lots of content
- Phenominal art direction!
- Many interesting places to visit and bosses to defeat

ELDEN RING as a whole took me away. The game can be pretty tough, you'll spend a while fighting most bosses but once you get it... it hits different. Exploring new places is usually very fun. The character designs and enviornments are beautiful, unique and interesting. The voice acting is just... incredible.

[h2] The bad: [/h2]

This section will be longer than the one above, that doesn't mean that Elden Ring is a bad game though. I just want to talk about this a bit more in-depth, at least as much as I'm able to. It's late.

Spirit summons are this games ''''easy mode'''', and I think they're not very well thought through. Some spirit ashes are extremely overpowered and carry bad players through the game. Even some of the less OP ashes can carry you a little too much. YOU'RE here to fight the boss, not other people. I wish the system was reworked a bit to make it a bit more interactive, alongside some nerfs ofc. Same thing goes for general summons. Player summons are a different topic.

The biggest issue with this game imo is that it focuses a bit too much on ''quantity > quality''. There's lots of weapons but many are outclassed, bad or just poorly balanced. There's many different dungeons to explore, but most of them look and feel the same. There's a whole lot of bosses to fight, but many are repeated encounters. Too much filler overall and it really brings this game down for me sometimes, coming from someone who explored the vast majority of this games available content.

I think the tutorial should be improved to be less wordy. I'd like to have it be longer though and maybe have it teach the player some mechanics better. Not too much hand holding though, one of the good things about ER is that it (usually) doesn't hold your hand.

Some other QoL changes would be nice, like having a pause screen, no input delay on rolls (would require some less restrictive input binding) and a couple of other things.

I think some boss encounters weren't that fun / had more potential, but most I enjoyed. I wish some weapons had cooler AoW / some type of AoW interaction [spoiler] (Dragon Greatclaw having Endure as it's only AoW is criminal) [/spoiler]. Torrent feels underbaked and is a more boring way of fighting some bosses. Having to click on a menu to revive Torrent is also a... weird choice. Quest design is needlessly confusing and the game not showing you numbers for talismans is weird - aka the game needs a wiki and that's lame!

[h2] Conclusion: [/h2]

Elden Ring is a great game, but that doesn't hinder it's weaknesses from bleeding through... even bleeding a little much sometimes. I enjoyed it so much despite those weaknesses, it was absolutely worth playing.

A mighty open world beast of a game.  That having been said, it plays less like Dark Souls 3 and more like a single player MMO RPG in which you explore big spaces, collect stuff, and then summon your phantom buddies for a raid boss.  Trying to play it solo is doable, and fine if you like that, but much of Elden Ring's nuances as a combat loop are how mounted gameplay and summonable parties transform combat.

If you forgo those, it plays like a less well paced version of Dark Souls 3.  If you include them, it becomes a more unique and memorable experience.  Also, this game is big.  No, bigger than big.  Bigger than bigger.  It is simply biggest.  As a result, having too much pride to use all your tools (magic, summons, Torrent,) in gameplay can very easily kill the pacing by having you get stuck on a boss.  This game is too big for mindless completionism or stubberness if you are not actively enjoying those things throughout the playthrough.  It's a game, play it how ever feels right in the moment and you will come to understand why it is a classic.  If you try to treat it like Dark Souls 4, it will likely just feel like slower paced DS3.

Big thumbs up overall.

Spectacle and buzzwords over substance. The open world is empty and repetitive, mostly just a time waster in between the real highlights of the game that they refer to as "legacy dungeons". Many parts of the world do look very good, but I would much prefer double the legacy dungeons which are generally well designed and engaging. The best this game ever felt for me was when I had a complete character in NG+2 and could just run past all the tedious open world stuff and not bother with any of the copy-paste dungeons or remote crevices where one useful item might be hidden. 

The game design is completely obvious, I feel no immersion because nearly every enemy and especially the bosses have been programmed based on the way players will react to them. Enemies hold their attacks for long periods of time or perform stilted combos designed to roll-catch and punish reactive or panicking players. Then there are large spectacle pseudo cutscene moves that are cool the first couple times and then just become boring and ruin the pace of the fight. None of them feel like an organic enemy in the world, just bare game design tuned to force rote memorization of their movesets or spectacle for the sake of it. I can appreciate the difficulty of it, but it ruins any kind of immersion or world-building for me.  

The story seems a level more depraved than any of the previous games, but you don't really have to pay attention to it. Overall a bad direction for the series and a major disappointment for me as a long time fan. I still like it better mechanically than Dark Souls 3 but find it to have less replayability because of Elden Ring's large scale making new character builds an incredible chore. The series has been on a downward slide since Bloodborne and this game is my exit point, I have neither purchased the DLC nor do I plan to in the future. There is plenty more that could be said, but its probably not worth it at this point. 

Some bonus gripes: Body Type 1 and 2 instead of male and female, expected from a game that is chiefly concerned with marketability, (buzzwords, flashy clips, difficulty memes) but still disappointing. Also as of March 2026, the game will not launch. It has an error after Easy Anticheat fails to initialize. I'm sure there is probably some sort of fix or workaround for this, but I now consider it a blessing that I was stopped from playing it again. I did a fresh install after not playing for year hoping to just mess around for a few hours and then it wouldn't launch making me realize immediately that I never want to play it again, and finally convincing me to put at least some of my thoughts on the game into a review.

Tl;dr Elden Ring is the best Souls game so far, it is very replayable thanks to its Ash Of War based gameplay.

Elden Ring, which has an eye-catching art style, has greatly increased replayability by making it feel different every time it is played, thanks to the many Ash of War content it contains. Since the main motivation of Souls games is that they make you feel like you are improving even more as you play with a different build every time you play and fight bosses, I can say that Elden Ring is the one that does it best.

There are two elements that can undermine replayability, one of them is farming items and the other is long runs. These two can undermine the feeling of replaying a bit, especially farming items, because if you research well enough in long runs, you will see that there is always a shortcut to your destination, but farming items is always torture no matter what you do.

Open world design decision is so good for souls games. You're already ready for search new things and open world game design let you do what are you want. 

Overall Elden Ring is the best souls game you can play and replay. Good bosses, good music and awesome art style, what more could you want in a game?

Elden ring is a game that you cannot pause, even in offline mode. Every other aspect of the game is permeated with this same sort of smug, sickeningly arrogant design philosophy. It's a game that totally realizes its vision, but this vision is so far beyond awful it is genuine difficult to describe how bad it is. It's central thesis is that what is obscure, cumbersome, or difficult is good. And that's it, there are no other design considerations. 

The game is terrible at explaining itself. Towards the end of it there is an area with invisible enemies. You can't see them without an item that is found very, very far from this area. No one so much as hints to the player where the item is, or even that it exists. If you do stumble on it, the default stats display for the item tells you nothing about it being special. Buried in a different menu page that normally just contains item related lore is a brief message telling you the item lets you see invisible enemies. Just awful design.

Staggering and being staggered by enemies is a *huge* part of the game. A weapon's stagger stat is probably more important than its ability to deal direct damage. Luckily, the equip menu displays this stat where it is easily viewable. Just kidding, there is no where in the game you can see this stat at all, for any piece of equipment, ever. At least you can see a stagger bar that shows you how close enemies are to having their stance broken. Just kidding, there's nothing like that anywhere in the game. But at least you can see a stagger bar for the player character. Just kidding...Well, you get it by now.

Elden ring just feels so, so sickeningly bad to play. Player movement is ponderously slow, and there is a noticeable delay before the player executes any attacks. I just can't overemphasize enough how *unmotivated* the player character behaves as they lethargically, limply swing their weapon. And that's not even taking into account the restrictive stamina system. 

But, if you spend enough time leveling up endurance, you can eventually circumvent this problem. Just kidding, welcome to "soft caps". Far before you can increase your stamina to the point the game doesn't feel like a slog, you start getting massively reduced returns. Like, you can still put more points into endurance, but it only increases stamina by one measly point per level.

In fact, Elden Ring mostly robs the player of feeling stronger as they level up. You can definitely find a lot of weapons, and those weapons can definitely be upgraded, but I've never seen a better example of illusory progression than the effect player attribures have in this game. Even endgame weapons that scale "well" with dexterity give something like a 0.33 percent increase in damage for every level of dexterity. There is also not even a remote semblance of different character attributes being balanced, the best build, for every type of character, is always one that emphasizes vigor to gain HP. Focusing on any other attribute instead is playing a challenge game. 

The worst thing about the game is how it generates difficulty. Remember how I told you that the player lacks any sort of agility? Well, the developers decided that meshed well with a lot of platforming and (usually lethal) fall damage. Enemies also have every movement related advantage that the player doesn't. In addition to turning invisible, they can charge, sprint, dodge quickly and energetically, teleport, and don't seem to care about stamina or MP. Another thing enemies do so often it I consider it to be the game's trademark, is attack the player from across the level with devastating ranged abilities. I'm talking about what basically amounts to artillery, and does tons of damage and knock the player down. And when I say "across the level" I don't just mean they aren't super nearby, I mean it is often genuinely difficult to figure out where these attacks are coming from because they originate so far away.

My favorite terrible thing the game does is this: player attacks terminate when weapon swing arcs hit an obstacle. The game *meticulously* checks for these collisions when the player attacks. And so, when I ended up in combat with an enemy on the other side of a wall, I thought "ah, I'm safe, the game is super careful to check if obstacles block swings." And then the enemy attack totally ignored the wall and hit me anyway.

Generating difficulty in games is both very easy and very hard. It's easy to put obstacles in front of the player, but hard to do it in a way that feels fair. Elden Ring feels like a game where the developers didn't come remotely close to understanding this, and instead generated challenge in the most lazy and uncreative way possible. It feels like the work of a self-absorbed amateur. 

There are so, so many more terrible things I could say about this game, but unfortunately I only have limited space.

Elden Ring is a perfect example of how an action RPG should be made. After several playthroughs, I can confidently say that it is one of the greatest games ever created.

The amount of content in this game is astonishing. Visually, the game is beautiful, with pleasant graphics and incredible art direction. At times the game looks absolutely breathtaking. I still remember the first time I entered Liurnia of the Lakes after defeating Godrick. I spent minutes just standing there and taking dozens of screenshots. The same happened when I first visited Nokron, the Eternal City. The views were unforgettable. I also remember the first time I entered Caelid. The atmosphere there is completely different. The region immediately creates a powerful sense of danger and hostility, especially when you encounter the very unfriendly wildlife that inhabits that land.

Every location feels magical and carefully designed. Wherever you go, you will always find something interesting. Hidden caves, ruins, unique landmarks, secret paths, and valuable loot are everywhere. The world constantly rewards curiosity and exploration. The number of points of interest across the map is enormous, and exploring never feels pointless.

The music and ambience add even more immersion. The soundtrack perfectly supports the atmosphere of the world and its mysterious tone.

Gameplay is outstanding. The player has access to a huge variety of weapons, spells, armor sets, and abilities, allowing you to create a build exactly the way you want. You can play as a heavily armored warrior who withstands powerful blows from bosses, strike quickly with a magic katana while dodging every attack, or become a powerful mage capable of destroying enemies with devastating spells. The number of possible playstyles encourages multiple playthroughs, and eventually you will want to try them all.

The story is also very interesting. Learning about the world, its history, and its characters feels rewarding. Every NPC you meet leaves some kind of impression, and many of them are memorable in their own way.

The game does have a few minor issues. Player versus player combat can sometimes be frustrating. If you play in co-op, you may be invaded by other players who are extremely experienced and focused entirely on defeating you. These encounters can interrupt your progress toward a boss and force you to spend resources dealing with invaders who constantly harass you during your run.

Despite a few minor imperfections, Elden Ring remains an extraordinary experience. Its vast world, incredible art direction, deep gameplay systems, and constant sense of discovery make it a truly remarkable game. It is a title that sets a very high standard for the entire action RPG genre and will be remembered as one of the greatest games ever created.

Elden Ring is not a video game. It is a trial of human existence - a digital divine judgment that tests your soul and decides if you are worthy, or if you need to die 73 more times before you get it.
The visuals are so breathtaking you wonder why museums still exist. Every landscape screams: "Stop, admire me - then die to a random enemy in the bushes." The world is vast, beautiful, cruel, and utterly indifferent to your suffering. Sunsets, castles, swamps, monsters - everything looks so epic that even while dying, you think: "Okay… at least that looked awesome."

Difficulty?
For newcomers, Elden Ring is a psychological experiment. For Dark Souls veterans, it's a sadistic comfort zone. If you survived Dark Souls 3, you enter with a weary smile, knowing: Pain is temporary, glory is eternal.
But beware - this game is a ticking time bomb for any social life. It can turn the calmest person into a screaming wreck. Neighbors may call the police, family will question your sanity, and pets develop anxiety. Controllers get threatened, furniture insulted, bosses personally hated.
This game demands sacrifices: time, patience, peace of mind - sometimes relationships.
Elden Ring should only be played by those who know how to handle frustration, defeat, and absolute injustice. Quick tempers risk not just rage, but diplomatic crises at home.

Verdict:
Elden Ring is a visual wonder, a gameplay nightmare, and an emotional punch to the face - and that's exactly why it's a masterpiece. Those who endure emerge not just victorious, but legendary.
Everyone else… dies. Again and again. 🪎👺👑🥂

Imma split my feelings about Elden Ring into two paragraphs. This is just my opinion, I recommend This game but can also understand why people don't enjoy all aspects.

[h1] MAIN GAME: 6/10 [/h1]
If you like high fantasy games you will probably enjoy Elden Ring. I personally had a hard time getting into it, I beat it, but damn did it feel slow at times. I think this was the easiest souls game so far, which isn't super bad, probably good for people getting into this kinda game, but it made some aspects of the story feel unsatisfying.

PROS:
- Awesome world building cut scenes
- Cool lore is scattered around forcing you to look for explanations to why things are happening (which i like exploring so that was cool)
- The open world is fun to explore and has a lot of areas to see with pretty views
- Most fluid combat system compared to older games
- You meet game changing NPCs early on
- Graphics were amazing

CONS;
- NPC questlines feel unimportant and unless you really wanna hear them out, or follow them, the game doesn't do a good job of making you care about them compared to other games.
- the first half of the game lacks direction
- The game is objectively easy. The hardest boss is optional which makes the main story feel weak. The hardest main boss is the first one you fight, after that they were super easy and didn't match the lore attached to them.
- The repeating nonmain bosses was annoying, i think i fought the ulcerated tree mini boss guy like 15 times in one play through. All in different areas, to the point where id finish a dungeon and be like hell yeah boss time and then just be disappointed that its another ♥♥♥♥ ass different colored ulcerated tree.
- The NPC quests are so hard to track without looking it up. I think that is why its hard to care about them. You see them in the [spoiler] roundtable [/spoiler] and then they are just gone somewhere on the large ass map, and if you end up missing them  because its a large ass map, then their quest line fails.

 i enjoyed it by the end, but i think it was the DLC that pulled me in. With out the DLC i was uninterested in the story. I can see why people enjoy it, but the main game alone to me was weak compared to other titles.

[h2] The DLC 9/10 [/h2]

The DLC for Elden Ring was fire. I really enjoyed exploring the new areas, learning about the NPCs views, and connecting the dots between the main games story and the DLC. The DLC Reminded me of how it felt to play DS3, so if you liked playing that you would enjoy the DLC

PROS: 
- boss fights had impact, they were hard, it felt satisfying to slay them and their fights made sense with story cues.
- the world was large but not large enough to lose story impact
- Graphics and cutscenes were amazing
- The story was easy to follow, i didn't ever forget what my objective was and puzzles were solvable without googling the quest i was working on.
- The DLC made the NPCs quests feel important, you see the NPCs in the DLC more then you see the main story NPCs in the main game and you can talk to them enough to have an opinion on their views by the end
- The big bad at the end is constantly hinted at everywhere, and makes you question if your doing the right thing constantly which made the DLCs story feel impactful

CONS; 
- The ending man, All that lead up and no cutscene at the end. You learn so much about the final boss leading up to it and there is no closure. Its such a hard fight too (which i liked btw), but no real closure or cutscene. i loved the reveal of the final boss just left wishing there was more after.

Over all Elden Ring was a good game, Id recommend it, it just was a little disappointing at times, and felt unsatisfying throughout parts of the story.

This game is art that I still lack the language to describe properly. Almost everything about the experience is deliberate. The depth of this game cannot be overstated because I'm not sure it has been fully experienced, by anyone. The amount and level of human skill, talent, effort, and love embodied here is a continually-unfolding treasure. After all this time, I still make new discoveries.

Of course, it's imperfect. In some ways it leans into this, which is itself beautiful. But this is sometimes done to a level that overshadows the experience.

Around mid-game the bigger problems start to pile up:

- Atrocious targeting
- Eaten or poorly-queued inputs (particularly jumps, jump attacks, flask uses, crouches, and steed whistle uses)
- Hitboxes that are too large on enemy attacks and too small on yours
- Basic enemies that read your animations in three frames and too often interrupt your actions at the last possible moment
- Basically scripted deaths, as the developers have explained, to give you stories to tell your friends
- Ranged attacks that are designed to fail under far too many common circumstances
- Boss fights that are unrewarding, monotonous, and performatively frustrating

As you move into later portions of the game these problems go from noticeable to oppressive.

The shadows lift once you learn to deal with these things semi-reliably, but it does take time.

This is a good game. Yes a good game not an excellent one. It certainly doesn't live up to its hype and one of its biggest flaw, actually being its open world.

But first lets get to the good parts of the game:
- combat: still works great, with a lot of different enemies and movesets to keep you busy experementing.
- legacy dungeons: these are smaller areas that kinda work as the level-like areas in former Dark Souls entries and they are most of the time very good, like you are used to, with shortcuts great enemy placement etc. Some of them are very short, but most of them are really great and are parts  where Elden Ring shines and shows that FromSoft is still capable of pulling that sort of quality out.
- enemy design: again one thine I really enjoy much also in former entries and here in Elden Ring the enemy designs show a great variety and range from standard soldiers to intersting fantasy species to creepy horror apperances. A little caveat come already here, when enemy types pop up at areas where they seemingly dont belong
- Mechanics: Overall I admire how much depths of mechanics is put into the game. You have upgrading, can change affinity of weapons, can calll Spirits to help, which you can also upgrade, you can mix your own potion, use great runes, make your own signs into the map etc.. - if you got runes you always find a way to spend them 
- variety of weapons: this is also sth I want to point out: you are faced with a huge amount of a great choice of weapons. There are over 300 weapons spread across 32 categories. Not all of them are useful and ofc most of them are useful more or less to a certain build, but you can pretty easily respec your char (which is limited) to try out different builds. I had a lot of fun experimenting with it, until I reached the point where every build I tested came to more or less the same dmg output just in different colors.

So far that all sounds very fun you might say and wonder where that negative criticism derives from. Well, now I will share the drawbacks of that game and they will become more and more significant the longer the game lasts:

- first of all the open world: this is an empty and hollow world with no real background living behind it or living behind the inhabitants of the world. It´s more like you travel from one diorama to the next. When you reach a certain trigger point that diorama sets in motion. This becomes even worse since the two first areas are very similiar to each other and very boring. The way you uncover this world is better than in most open world games, yes, since you dont have your map cluttered with items, but still its a shallow world
- Questdesign: this is also a huge problem. FromSoft stayed with their established formular of stumbling into NPCs which then give you cryptic instructions (well a bit less cryptic than in former games, but still very cryptic). Then you are left up with trying to figure out where to find this NPC next. Only problem is, since this game is open world and these NPCs sometimes travel to locations you already have been, you might never find them again. Also if you reach certain areas before you met this NPC you will miss the entire questline. Since I want to see as much content as possible and not that guy who plays a huge open world game a second time, I was lot reading where to find all these NPCs, which I think is not fun anymore at a certain point. Also the quests also lead to the same fate for their protagonists.
- Dungeons: and here I am not speaking of these level-like dungeons but of the smaller dungeons which are all around in this world. There are four or five types of dungeons which are all build very similiar and follow the same formular. At the end you will always find a boss or chest with some loot. They get boring very quickly and feel like a classical filler of a too big open world. In most dungeons you also find the same enemy types which even more make them boring. 
- enemy variety: yes you read it right. I praised the variety further above, but its just the overall variety. So here are more dffetnt types then i.e. Dark Souls 3. But the longer the game lasts the lesser the variation gets, since in new areas are all the same enemies just in different combninations. They also just have more dmg output and a higher healt bar, which make progress seem pale because you wonder why this enemy takes so much more hits than he needed two areas before. Also, some stroy-unique bosses get reused, which make them feel less unique. I dont have a problem with mini-boss reusage if it fits the scenario, but story important characters reused breaks the immersion and the meaning.
- Bosss-fights: Speaking of bosses, the boss-fights are some of the weakest parts of the game. Either you are most of the time overpowered for the average mini or dungeon bosses or you run into annoying boss fights which have the following problems: the bosses spam aggressively their attacks with no stamina constraints. They use input reading which means they don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. This also becomes relevant when they use their huge wind up to delay their attacks. If you cant stand the tensions and press the dodge button they turn towards you and strike their attack just in that moment. These wind-ups mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight, which also becomes very unnatural since you dont react to what the enemy does but more try to guess when his delayed will finally come down to react.
- Upgrading: I said I had a lot of fun experimenting with weapons, which is true, but there is also a caveat to the system. Upgrading material is scarce, you can find items which allow you to buy these materials at a special merchant, but grinding for upgrade material can become tedious. But its neccassary, since if you change your build you will need your new weapons at the same level as your weapons you had before, because otherwise you wont deal enough damage.
- Bonfires: this is one of the biggest problems, which is a result of an open world. There are bonfires everywhere. The problem that encompasses this design is, that there is no real tension if you die, no real meaning for shortcuts. The amount here is ridiculous. There are some areas where bonfire placement is scarce and they are great for that, but overall it breaks the mechanics  for a soulslike.
- Music: the music is lackluster. Music playing in different area is just some annoying ambience rattle, which gets nerve-racking pretty quickly. The music of boss-fights is mostly very uninspired and just gets better towards the end. Only good titel here is the main screen music in my opinion. If you wanna here good background music which is fitting for each area you should try out Tainted Grail: Fall of Avalon, which does a formidable work in this aspect.
- PVP: this is a double-edged sowrd, but as so many of these criticims it becomes worse the longer the game lasts: you cant play in a relaxing coop, because if you do, you will always almost instantly get invaded. Either you fight some hardcore-super-pros which will kill you instantly, what will be almost the best outcome, because there is a bonfre nearby and you can go on. But often you get invaders which will hide somewhere or runaway if they realize they cant win. Thats a problem because invading closes the area and you cant leave until invader or you is deafeated. From my almost 200 hrs you can easily discount 40-50 hrs of being invaded and need to find or follow invader and then regroup with teammember. Because if you die you have to summon your friend again, which often doesnt work to disconnects, then you need to restart the game - so after hundreds of invasions where you actually dont fight - no fun!

So after all I would not recommend the game to anyone who has the inner commitment to fully complete a game (as I do) because it becomes more and more a chore. 78 / 100

To preface this, I put over 120 hours into this game in 2022 on console. I love this game.

However, I don't recommend this game on PC. It was not designed for PC. The game/animations are max 60 frames (or it will break the combat systems, a massive pitfall of FromSoftware game design), and the game has limited settings available to configure the game correctly for a PC level of experience. The default vsync function does not work, the game resolution breaks completely if you try to play it while you have more than one monitor connected, and you can't click off the game screen even when it's in windowed mode. There are so many issues with the PC port of this game it genuinely ruins the experience. I paid good money for both the base game and the DLC, I should not have to be troubleshooting workarounds to fix basic functions of the game. 

This is a souls game, therefore it has a level of difficulty that's unmatched by any other game. BUT, on top of the actual gameplay difficulty, the developers couldn't be bothered to finish certain functions of the game so that they work properly. The lock on system is a prime example of this. It is nearly impossible to lock on to the target you want to hit. You'll be locked onto an enemy, and another will attack you from another direction that you can clearly see coming, but you can't do anything about it because you're frantically cycling through locking on all other enemies before you reach the one that you need to hit in that moment. Game difficulty is a lazy excuse for an incomplete game. It should be difficult but feel good to play. This is not the case for this game on PC.

A complete game should never be at a point where you have to do actual research before your every move to make sure you are not breaking questlines. Unfortunately, you can break questlines permanently in this game. You can't just save the game manually before doing something and reload if it destroys your whole playthrough. The only way to save the game is by saving AND exiting. This is not a game you should play for the story, but the rewards earned by completing quests warrant a complete and functional questline system.

This game's exploration, content quantity, and graphics are incredible. That being said, this game is incredibly overrated. I sincerely hope FromSoftware fixes this PC port, even if they have to re-configure their game engine. That will likely never happen. Do not buy this on PC if you want the proper Elden Ring experience.

Beautiful and maddening game. If you haven't played a Dark Souls type game before, just be prepared: you will die. A lot. It's part of the gameplay mechanic. You die, you respawn, you try again. And eventually you either win or give up. Visually very impressive and creative. 

Gameplay mechanics could use some work, as the sprawling open-world map makes it difficult to understand where you are, what quest you are on (hint: there is no quest tracking at all), or where to go next. 

A lot of the game is rewarding discovery, but at a certain point, that begins to feel more like a chore than a game. Sometimes it's a simple thing like forgetting to cycle through all dialogue options with a NPC, which you may not know about since it frequently ends the dialogue chain until you start it anew and realize they have more to stay. Only once they start to repeat themselves have to exhausted all options. 

The real winning formula here is the mix of beautiful graphics, creative enemy design, and fight mechanics. Learning how the fight mechanics works can be frustrating, and learning to dodge and parry at the right time can really have you question your sanity. It's not logical fighting by any means -- you are fighting giant creatures and dragons and monsters that are 10-50 times your size, yet all you need to do is hack away at their legs or feet and that is usually enough to bring them down. Dodging into an attack is often rewarded here, which is unusual. In my head, this would just end up getting myself into worse position, but in Elden Ring, it has almost the opposite effect. Learning to roll into an enemy/boss rather than away from them takes effort if you have spent most fighting games doing the opposite.

我在23年的时候就接触到了这款游戏，实话实说给我带来了不小的震撼，没有想过一款开放游戏可以做到这样的地步，战斗系统对于前几代魂类游戏的优化与进步，地图的宏大以及内容的丰富，作为新手的第一款魂类游戏也再合适不过了。但是同时也是一款优缺点明显的一款游戏，并非是游戏性上的不行，而更多是魂类游戏所遗留下来的“传统”。
在战斗系统上武器以及等级使游戏内部出现了许多不同的流派，也有轮椅级武器可以让大家来尝试通关，战斗上依旧保持着高难度的水准，以及恶心的快慢刀，其实很劝退手残党，但是BOSS战的爽感是没有游戏可以比拟的，失败之后一次次的挑战，最终战胜时的喜悦总是让人难忘。
魂类游戏优秀的宫廷设计依旧在本作中展露无疑，但是游戏副本的恶心程度不是一般的高，地图里老是设计和塞入一些恶心的怪用来满足宫崎英高变态癖好，我只能说这就是老贼你以前的回家路，三狗屠仙阵也肯定是你小时候被狗咬过是不是，“门不能从这一侧打开”。。。。。。你在开什么玩笑混蛋。
故事内容以及美术设计依旧顶尖在位，DLC里加入的剧情也算是完全将剧情给“希腊化”，后面填的坑自己埋不上，以为是高速公路，实则是乡间小道，也是让我无力吐槽了，但是瑕不掩瑜，任然是2022年的神作。
还有我知道fs社现在是想把魂类游戏给做大，但是黑环这托大的也真是挺大的，如果老高想要更多的新鲜血液流入，首要任务是降低难度，特别是小怪难度，但是BOSS战的爽感也丝毫不能减，还有就是更明确职业划分，不要老是分工不明确，增加联动体验，在去掉糟粕的同时可以保留原汁原味的战斗才是最重要的。
也希望fs社可以在未来给我们带来更多优秀的作品，也希望Switch2上老贼的多人联机魂类游戏项目大获成功。

I have played this game a lot, both with and without mods. I'll be blunt: it's a good game overall, but it has a lot of things dragging it down. Some say it's a 10/10 game, but I disagree. First of all, the biggest issue with this game, is input reading. Enemies and bosses don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. The enemy in Fort Gael is a good example: I try to shoot it with a crossbow, but it evade the moment I press the button, wether I'm aiming at it or not. This is dumb. -1 point.
Next is wind-up attacks and tracking: a lot of bosses and enemies have ridiculous wind-ups that mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight. And if you try to reposition to avoid it completely, they will simply turn around 180 degrees and hit you with that attack anyway. This is cheap, not difficoult. -1 point.
Then there is the game balance: it feels like they spent less than 10 minuttes to balance this game. In a lot of late game areas, enemies are just basic scrubs that do nothing, while a mid game area might have enemies that will utterly destroy you regardless of stats and defence. Bosses also do WAYYYY too much damage in proportion to how often they attack and how long their combos are. They get to kill me in 2-3 hits while being able to chain 3-7 attacks in a row, while I'm lucky to land 1 single hit before they jump away from me and just stare at me from the other side of the area. This is utterly stupid. -2 points.
Next is the ability to respec, upgrade weapons, and change builds: this is hopeless.... the game is incredibly stingy with upgrade materials, and even if you obtain the bellbearings, the mats get increasingly expensive. You need a total of 12 of each basic smithingstone to max a weapon, from lvl 1 stones to lvl 9 stones. And lvl 8 stones cost 30 000 runes a piece, just to give an example. This discourages experimentation in a game with over 100 weapons. Respecing is also limited, as there is a fixed amount of larval tears you can obtain in a single playthrough. This can hardlock you to stick with the same build through the whole game. -2 points. 
Now we are down to 4/10. Now lets add the good things: The world is big, with lots of things to discover around every corner. Everything from weapons, mats and spells, to catacombs, castles and dungeons. Exploration is very rewarding. +2 points.
Buildvariaty: if we look away from the horrible upgrade system, there is a lot of different ways to build your character. You can go pure meele, or pure spell/incantation builds, or heavily focus on status buildup, or make a combination of either of them, and much more. +1 point.
Encounters: there are many npcs to stumble upon in this game, most of wich leads to new side quests or detours, or even new areas. Some are missable, wich can lead to missing out on certain questlines or items, but this isn't really a problem. The npcs of this game are fairly interesting, and some will even fight alongside you at certain bosses if you summon them. +1 point.
Now we are at 8/10. There is a lot more that drag this game both up and down, but these are my takes. Personally I give the game a 7/10. It's an overall good game, especially with certain mods, but it can be really frustrating at times, and I can't really think of anyone I would ever recommend this game to. I had my fun, along with much frustration.

Edit:I changed to thumbs up, simply because I actually found someone to recommend the game to. So now the answer is "yes, I will recommend this game with or without mods to someone".

Look, I'm bitter, but my save data was just corrupted after 470+ hours of playtime. (It's probably closer to about 400 hours, as there were several points where I just had to step away for a while when the game was running.)

The fact that the lost save data can happen feels a bit ludicrous, especially when other players have experienced the same thing and cite a.) fully manual attempts to recover and b.) very low probability of success in recovery.

(Yes, I tried several things, and, no, none were successful. Also, no, I don't use any mods.)

I had started a second character, and that character was my first time going through the DLC. I'm getting kicked out of playing just before I got to experience the last couple of bosses -- the really big ones for the story that would finally test my character and play.

It's all pretty devastating, and it's enough so that I'm willing to just go ahead and leave a negative review for the fact that I could have had this deeply unsatisfying conclusion at any point after being many hours into the game.

The game needs better save management so that this doesn't happen. The game itself crashed during the DLC several times and always yelled at me when I logged back in, and now I would have to start over on hundreds of hours worth of work if I wanted to see this through.

That, to me, with even just a 1% chance of happening, is a pretty bad thing to let happen to many paying players.

You want to know about the game itself?
It's very Fromsoft, and it has an absolute ton of things going for it.
That said, on a per-hour-of-play basis, it's below any Dark Souls title or Sekiro for me.
You're getting a ton if you get the game, but you're also getting some baggage and the risk of losing your save like I did.

10/10 – Nearly 1,000 Hours Across Platforms

I don’t throw this around lightly: this is one of the best games I’ve ever played.

Across multiple platforms, I’ve accumulated nearly 1,000 hours in Elden Ring. My first playthrough alone was around 170 hours. Later runs went over 200. Most recently, I completed a 3-hour NG+2 speedrun to finish every achievement.

A game does not hold your attention for 1,000 hours unless it’s doing something special.

The World

The Lands Between is one of the most rewarding open worlds in gaming. It doesn’t hold your hand. It doesn’t flood your map with meaningless icons. It lets you explore naturally.

Every region feels distinct. Limgrave feels like discovery. Caelid feels oppressive. Leyndell feels earned. Exploration isn’t filler — it’s progression.

On my first run, I explored everything. Every cave. Every boss. Every hidden path. And even hundreds of hours later, I was still discovering things I had missed.

Combat & Build Variety

The build depth is absurd.

Lightning, faith, bleed, frost, magic, strength, dex — almost anything is viable if you understand the mechanics. I’ve experimented with high-damage lightning builds, buff stacking setups, hybrid stat spreads, and Ash of War nukes just to push damage numbers as far as possible.

The game rewards experimentation. It rewards knowledge. It rewards mastery.

Watching your character evolve from struggling through early bosses to routing NG+ cycles efficiently feels incredible.

Difficulty & Freedom

The difficulty is challenging but fair — and more importantly, flexible.

If something feels impossible, you can leave. Level up. Change builds. Explore somewhere else. The game respects your time and your decisions.

By NG+2, I wasn’t just surviving bosses — I was executing clean runs.

That progression feels earned, not handed to you.

Replay Value

This is where the game truly stands out.

It transforms depending on how you approach it:

First run: exploration and survival.
Second run: optimization.
Later runs: experimentation.
Endgame: speed and efficiency.

I went from a 170-hour immersive first playthrough to a 3-hour NG+2 clear. That kind of growth doesn’t happen unless the game systems are deep and well-designed.

Very few games evolve with the player like this.

Final Verdict

This became my first fully completed achievement game — not because I forced myself to finish it, but because I genuinely didn’t want to stop playing.

If a game can give you nearly 1,000 hours of enjoyment across multiple platforms and still make you want to start “just one more run,” that’s not just a good game.

That’s a masterpiece.

Nearly 1,000 hours later, and I’d still press “New Game” again without hesitation.
Just might be the best game ever made.

This is my first fromsoftware game that i have tried  and it is really nice game with many gimmicks and mechanics. The world is beautiful and one of the most detailed worlds that I have seen in a game. The open-world is really vast with many quirks. The boss fights are very well crafted and rememberable.

Elden Ring ring is a mostly good game. I say "mostly" because one of the things that the game puts a heavy emphasis on is also one of its serious downfalls. That being the bosses.

[b]Pretty much every dragon boss is a copy and paste of the last with a different status effect.[/b] It really makes dragons feel like more of an inconvenience because you'll get good at fighting them by your second or third dragon boss. They should be way more threatening and keep you on your toes with mixed up movesets. Instead, they become old very quick. (this doesn't only apply to dragons, however they make for a great example)

[b]Elden Ring also has some of the worst implementations of duo bosses I've seen in the series.[/b] Duo bosses' attacks don't compliment eachother whatsoever, they're too independent to the point where it's like you're fighting two boss battles at the same time instead of a single 2v1 battle. The constant rushing of some bosses in this game really doesn't help either.

I'll use Valiant Gargoyles as an example:
One of their attacks is an AoE that does both instant damage and poison build up, which is fine. We've seen attacks like that hundreds of time before. Where the issue lies though is that you're sometimes put in a situation where this AoE attack is near unavoidable because the second Gargoyle wants to get up your backside CONSTANTLY, which leads you to being stuck in a poison AoE whilst also try dodge wild swings from another enemy. You're pretty much guranteed to take damage and you just have to take it. That's not a "git gud" moment, that's just poor boss design.

[b]Some boss strings are so quick they're almost impossible to dodge completely.[/b] This wouldn't be an issue if dodging the first attack of a string would give you an improved opportunity to evade the rest of said string, but with some bosses that isn't the case. The player's movement doesn't match the speed of some of the flurries thrown at you.

Luckily, this is a pretty uncommon occurrence and so it doesn't affect the majority of bosses, but it is still a very clear issue with balancing in this game...

[b]With all that being said, Elden Ring is still a very fun experience.[/b] Moving to an open world map offers for a lot more exploration and secrets that previous souls games. There's a whole bunch of NPCs to interact with and side quests to complete, which will keep you occupied for hours. There's a huge range of weapons and spells to find throughout your playthrough which really adds to the freedom of stylising your builds.

I do have other critiques and complaints about this game but it'll turn this into a much longer review than I'd like to make it.

And if you're someone who has already played Elden Ring and hasn't given the Dark Souls series a try yet, I highly recommend you give it a shot. It's a much more linear and more hardcore experience than Elden Ring but it makes beating it all the more satisfying.

[h2]Elden Ring is a great game, yet with glaring issues when you scratch the surface! Oh thee, lowly Tarnished...[/h2]

Elden Ring was my first Souls game, yet I've seen playthroughs of the Dark Souls games, so I was pretty aware of what to expect when I started playing. Struggle... struggle... and yet more struggle. My aim was to do a blind playthrough, but I quickly decided to check out some "non-spoiler" guides to actually enjoy the game. Overall I did have a great time, yet at times the game was insanely frustrating and unfair, which was to be expected. The game is wellmade, yet has some glaring issues...

[h3]Positives:[/h3]
1. The combat: Overall a great feeling when you manage to progress through parts of the game or killing a hard boss that you've been struggling on. There's a lot to learn and master, which improves your performance over time. Just get to grinding!
2. Builds: Anything and everything can work on any build, some things are obviously better (even broken) than others. You can choose yourself if you want to play with them and cheese bosses.
3. Difficulty "settings": Being able to play with OP builds/weapons, summons (spirit ashes) increased my enjoyment by a lot! I would've needed probably around 200-300 hrs to finish the game without them. Wiping on bosses for 100+ wipes is simply not enjoyable for me, but hey if you like that, go for it! "Unless you kill the boss on first try without summons and being full-naked with no weapons, then it's not a legit kill!", just touch grass lol!
4. Exploration & The Aesthetics: The Open World is simply amazing. I spent the first ten hours just exploring Limgrave (1st zone) and bonking around. It was great and I kept finding new secrets all the time. 

[h3]The negatives:[/h3]
1. Reused assets: There's simply *too much* in the game. Side content such as catacombs, mines, mobs etc are just copy+pasted in several locations. The first few "secrets" are hype to discover, but finding the roughly same layout of catacombs with the same boss after 50+ hrs is simply not fun. I think the game would've been better with a smaller and more compacted design (fewer unique bosses/zones), with a smaller map. 
2. Controls: The mount (Torrent) is amazing, but the [b]mount controls on PC are HORRIBLE![/b] I can't count the amount of times I've died due to the goat simply jumping off the map, even if my input was the opposite way... Not to mention the JP-path to the [b]Frenzied Flame in the severs... I spent like 30 mins and 20+ deaths trying to get down there, because my character randomly kept overshooting/moving on landing etc[/b]
3. "Punishing gameplay": The difficulty of the game is FINE and Souls games are supposed to be challenging and punishing. To a degree I would even say that they are supposed to "waste your time", until you "git gud". However... there are a lot of elements that are simply unfair. Many aspects (maps, bosses, mobs) are deliberatly designed to make you ragequit. I don't mind the challenge, but it should at least be a "even playing field", where you can learn.
4. The tryhard community: Holy... reading the input of parts of the Souls community makes me question my life choices. Can you just let people play the game THE WAY THEY WANT. If you want to play it as a "no-hit, naked, no ashes"-playthrough, then do so. Stop bothering people who use spirit ashes, summons etc. You can enjoy the game the way you want, and others are entitled to the same...

[h3]Overall a very solid game. Punishing & challenging, yet very enjoyable. Would strongly recommend, even though its apparant flaws![/h3]

I love it when multiple aspects of a game combine together to form a cohesive whole that exceeds the sum of its parts. Elden Ring, unfortunately, failed do that for me. And while I don't want to not recommend a game I had a lot of fun playing, there are just too many seemingly small irksome factors here that compound to produce a somewhat tedious experience for me where every time I'm about to enter a boss arena, I shudder at the thought of having to spend the next hour or two (or four) grinding that boss. Keep in mind that I'm no expert at this game, obviously; I've yet to beat R+EB & M (I'm sure everyone understands who I'm referring to). I simply did not have the heart to continue playing Elden Ring and this review serves as my closure so that I don't keep ruminating over it afterwards.

As I stated before, I have many "minor" gripes with this game.
[spoiler]
[h2]1. The Gear Upgrade System[/h2]
Let's start with an easy one. Elden Ring, is significantly more open than previous games. It has a bunch of cool weapons, spells, incantations and items to enable further exploration and every time I see a new exciting looking item, I want to try it out immediately and to this end, ER does have a re-spec system. But in classic FromSoft fashion, it is quite limited.

I can only re-spec my character if I have a larval tear in my inventory. So, every time I want to change my build after finding a new item or in response to a boss, I need to go take a massive detour and try to find larval tears on my own, or look up the wiki and go on a much smaller detour. You can guess my preference. Not only that, after the re-spec, I also need to upgrade my new shiny weapon/staff/seal so that it does not do terrible damage, which means, you guessed it, more massive detours (or wiki-powered smaller detours).

I just wish that ER had the following two QoL upgrades in order to incentivize exploration, if at least for the first playthrough (I know that during subsequent playthroughs, players either look up or cook up a build and beeline towards the items they want while ignoring everything else).
[list]
[*][b]Free re-specs[/b], similar to games like Divinity Original Sin 2.
[*][b]Smithing stone transfer[/b]: If I am to re-spec my character, chances are my previous fully upgraded weapon is now completely unusable anyway. So why not just let me transfer the +X upgrade to my new weapon. Of course, if I have two +25 (or +10) weapons and I want a +25 seal on top of that, I [i]have[/i] to farm, but exchanging one +25 weapon for another +25 weapon does not feel "unfair" to me at all. If I lose the ability/desire to use a certain weapon, having it rot in my inventory while I have to either find more stones or farm more runes to buy stones feels tedious.
[/list]
[h2]2. Enemies[/h2]
[h3]2.1. Design[/h3]
To me souls games live or die by their enemies. These games are not the most flashy/combo-driven and have relatively simple weapon movesets so most of the fun comes from fighting interesting enemies. But enemies in ER just have ridiculous physical form and movesets. Some of the most annoying enemies are either massive and have hitboxes that greatly exceed the dodge window or are so ridiculously fast that they attack non-stop and constantly hitstun. Allow me to list out some [b]large[/b] enemies that have what feels like a million health and also do a million damage.

And then some ridiculously fast/multi hit enemies like rats, the blob with a million arms that has a wild combo, Grafted Scions, black-knife assassins and the insect guys that shoot the 100 needles also fit this mold. And then, in classic Souls fashion, there are enemies that cast insta-kill clouds.
[h3]Placement and Scaling[/h3]
Outside of some enemies being inherently annoying, their placement and scaling, especially in late game areas, feels to me as if I'm supposed to avoid them altogether. In the mountaintops, the only enemies I found were giant crows, giant t-rex dogs, giant hands, rune bears and so forth. Catacombs now have the giant stone dogs as normal enemies. The Zamur heros are also just normal enemies now. The haligtree branches also has those massive trumpet bubble guys. Not to mention the giant ants in Ainsel that do a ton of damage.

On top of this ridiculous placement, the damage they deal is also outrageous. One strike from any of these enemies does like 50-75% of my health bar at 50 vigor. Some kill in one hit or one hitstun combo. Fighting one such enemy takes like 2-3 charges of my flask on a good day which quickly gets tedious.
[h2]3. Bosses and Rhythm[/h2]
ER has good bosses, outside of the obviously annoying ones. But I can't help but notice that every boss has an unstoppable flurry of 5-7 piece combos paired with a highly off putting rhythm. ER almost feels like a turn based game to me where the boss does a 7 hit combo while I dodge, then I get like two seconds to counter-attack wherein if I am not in the exact place to strike back, I lose that opportunity. Even staggered bosses require stamina to reposte, so while I stand around recharging my stamina for one second, the boss has already recovered.

The rhythm of the fight also just seems to demand rote memorization. I can't seem to extrapolate the rhythm or tempo of the whole fight by sampling a handful of random moves in my first few attempts. I just feel like every move is uniquely timed to catch rolls and dish out maximum punishment. Unless I can just out damage the boss, and there are builds capable of doing that, I just feel like I have to experience every single move first hand over the course of 2-3 hours before I can finally make any progress. This has been a real bummer for me, especially in the case of Rhadann (Starscourge), Maliketh, Godfrey, Malenia and Mogh (sewer and palace). The attacks these bosses do seems almost randomized where sometimes the exact same combo ends after 3 hits and other times is immediately followed up by another combo basically obliterating my punish window, punishing me instead for daring to attack after what felt like (and was in 60% of the cases) the final hit of the combo. After this happens a couple times, I am just afraid to go in again, what if there are more follow up hits? After like 20 attempts of failing to make heads or tails of the fight and making zero, I am forced watch a YouTube guide breaking down every single move and possible follow up which I then internalize and beat the boss in the next 5 attempts. This does not feel fun to me, it feels like I'm learning an instrument that I can't even play a song in.

Just for illustration, the rhythm of these fights feels something like this:

one . . . two . . . . . . . . three FOUR . . five

orr, maybe like this:

. . . . one TWO THREE . . four . . . . . . five

or perhaps:

. . one TWO . . . . three FOUR

or most likely, all of the above in a single fight, where every single move has a distinct rhythm and the rhythm of one chain of combos simply does not apply to another. I could go on but I am literally hitting the character limit.
[/spoiler]
[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
I really want to like ER. Heck, if I persisted, I could probably beat both M and R+EB in due time but I just couldn't bring myself plough on; it does not feel rewarding for me to do so. This is also, in part, because the DLC seems to exaggerate the exact same things that I've disliked about the base game. Maybe I can come back to it in 6 months and enjoy it again in the way I have enjoyed the earlier parts of ER but for the time being I feel like I'm done.

Elden Ring to jedna z tych gier, które jeszcze przed premierą zostały wyniesione na piedestał. Produkcja studia FromSoftware, twórców serii Dark Souls, była zapowiadana jako rozwinięcie znanej formuły w otwartym świecie. Efekt końcowy jest jednak bardziej złożony. To gra z wieloma świetnymi pomysłami, ale jednocześnie z wyraźnymi problemami projektowymi, które często wpływają na komfort rozgrywki.

System rozwoju postaci

Jednym z największych atutów gry jest ogromna różnorodność buildów. Gracz może rozwijać postać na wiele sposobów, od klasycznego wojownika z ciężką bronią, przez szybkie buildy zręcznościowe, aż po potężne postacie oparte na magii. System rozwoju daje dużą swobodę i zachęca do eksperymentowania.

Problem pojawia się jednak w trakcie rozgrywki. Dość często okazuje się, że build, który wcześniej działał bardzo dobrze, nagle przestaje być skuteczny. W pewnym momencie trafiamy na ścianę i przeciwnicy lub bossowie zaczynają być wyraźnie trudniejsi dla konkretnego stylu gry. W efekcie gracz zamiast rozwijać postać według własnej wizji zaczyna dostosowywać się do wymagań konkretnych walk.

Oprawa wizualna i świat gry

Pod względem artystycznym gra prezentuje się znakomicie. Świat jest ogromny, różnorodny i pełen charakterystycznych lokacji, a każdy region ma swój klimat i wizualną tożsamość.

Na uwagę zasługuje również historia świata współtworzona przez George R. R. Martin. Lore jest ciekawy i intrygujący, choć duża część fabuły pozostaje ukryta w opisach przedmiotów i fragmentach dialogów. Dla jednych jest to element budujący tajemnicę świata, dla innych bariera w odbiorze historii.

Problemy z kamerą

Największą wadą gry jest kamera. To właśnie tutaj pojawia się najwięcej sytuacji prowadzących do frustracji.

Podczas walki z przeciwnikiem można zablokować kamerę na celu. W teorii ma to pomagać w śledzeniu przeciwnika, ale w praktyce często prowadzi do chaosu. Kamera potrafi się gubić, nagle zmieniać pozycję albo ustawiać pod dziwnym kątem. W efekcie gracz nie widzi ani ataków przeciwnika, ani czasami nawet własnej postaci.

Problem szczególnie nasila się przy dużych przeciwnikach. Kamera potrafi wtedy ustawić się tak blisko modelu bossa, że trudno ocenić sytuację na ekranie. Próba grania bez blokady celu również nie rozwiązuje problemu, ponieważ kamera nadal potrafi poruszać się samoczynnie i nie zawsze pozostaje tam, gdzie gracz chciałby ją ustawić. W praktyce oznacza to, że część zgonów nie wynika z błędu gracza ani z poziomu trudności walki, lecz z problemów technicznych i projektowych.

Powtarzalność przeciwników i bossów

Kolejną wadą jest design przeciwników oraz powtarzalność wielu walk. W wielu miejscach widać wyraźne użycie metody kopiuj i wklej. Boss, z którym wcześniej stoczyliśmy efektowną walkę, później pojawia się jako zwykły przeciwnik w innej lokacji.

Osłabia to poczucie wyjątkowości starć i sprawia, że niektóre momenty przestają być tak znaczące, jak powinny. Walki bywają widowiskowe, ale to nie zawsze oznacza, że są dobrze zaprojektowane. Niektóre starcia sprawiają wrażenie mocno oskryptowanych. Czasami wygląda to tak, jakby można je było przejść sensownie tylko jednym konkretnym stylem gry, ponieważ inne podejścia są znacznie trudniejsze.

Podejście do nowych graczy

Gra nie szanuje również graczy, którzy wcześniej nie mieli styczności z tytułami typu Souls. W wielu momentach zakłada się, że gracz już zna mechaniki charakterystyczne dla tego gatunku. Systemy gry są słabo tłumaczone i wiele rzeczy trzeba odkrywać metodą prób i błędów.

Popularność marki w dużej mierze opiera się na opinii o jej wyjątkowej trudności. W praktyce jednak spora część tej trudności wynika z problemów projektowych. Nieczytelność walki, problemy z kamerą czy niespójne decyzje designerskie sprawiają, że gra bywa wymagająca nie dlatego, że przeciwnicy są świetnie zaprojektowani, ale dlatego, że niektóre elementy gry utrudniają komfortowe granie.

System punktów odrodzenia

Dobrym przykładem niespójnego designu jest system punktów odrodzenia. Czasami ognisko znajduje się dosłownie przed areną bossa, a dodatkowo mamy jeszcze statuę, która pozwala odrodzić się jeszcze bliżej. W innych sytuacjach po każdej śmierci trzeba pokonywać długą drogę z ogniska do bramy bossa.

Przy trudniejszych przeciwnikach, takich jak Malenia, Blade of Miquella, oznacza to, że spora część czasu nie jest poświęcona samej walce. Zamiast tego gracz biegnie z powrotem do areny i ponownie nakłada buffy przed starciem. W efekcie nawet jedna czwarta czasu spędzonego przy bossie może polegać po prostu na powtarzaniu tej samej drogi.

Podsumowanie

Elden Ring jest produkcją pełną kontrastów. Z jednej strony oferuje piękny świat, ciekawy lore i ogromne możliwości budowania postaci. Z drugiej strony cierpi na wyraźne problemy projektowe, takie jak praca kamery, powtarzalność przeciwników czy niespójne rozwiązania w designie walk.

Nie jest to zła gra, ale zdecydowanie nie jest też tak bezbłędna, jak sugerują niektóre opinie. Część graczy wynosi ją na piedestał głównie ze względu na renomę studia FromSoftware, a niekoniecznie przez faktyczną jakość wszystkich elementów gry. To tytuł, który potrafi zachwycić wizją świata, ale jednocześnie momentami potrafi też bardzo frustrować.

My first dodge-based souls/souls-like game, I found the game overall great (I still prefer parry-based systems like sekiro/lies of p). By far the best aspect is the open world exploration and subtle worldbuilding, but I would've enjoyed to see more of a narrative/story. The environments are gorgeous and the game runs well on PC. The music is good too, although not much was memorable. Unfortunately, I knew of some of the bosses and a couple areas from social media (like sword woman, blood man, first couple major bosses, and final boss), but the exploration was still top tier, as most areas I have not seen. This game is the game to play if you are looking for exploration. Another pro is the gameplay; the game feels snappy and responsive, very cool enemy designs, and it is overall satisfying to play. 

There are also some cons. The main, unavoidable one is having an open world souls game, as that makes some areas you explore "out of order" easier or harder than "intended". For example, I followed the main quest for a little, then I went back to the starting region and found the rest of that region really easy. Similarly, since there are so many extra places and things to do to earn souls, I got to a high enough level starting at the midgame that I could beat every boss in one or two attempts, and a lot of the endgame bosses also became too easy aside from malenia (beat blood man, and the final few bosses all in 1 or 2 attempts). There were no exceptionally difficult bosses, as I only had 3 bosses take around 2 hours (malenia, 1st tree sentinel, and a black blade kindred), but I think it is hard to make an exceptionally difficult boss because of the open world nature of the game. The other primary con I had was the parkour/jumping was janky, which was sometimes frustrating. 

Overall, if you like exploration and some challenge, this is the game for you (or you could use summons to make it easier). However, because of the open world, many of the bosses will end up being too easy if you choose to explore a lot. If you are looking for a challenging souls game, you can get that as long as you choose not to level up as much, otherwise the main draw of the game is exploration.

What else can I say other than that this game is a modern classic. I love how open ended and expansive the game is with there being so many options on how to tackle the humongous world. I've done multiple playthroughs of this game on different platforms and each one always leads to new discoveries and challenges. From spirit ash summons, swappable ashes of war/special attacks, the wonderous physick, new weapon and spell types, and multiple accessible areas of varying difficulty at the start, the game is yours to customize to your taste with no need for traditional difficulty options. Those who want an easier time with magic and the like will also have to do a lot more exploring which makes it feel much more like you have earned your power instead of gaining power by just getting a bunch of money and making a number go up (and before you ask, yes my first playthrough was done with a no summon, no buff, pure strength melee run with the bastard sword so I think I've earned my right to have fun). The game also hides many large areas behind side content, hidden walls, and quest lines which is a double edged sword since it can mean you find hours of new content on repeat playthroughs, but at the same time it means that many useful items for builds may never be found if you don't look in the right places or use a guide.

My main problem with the game is you'll encounter the same couple bosses (many of which become normal enemies) over the course of the game and that lots of the side areas have copy pasted layouts, gimmicks, and enemies (although much of it is designed with some intentionality which I will take any day over the god forsaken chalice dungeons of Bloodborne). I'd highly recommend anyone who plays to pace themselves and to vary up what side content they engage with or you'll be in for quite a few boring hours. After the first playthrough, making a new build can also be less interesting as the game just becomes a checklist to get whatever you want for a certain loadout. My last problem off the top of my head is that multiplayer has been gutted quite a bit with what would traditionally be covenants in the souls games now being reduced to questlines and player invasions only happening to players with summons. The "covenants" in the game are also quite meaningless since you can just join every faction you come across freely with no penalty or rivalry between them, losing much of the identity and focus of what was in the souls games.

Overall, although the game isn't absolutely perfect I still think that the quality shines through and it is worth at least one playthrough, if not more.

Elden Ring is, quite simply, a masterpiece and easily a 10/10 experience in my book. It stands as one of the most complete and ambitious action RPGs ever created and firmly sits in my personal top 10 games of all time.

The most immediate achievement Elden Ring delivers is its open world design. The Lands Between feel vast, mysterious, and endlessly explorable without ever relying on traditional map markers or hand-holding. Discovery happens naturally through curiosity, whether stumbling upon hidden dungeons, unexpected bosses, or entire underground regions that feel like secrets waiting to be uncovered. Exploration consistently rewards players with meaningful encounters, gear, lore, or progression opportunities, making nearly every direction feel worth investigating.

Combat builds upon the refined mechanics seen in previous FromSoftware titles while expanding player freedom dramatically. The variety of weapons, Ashes of War, spells, summons, and build paths allows players to craft highly personalized playstyles. Whether leaning into melee mastery, magic dominance, hybrid experimentation, or unconventional approaches, Elden Ring supports creativity in ways that feel empowering rather than restrictive.

Boss design is another major highlight. The game features some of the best encounters FromSoftware has ever produced, blending spectacle, mechanical challenge, and strong thematic presence. Many fights feel like climactic moments that reflect the world’s mythology and decay, creating victories that are both mechanically satisfying and narratively meaningful.

The lore and worldbuilding are equally exceptional. Elden Ring presents a layered mythos filled with fallen demigods, fractured powers, and cosmic influences that players gradually piece together through exploration, dialogue, and item descriptions. This approach preserves the studio’s signature interpretive storytelling while scaling it to match the game’s massive world.

Atmosphere and art direction further elevate the experience. Every region carries a distinct identity, from golden plains to scarlet wastelands and haunting eternal cities. The visual variety ensures that the world rarely feels repetitive despite its size, maintaining a constant sense of wonder and discovery.

In terms of flaws, there are very few that significantly impact the experience. Crafting stands out as the most noticeable limitation. While it functions as a useful supplementary system, many players can progress comfortably without relying heavily on it. As a mechanic, it feels like it had potential for deeper integration into gameplay loops, but its current implementation often makes it optional rather than essential.

Even with that minor criticism, Elden Ring succeeds on nearly every level. Its world design, combat depth, boss encounters, lore, and atmosphere come together to form an experience that feels both expansive and cohesive. It captures the sense of adventure and discovery that defines the best RPGs while maintaining the challenge and identity that FromSoftware is known for.

Overall, Elden Ring is a landmark title that represents the peak of modern action RPG design. With unforgettable exploration, some of the studio’s strongest bosses, and deeply compelling lore, it stands as an easy recommendation and a game that will likely be remembered as one of the defining releases of its generation.

The narrative atmosphere is strong but distant. Lore is delivered cryptically, requiring significant interpretation, which can enrich immersion but also reduce emotional engagement. Smaller design issues clunky menus and sparse system explanations add friction.

I liked aspects of it, particularly the art direction and moments of discovery, but the overall experience feels mechanically stagnant. It is polished and competent, yet rarely transcends its core loop or delivers sustained innovation.

A recent return to Elden Ring finally helped me understand what so many players have been praising for years. After multiple past attempts where the magic just didn’t click, this latest playthrough opened my eyes to how remarkable the game truly is. The world is stunning, with sweeping vistas, intricate ruins, and atmospheric lighting that make every region feel alive. The sound design elevates that sense of place even further—haunting ambient tracks, thunderous boss themes, and crisp combat audio all work together to pull you deeper into the Lands Between.

The combat is where everything really came together for me. It’s challenging, sometimes brutally so, but it’s also deliberate, responsive, and endlessly rewarding once the rhythm sets in. What made the difficulty feel more manageable this time was embracing both player summons and spirit ashes. They don’t trivialize the game, but they smooth out the rough edges enough to let the brilliance of the encounters shine through instead of feeling like a wall.

After finally “getting it,” I can confidently say Elden Ring is an exceptional experience—one that rewards persistence with moments of awe, triumph, and discovery. 9.5/10.
