[h1] One of the greatest and highest-quality games ever made. [/h1]

I’ve been putting this game off for a long time because, honestly, I’m not a big fan of open-world games. Too many of them feel bloated, repetitive, and filled with busywork and i get lost and frustrate easily. Elden Ring is different. This is open-world done right. The map is massive, but it never feels like lazy copy-paste filler. Every region feels distinct: different enemies, different bosses, different environments, and different challenges. Exploration is constantly rewarded—whether it’s a powerful weapon, a new spell, a hidden dungeon, or lore that makes you stop and think. You’re not just wandering for the sake of it; the game respects your time and curiosity.

Elden Ring doesn’t rely on cutting-edge, photorealistic graphics—and it doesn’t need to. The art direction is absolutely stunning. There were multiple moments where I literally put the controller down just to stare at the scenery. This game is living proof that art direction > realism every single time.

The character and boss designs are incredible. Every major boss feels unique, intimidating, and straight-up badass. Add in the phenomenal soundtrack, and every boss fight feels like an epic event. Even when you’re getting absolutely destroyed, you can’t help but appreciate how cool everything looks and sounds.

The combat is easily the best part of the game. The combat is deep, satisfying, and insanely flexible. There are countless ways to play: different classes, builds, weapons, spells, and playstyles. This gives the game ridiculous replay value—you could finish it multiple times and still feel like you’re playing something new.

Boss fights are intense and memorable, but also frustrating as hell—sometimes in the funniest way. Some bosses will start an attack, stall for what feels like 20 years (just like my government), and then drop it on you the moment you least expect it. Painful? Yes. Memorable? Absolutely.

I’m not going to sugarcoat it: this game is hard. That said, it’s more forgiving than other Souls games thanks to mechanics like spirit summons and co-op options. The difficulty feels challenging rather than unfair, and the game gives you tools to overcome obstacles—if you’re willing to experiment and adapt.

The story is dark, mysterious, and incredibly alluring—but it won’t hold your hand. There are no 20-minute cinematics explaining everything, no quest logs telling you exactly where to go. If you don’t pay attention to NPC dialogue, item descriptions, and environmental clues, you will get lost.

The narrative is told in fragments, pieced together by the player. It’s written by Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R. R. Martin, so expect heavy themes of decay, tragedy, and a world on the brink of collapse. If you want a straightforward, cinematic story, this isn’t it—but if you enjoy deep lore and worldbuilding, it’s one of the best in modern gaming.

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]

If you have the patience of a saint and the curiosity of a cat, buy this game. If you value your blood pressure, maybe think twice. But skipping Elden Ring means missing out on one of the most ambitious, rewarding, and unforgettable gaming experiences ever made.

This is my first Souls-like game, so I’m leaving comments open in case someone wants to share their perspective or maybe spark my interest in the genre again. That said, I genuinely don’t see the appeal.

I played fairly deep into the game, far enough to defeat major bosses, slay something massive, and set something important on fire (no spoilers). So this isn’t a surface level take.

Story:
There barely is a story. What’s there feels vague and disconnected, more like a sequence of boss fights than a narrative. Lore exists, sure, but it’s buried so deeply that it never felt engaging or motivating to me. I never felt invested in what I was doing or why. Is it the genre? Like racing games where lore and story is not the point? 

Combat:
It’s… fine. Rarely exciting. The biggest issue is rewards: you’re showered with an overwhelming number of weapons, most of which feel completely pointless. Beating around 95% of bosses gives you nothing meaningful, which is a big problem when the game is essentially a boss-rush experience. Progress often feels hollow.

Setting:
The world is technically open, but it feels lifeless. There are almost no people, no real villages, no towns just ruins and enemies. Exploration didn’t feel rewarding or immersive, it felt empty. An open world should invite curiosity, not make you feel alone in a dead museum.

Overall I don’t understand the obsession. For me, Elden Ring feels more like endurance than enjoyment and I will not be returning to the genre again... Maybe for that Napoleon era game.

Elden Ring is an exceptional entry in the Soulslike genre and one of the best executions of its formula to date. It’s demanding and opaque, but far more approachable than earlier titles, making it a strong—if still challenging—entry point for newcomers willing to engage with its systems. I waited until a second playthrough to review it, and it genuinely may be one of the greatest games ever made. That said, meaningful criticism is often dismissed with “get good,” which does the game no favors. The story and worldbuilding are genuinely interesting, but deliberately esoteric. Lore is fragmented, subtle, and easy to miss if you don’t already know what to look for. It can feel scattered and opaque, but that’s very much how these games operate—and for many players, that mystery is part of the appeal.

Brief note for new players: ranged magic builds are extremely powerful but hard to set up without deep game knowledge; melee builds are easier to start with, but significantly harder to master in practice.

Love this game. I hadn't played any of the souls games before getting Elden Ring, and I feel like it's a perfect introduction to the series/genre. There's just enough tutorial and guidance to give the player the tools needed to progress but it's still vague and difficult enough to maintain the challenging nature these types of games are known for. I've played a lot and it's been really fun and motivating to improve at the game. Now, with just over 200 hours, I've gone from not knowing that the roll was a dodge to getting close on my first no-hit run and I'm still loving it.

The DLC, Shadow of the Erdtree, is much closer to some of the other souls games in nature. It's significantly more difficult than the base game, and much more confusing to piece together the narrative and even figure out where you need to go. There were several major areas and bosses that I completely missed my first time playing through the DLC, whereas I found almost all of them in the base game even with no souls experience. 

All in all, I'd give the game a solid 8/10. I'm taking one point off because perfect games don't exist, and another because there are a few annoying aspects of some of the major boss fights. They aren't difficulty problems so much as they are things that just make the experience of fighting those bosses less enjoyable than they could be (i.e. Godskin Duo's inconsistent AI, the fire physics, Divine Beast Dancing Lion's existence...), so other people may think differently.

Elden Ring + Shadow of the Erdtree was my first Souls game and I wasn’t fully prepared for either the combat or the storytelling. I went in with guidance from an experienced player, and looking back, I probably should’ve kept a death counter. Frustrating at times, but also a clear marker of progress as those deaths slowly became fewer.

The world design is visually stunning. I had multiple moments of cresting a hill and just stopping to take it all in. Sometimes breathtakingly beautiful (notably for me, Limgrave, Liurnia, Gravesite Plains), other times deeply unsettling (horrid and grotesque Caelid). The underground areas, especially Nokron and Nokstella, felt other-worldly and remain some of my favorite locations in the game.

Boss designs are massive and intimidating, making each fight feel truly epic. The music complements this perfectly: choral, gothic, and atmospheric when needed, then swelling into dramatic orchestral scores during combat without overwhelming the scenery.

Cons 
- Story is obscure and difficult to follow (I had expected more cnematic cutscenes similar to that of the beginning sequence introducing the world, but it only happened like that at beginning).
So, if you’re looking for a clearer or more accessable narrative, this probably isn’t the game for you.
That said, it didn’t hurt my enjoyment much, since my focus was learning combat and exploring the world.

- Wish there were an option to replay cutscenes (some moments I wanted to really re-visit)

Overall, Elden Ring (and its DLC) delivered an incredible sense of escapism. Between the hauntingly beautiful world, immersive music, and colossal bosses that tested my persistence, it was a rewarding experience.

Playing Elden Ring as an Intellect build completely changes the mechanical experience, and it’s incredibly satisfying. Combat shifts from melee pacing to high-stakes spellcasting, where timing, positioning, and resource management dominate. Spells hit hard, but each cast requires careful spacing, FP management, and awareness of enemy attack windows, turning every encounter into a tactical puzzle.

Sorceries, catalysts, and buffs feel distinct and meaningful. Selecting the right spells for range, crowd control, or single-target burst is crucial, and experimentation with combos like Glintstone Barrage followed by swift melee or ranged backup is highly rewarding. Spellcasting is not just powerful — it’s a mechanical system that encourages creativity and adaptability.

Movement and positioning are critical. Intellect builds rely on kiting enemies, reading attack patterns, and controlling engagement distances. Dodging and rolling aren’t optional; they’re key tools to survive while channeling high-damage sorceries. Mount combat also opens interesting tactical options, letting you cast and reposition simultaneously in open-world encounters.

Resource and cooldown management adds depth. FP consumption, catalyst upgrades, and buff durations create constant decisions about when to commit, retreat, or change tactics. Even boss fights feel like complex mechanical challenges, rewarding smart spell rotation, precise timing, and environmental awareness.

Elden Ring’s RPG systems shine for magic builds. Gear, talismans, and Ashes of War all meaningfully impact your playstyle, letting Intellect characters feel powerful without breaking combat balance. Every fight, exploration moment, and encounter is a test of skill and strategy, making victories feel earned.

10/10 — precise, tactical, and mechanically brilliant for spellcasters.

[h1] Its alright, I guess [/h1]
Fresh off the back of getting all achievements for Dark Souls 3 & Dark Souls Remastered (I've also completed and loved Sekiro), I decided to give Elden Ring a crack.

Elden Ring is arguably the culmination of lofty developer ambitions, twinned with game design trends of the time. A classic Dark Souls game (big dungeons, unforgiving combat, vague narrative and beautiful world design), but bigger and better, with an open world, teeming with optional content and areas to explore.

You play as 'Insert Name Here', who's a generic nobody, in a world that is uncaring. Along the way, to your vague goal, you meet various NPC's, conquer large dungeons and multiple mini-dungeons/tombs and get your bootay handed to you on many an occasion. Do you play melee warrior, ranged mage, or something in between? The choice is yours. It still won't help you 'git gud'!

I absolutely adore the world itself. It's beautiful, with some great setpieces (Stormveil & Raya Lucaria), a great soundtrack, and great variety in enemies and how you build your character. There's a good variety in bosses too. The soundtrack is really really great too, as with all Souls games.

Where I think this falls apart, is the open world. I don't think it adds anything, and coupled with the many many smaller dungeons scattered across the lands, I feel it causes the game to lose pace. I decided to clear all dungeons and kill all bosses (including mini-dungeons), getting every item available, which no doubt led to fatigue, and influenced my opinion on this, as I wanted to make sure I experienced everything the game had to offer.

I think the inclusion of a vast open world, works against the game and is very much a product of design trends at the time. What it does well, is the large, sprawling dungeons (classic style), along with music, area design and world building. I did however decide to skip the DLC, as I was so burned out at the end of NG, I didn't want more of the same.

I found that fun did return, once I was steam rolling NG+2 and NG+3, blitzing my way to the end and focusing on core objectives, having all the items I needed to just ignore optional areas/smaller dungeons altogether, and this ignoring all optional content, reminded me of why I liked previous games. It felt tighter, easier to get around, without the open world padding.

Each to their own, but I was disappointed by this, but then again, I was also disappointed by Breath of the Wild, because of how samey the mini-dungeons were, bar one or two which actually did something to differentiate themselves.
 

[h2] Summary [/h2]
[h3] Pros [/h3]
- World building
- Music
- Clean and responsive combat
- Multiple ways to build and play your character
- Lots to do
- Rani


[h3] Cons [/h3]
- Mini-dungeons feel repetitive and uninspired
- Traversing the open world gets really boring, really fast
- Invisible Scarabs
- Feels like there's too much to do, it's easy to lose track of key objectives

[h2] Final Verdict - 7/10 - Good Game [/h2]
This game is really worth a look at, if you're in need of another SoulsBourne title, and love open world games (e.g. Breath of the wild). If you don't like open world games, that is a major detracting factor, which will annoy you. So much of what there is great, but it's the middling areas in between, which feel like unnecessary padding, which work to its detriment. At 120 hours I really really wanted to love it, and gave it enough of my time to win me over, and went to great lengths to complete everything, but it just never clicked, and I think the open world is the reason. I'd rank this 45th best Souls game that I've completed (for me), with my order of Best > Worst games being Sekiro > Demons Souls > Dark Souls Remastered > Dark Souls 3 > Elden Ring.

It's a great experience. The combat, which I always thought at a glance looked a little boring, is in fact some of the most satisfying combat I've ever played. The variety of weapons are great, and they really feel good to use. I feel like anyone who wants to play a spell slinging, hack and slash game, anyone who ever dreamt of being a Merlin, or King Arthur, any dark, grim, knightly fantasy needs to play it. The enemies and bosses look wonderful. I'm not going to go too much into the good, you'll know it as soon as you start playing, and I think you should. I'm going to go through some bullet points of the bad, so that some people understand them.

-Some of the bosses are hard, simply for the sake of hard. Don't matter how big they are, they'll be able to move better than you, throw out more attacks faster and more often than you. It's not all bad, it can just get tiring after enough of them.

-The world is fairly massive, which is great, however, the verticality of it can get frustrating as can be. You'll see so many places, that look so close, but are so very hard to reach. When you start wanting to explore all of the Volcano Manor area of the map, you'll really understand what I'm talking about. Many hours were spent just figuring out, how I could get to places.

-This is both a positive and a negative. The game is completely open world. There is no journal or quests in the modern way we know them. This game is more related to the games of long long ago where if you want to know and understand the story, you're really going to have to pay attention and remember things, and I've found on a first play through, when you're so busy trying just to survive, and figure out how to get where, that it can be hard to do, so a lot of the time, I had a really vague idea on what was going on, who hated who, who loved who, and the reasons why. Not with everything and everyone, but enough for it to be kind of sad. 

-My biggest complaint and let down, is the ending I got, and I'm sure the others, are God awful. Short, open to interpritation, which makes me wonder if even learning all the lore is really worth it given the ending. It really irks me because of how much challenge, and how many hours you're going to drop into this game to be given next to nothing at the end of it. I mean that whole heartedly, next to nothing.

That said, I don't regret a minute of my playtime. The world is worth exploring, and the fights are worth fighting. The gameplay is fantastic, and it's presented something I hope future games emulate, just improve upon.

Elden Ring is special. I feel like FromSoft has been building up to this game since the first release of Dark Souls, possibly longer. This game is extremely well made and stunning in every sense of the word. I can talk about how beautiful the world is, how amazing the story is, how fine tuned and gratifying the combat is, how much fun it is to explore but I know you have heard that all before.

As someone who has played DS1, DS3 and Bloodborne I am used to some of the basic knowledge of how these games work. It is tricky though, because this game falls victim to one of the sharpest learning curves out there. It is difficult to call this a negative because I feel that this is part of what makes this game so special. I am a firm believer that this game would not work in a world without the internet. I feel like the meta of searching how to do some niche thing and finding an entire community of passionate people enjoying the game is part of the experience itself. Talking with your friends who have played it and explaining different tactics, gear, secrets and more is part of the fun. This game is not friendly, and I am not referring to the fact that it is "hard", but that it intentionally does not guide the player in any way. Yes there is a tutorial but most of the games mechanics are not explained in any way and just left for the players to experiment and find themselves. I spent my first 30 hours in the game when it first came out not understanding how Ashes of War worked. Not until I picked the game up again and started over recently did I start to understand how the combat worked fully.

I think the best example of this is the story of Elden Ring itself. A player can play hundreds of hours of the game and not understand a single thing of what's going on. Not understanding what NPCs are talking about, not understanding the overarching plot, maybe they dont even understand who Michela is (the key character in the story). Not until I started watching lore videos did I start piecing everything together and start to appreciate the impact someone like George RR Martin had on the creation of this game. Everything is not there to serve you, it just is. I think this is kind of magical in a way, breathing a sense of life into the world, as if it has always been there and you are just a passerby of this breathing beautiful world.
This is how all of the mechanics in the game feel, from the exploration to the combat to the obtuse side quests. Its tricky because if it was executed in any other way I would say this is just bad design but I believe it is the intentional fun of it. They want you to research, they want you to learn. By the time you finish Elden Ring for the first time, if you start all over from a new save you will undoubtedly be a better player because you have taken the time to learn and understand how the game works, not just because your end game character is level 150+.

This game is not for the causal player, and I am not saying that to gatekeep, I am saying that because I don't think you will be able to enjoy Elden Ring in any casual way, you absolutely have to “lock in”. It's funny to see when people are in the middle of their first playthrough because I have seen it basically take over their consciousness, once it starts, it works its way into your brain and it's hard to not stop thinking about it. I know that happened to me.

If you are willing to give Elden Ring your time and energy, you will not regret it. It is absolutely fantastic.

Не буду уподобляться игрожурам диванным, которые бы вычленили каждый аспект и оценили их отдельно по мнимой 10-балльной шкале или шаблону. Искусство судят в целости. Обзор представляет из себя хаотичный поток мыслей, посетивших автора на всех этапах игры. Это взгляд с перспективы человека, в чьей жизни Elden Ring не является первенцом из серии Souls. 
Игра удивительно хороша подкована технически. За всё время в ней я ни разу не сталкивался с вылетами или грубыми падениями кадров. Подловил себя на мысли, что ПК релиз, функционирующий настолько же безукоризненно как на эталонных консолях, сейчас уже как что-то из ряда вон выходящее. 
Японцам удалось нащупать баланс между плавной игрой и безумно красивой, местами гиперреалистичной картиной. Учитесь, янки!
При исследовании очередного сегмента карты, приходящейся лишь крупицей исполинских габаритов открытого мира, я думал: "А насколько большой и величественной архитектура тут ещё может быть?", наравне с мыслью "Насколько долго я могу просто бездействовать и созерцать?". Множество сюрреалистичных замков, крепостей, священных башен с величавыми мостами. Обожаю! Эта игра - как кладезь архитектурных изысканий, которые бы никогда не увидели жизни в нашем мире. В купе со своей дальностью прорисовки внушает тебе свой подлинный масштаб, свободный от игровых условностей. Столица Междуземья, Лейнделл - Город, обрамлённый золотом. Город Богов. Одним своим видом он заставляет тебя, сновидца, поверить в события, предшествовшие твоему появлению, как и в те, приведшие к его падению. Нарратив через левел-дизайн работает здесь на полную катушку. Elden Ring не ставит себе целью объяснить игроку все происходящее. Игра не использует кат-сцен, диалогов(за исключением немногих, которые ничего не объясняют), или рассеянных записей с информацией. Вместо этого она подогревает и дает пространство для воображения игрока, как сновидца. I have never properly played a Soulsborne game before and this is my entry into the series. I however do have some familiarity with other Soulslike games (Black Myth: Wukong, Silksong?) and have a FCG (fighting game) background. Please understand that my opinion comes from [b]my perspective as a hardcore gamer who has never played a FromSoft game.[/b]

First off, the negative: This game... is frustrating. Really frustrating. I understand to that players of the game love to make the argument that you can just make an OP build and explore and level up so that bosses get easier. While this works decently well in the early game, even without knowledge of how to make a build, in the later game, it is very difficult. Especially if you don't know what sort of armaments or talismans exist, didn't learn important mechanics in the early game when you were a bit information overloaded (as a new player to the series), or simply missed important things during exploration, with it so easy to forget or not know where there still is to explore. Nearing the end game, I found myself so frustrated with the final boss that I ended up searching up online on how to beat it [spoiler]-- getting in-game practice was tough since I had to beat Radagon every time beforehand to even get an attempt at Elden Beast with my melee only build. I eventually I searched up where to find Holy defense, good holy armor, etc., [/spoiler] As a gamer who likes to not rely on external learning outside of the game for singleplayer experiences, this felt like a huge defeat for me. The same happened with me missing the summoning bell. Since the final boss was the last part of my Elden Ring experience before writing this review, it did leave a bit of a bittersweet taste in my mouth. I did not feel a great sense of satisfaction for beating that final bit in the way that I did. 

With that out of the way, the good: Due to the fact that the bosses and enemies are so hard and how FromSoft designed the world, the world does feel more full and rich. You are just a tiny feeble speck in this massive world where castles and bridges and foes are consistently 5 to 10 times the size of the player. You often don't feel like an overpowered god and it brings a sense of overcoming hardship that ties in really well to a lot of the reasons we as players play games at all: A sense of achievement. Making your unique build (even if you don't really know what you are doing) is still fun as a new FromSoft player, and most bosses do make you feel amazing after you try again and again to eventually overcome, (whether through how you speced your build in its RPG mechanics, or just through learning boss patterns and punishes.) Seeing familiar concepts from fighting games (iframes, recovery, startup, active frames, hitbox analysis) is nice and some new ideas to me like stance and stance damage make for a really clean combat system.

Aside from praise, some small nitpicks:
[list]
	[*] A lot of the mine areas felt very same-y and didn't feel as fresh and give that amazing feel of exploration that the bigger castles/areas do. Going from mine to mine feels very bland and formulaic. Same with some of the minor bosses, which feel a bit cut and paste.
	[*]Due to how FromSoft tackled open-world level scaling, some areas you come across late in your playthrough sometimes are way too easy and lose that sense of wonder that you get when discovering an area roughly when you are supposed to for the first time.
[/list]
But with all my frustrations and nitpicks aside, my overall experience of playing the game was very good and I still think the feelings I had overcoming bosses and exploring the grand world more than makes up for it and this is definitely one of the better games of this gaming generation. Is it a masterpiece like they say? Idk, but it sure is a fun game to play.

If you are a new player to FromSoft games like I was and considering buying this game, I do NOT recommend it if:
[list]
	[*]You dislike games with very precise combat systems.
	[*]You aren't OK with some repetitive grinding of tech skill AND you aren't willing to seek help outside of the game.
[/list]
[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
	[*]Beautiful art design, sound design, open-world level design, and overall well executed on most fronts
	[*]Rewarding RPG mechanics as well as rewarding Boss/ combat encounters
	[*]Quite content-rich
	[*]Unique and rewarding experience of overcoming hardship that is very hard to get from any other AAA developer.
[/list]
[b]Cons:[/b]
[list]
	[*]A lot of important systems are easy to miss or hard to learn without external help (wiki, youtube, a friend watching you play, etc.)
	[*]Chance of repetitive or poorly balanced "side" content
[/list]

First of all, the first gameplay experience is unmatched.
The world is insanely beautiful, the characters are memorable, and the voice acting is perfect. Every line feels heavy and meaningful. The dialogues hit hard...you can feel the weight behind them.

About the Difficulty :

The game’s difficulty depends entirely on how you choose to play.
Yes, skill matters...but even a noob like me can finish this game.

If you decide to fight bosses without summons or without some broken one-shot build, the game becomes hard as hell. You’re forced to rely purely on skill.
Summons, on the other hand, make the game much easier.

For me, Mimic Tear carried my entire playthrough, even against Malenia, and I was using a pretty random build to be honest.
For some reason, Mimic Tear didn’t help much in the Radagon fight...but Tiche absolutely did.

I personally don’t want to spend hours fighting a single boss. My first playthrough took 94 hours, and even with Mimic Tear helping me, it already took a long time. Without Mimic Tear, it would’ve taken me way more than that...there’s honestly no way I could’ve completed the game.
That said, there is one thing that genuinely made the game harder for me...and I’ll explain that in the “What I Hate” section.

What I Loved About the Game :

The beautiful environment goes without saying, but exploration is the real star of Elden Ring.

This is the only game where I explored this much. I’ve never explored any other game the way I explored this one...not even Red Dead Redemption 2 or The Witcher 3, where exploration is also a huge focus. Everywhere you go, something is waiting for you...a boss, a weapon, a Somber Smithing Stone, or even something you didn’t know you needed.

Even when I found items I wasn’t interested in, it still felt satisfying. Exploration never felt wasted.
Even after exploring for hours, I still feel like there are so many things left to discover.

Honestly, 60–70% of my playtime was just exploration, not boss fights ...and I loved every second of it.

One more thing I absolutely loved was weapons, especially my favorite one.. the Uchigatana with the Unsheathe skill.
I honestly can’t explain how satisfying that weapon feels. I used the Uchigatana for almost every boss in the game, right up until I found Rivers of Blood. The Unsheathe skill just hits different.

I know the Uchigatana isn’t really a late-game weapon...at least not with the skillset I have...but it’s still my favorite weapon in the game, no lie.

As for the story… I’ll be honest I barely understood anything except “Put these foolish ambitions to rest.”
I’ll definitely watch lore videos later. I’m just bad at grasping stories when the narration isn’t direct. But I’m sure it won’t disappoint.

Boss designs and movesets are also fantastic.

What I Hated About the Game :

This is purely my opinion nd you don’t have to agree.

The combat.
I don’t enjoy dodging 3–4 attacks just to land one hit or only to get interrupted or staggered while using a skill attack. Many weapons have amazing movesets, but the real question is ...can we actually use them effectively? I’m not so sure. Maybe skill issue from my side ..but srsly.

Another thing I hated was how the dodge  works.

Dodging doesn’t always respond instantly if you’re already attacking or stuck at the end of an animation and that often gets you hit.
My first Soulslike game was Black Myth Wukong, where dodging is instant. No matter what you’re doing...if you press dodge, you dodge.

That’s why combat in BMW feels so much better and more satisfying to me than in Elden Ring.

That’s exactly how I wanted Elden Ring’s dodge to feel.
If dodging worked like that, half the game would instantly feel easier. And that’s why BMW felt much easier to me compared to Elden Ring. If instant dodge were removed from BMW, it wouldn’t be any easier than Elden Ring at all.

This is honestly the only major thing I hated about the game.

Final Verdict :

Despite my complaints, I absolutely loved exploring this world, and overall, I enjoyed the game a lot.

I’ll still say it straight: Elden Ring is a 10/10.
You won’t regret buying this game and giving it a shot.

Awhile, being 50 hours on my first character that made any significant progress in the game and even then many would argue I had not even made it halfway on that character. Every few months I would try making a new character and playing through Limgrave to see if this was the time I would beat the game. For over three years this went on. I even bought the game again on PS4/5 to see if having it on the 'big screen TV' would be enough. But it wasn't until the tail end of 2025 going into 2026 that I finally played through on a new character and beat the game. I honestly could not tell you what was different about this playthrough compared to previous playthroughs, but the aspects of the game that bothered me before just... didn't this time. And this inner turmoil surprised me as a veteran of From's Soulsborne games. I've beaten all of them multiple times (Sekiro on PS4, requires a new playthrough on PC for fresh thoughts) and far and away my favorite has been Bloodborne. So much so that game has over 800 hours from me and has been platinumed for years. This game, Elden Ring... sits just below Bloodborne for me, after all this time. It all just made sense in a way it never had before, and I enjoyed it thoroughly and am already planning character builds for multiple playthroughs. The fallen leaves tell a story. A story of the lands between. And it is certainly a story to behold.

But this is a thing to talk about later. For now... you hate yourself? You're a masochist? Or do you simply love to take on fights where the odds are stacked against you? In any of these cases, you're certainly made for this game.

Aspect one: Gameplay
If there is such a thing as a gameplay loop, it can be summed up with the following: Attack overwhelmingly strong boss enemy -> Miss a single dodge -> die -> repeat. Sure, some are easier on you than others, but this is generally the way a game of the soulsborne genre works. And if you for some reason do manage to defeat said foe, there's one just as dangerous if not worse pretty much just down the road. Which can get frustrating if you get stuck on the same guy for several sessions of playing.

The odds that are heavily stacked against you though make it incredibly rewarding when the guy you have been trying to defeat for - and I have to say it depends on the individual boss - up to several hours finally perishes. (Yeah, f*ck you Astel.) Which I would expect is why so many people play this type of game. Apart from just constantly fighting one of the more than 100 bosses however, there is an expansive open world to discover and explore. Literal thousands of both openly visible and incredibly hidden details tell a story about the Lands Between. All 13 main areas are filled top to bottom with secrets to find. Be it just another main area, a dungeon hidden away behind a fake wall or one of many catacombs, just to name a few, every time you can find a place filled to the brim with enemies and loot as well as just a wonderful vibe. And, despite me probably spending a full paragraph two categories further into this review, I have to say that this vibe and some wonderful cinematics extend past the catacombs, caves and dungeons and encompass literally the entire map.

There is one caveat to fighting the big guys, however, and that is directly tied to the cinematography that I just praised: you more often than not can't see much of the wonderfully staged boss because you are very often just sitting below them attacking their legs with no way of telling what attack is coming next. Also, just in general, the camera has taken up the mantle of being the ultimate final boss of Elden Ring, at least to me. Yes, I am incredibly bad at playing with the free camera, I need to fix my camera on the boss to be able to fight it. But randomly losing the guy from focus, running around a corner into a problem I couldn't see because I couldn't get my camera to cooperate or just straight-up running off a cliff because I couldn't turn around in time did get me very frustrated at times. However those two things are my only complaints about the gameplay.

Fighting in general gets the biggest variety of all soulslike games developed by FromSoft yet, because of the large amount of different, varyingly conventional weapons, as well as a bunch of weapon talents, sorceries and incantations. Whether you want to be a mage wielding incantations and sorceries from a little distance, dodge around enemy hits with straight swords and shields or just be the gigachad that ignores everything and one-shots everything with a colossal weapon or one to two greatswords, you can personalize the fighting style to be uniquely yours. It is the most accessible, so if you want to get into the genre this is the game to do it with.

Aspect two: Story
Yes, to the first-time player who doesn't look into every nook and cranny the story is confusing as sh!t. Until I started researching online I just understood maybe 50% of everything shown. But if you immerse yourself a little in the story itself, you can expect one of the deepest stories you can find. You are a Tarnished who returns to the lands between after ages of exile to become the new consort to the Queen of the Lands Between. That is all you really need to know in order not to get lost in the present-day story. Take a look into the deeper levels of the story and you will fall in love. Trust me.

Aspect three: Graphics and Sound design
I already teased on my love for the cinematography in this game. FromSoftware really knows how to stage every area of the map in its own way. There were so many times when colour pallette, vista and music came together to create the perfect vibe that stopping momentarily just to enjoy the view became a routine thing for my playtime. All that despite the texture blurring in the distance and graphics not exactly being a 4K picture. But realistic 4K or more in terms of resolution is not neccessary. And FromSoft understood this perfectly well when creating this game.

And the soundtrack just adds to this in the perfect way. There are so many different things happening just OST-wise that I just can't put into words, but they support the cinematography that I just praised again perfectly, and when "that one theme" (take your pick) is supplementing your fight against a perfectly staged boss it feels like you could slay a god or become one yourself.

Conclusion
A wonderfully crafted world and over a hundred bosses, most staged with perfect cinematography. Added to that an epic soundtrack and the unparalleled feeling of defeating even the largest of guys just by yourself. It is the perfect package if you love fighting big bosses.

10/10, I recommend.

Elden Ring makes a strong first impression, but the longer you play, the more you notice that something feels off. The world is huge, yet strangely artificial — nothing in it feels truly alive. Locations are empty, often poorly detailed, as if stretched out just to look big. It’s a stark contrast to Dark Souls, where every area was meticulously crafted, full of details, shortcuts, connections, and atmosphere you could feel instantly.

Here you get a massive map, but without the soul that made exploration in previous FromSoftware titles so memorable.

Bosses
Boss fights in Elden Ring are another issue. Arenas are often cramped or unclear, and some encounters feel rushed. On top of that, many bosses repeat — the same enemy appears in a different cave, dungeon, or context. Sure, it’s a necessary filler in such a large game, but after a few repeats it becomes dull.

The biggest problem lies in the flow of combat. In Dark Souls, bosses had rhythm and patterns you could learn. Here, many bosses spam attacks nonstop, as if the game wants to overwhelm you with animations. There’s little breathing room, few clear openings, and rarely that satisfying moment of “okay, I’ve figured him out.” Sometimes it feels like side bosses were added out of obligation rather than as meaningful encounters.

A few great bosses… but they’re exceptions
Of course, there are standouts — the main story bosses are on a much higher level. You can tell they received time, budget, and attention. The problem is that the rest pales in comparison.

And that’s the shame: Elden Ring had the potential to be the absolute king of the genre. But the uneven quality of its locations and bosses makes the experience feel disappointing.

Summary
If you want a truly great FromSoftware game that maintains quality from start to finish, play Sekiro, Dark Souls 1, or Dark Souls 3. Elden Ring is an interesting experiment, but it doesn’t reach the heights the studio is capable of.

Still, despite all its flaws, I have to admit that I did enjoy my time with it. There is something captivating about the atmosphere, the music, and the freedom the game gives you. And even though I see its weaknesses clearly, I know I’ll return to Elden Ring again — not once, but many times. There’s just enough charm in it to pull me back, even if it’s far from perfect.

At the time of writing I haven't yet finished Elden Ring, but with well over 100 hours of playtime and multiple possible endings I feel like I've got a good enough handle on the game to give it a fair review.

I played on my Steam Deck OLED in both handheld and docked modes.  The game defaulted to the “High” preset and ran great.

[h2]Game Design[/h2]
Elden Ring is a what you would get if you combined “Dark Souls” with “Skyrim” or “Breath of the Wild”.  It’s an open world take on the “souls-like” formula that works surprisingly well.  Once you finish the optional tutorial, stepping out into Limgrave feels a lot like the first time I stepped out of the resurrection chamber as Link in “Breath of the Wild”.  It’s your first breathtaking look at an expansive open world that you’re free to explore at your leisure.

The thing about open world games is that they’re easy to get wrong.  It’s easy to have a big map with nothing fun or interesting to do in it.  Thankfully Elden Ring delivers.  There’s constantly something to collect, enemies to fight or avoid, caves or castles to explore, etc.  Being open world gives you the freedom to approach challenges in your own way.  There are some moments where the game will funnel you thru an expected route, but there's often alternatives if you pay attention.  When I played Dark Souls it was cool that its world was fully connected and seamless without loading screens, but it still felt like a series of interconnected corridors and fast traveling isn’t unlocked in Dark Souls until very late game, so if you want to go explore a different area, talk to a specific person, etc., you’re physically walking the whole distance and fighting every enemy on the way.  Elden Ring on the other hand isn’t just huge and seamless, it gives you agency over where and how you navigate. There is the occasional elevator or door-opening animation that probably serve as loading screens, but you never have your agency or ability to control your character taken.  Even the act of opening a large door into a castle or something happens in real time, and once it’s open you’re free to come and go between that area and the rest of the world.  One of the coolest features of this open world is that besides the caves and castles of the overworld, there are multiple massive underground areas that exist completely parallel to the overworld.  These underground areas are, each, multiple hours worth of gameplay and lore that could almost be entire games or DLC content all on their own.  It’s really impressive just how much stuff they managed to cram into this game.  There’s also large elevated plateaus that go over top of other areas, so between those and the caves and underground areas, there’s actually quite a lot of verticality.

Weapon durability is also gone, and like Dark Souls, you don’t “have” to upgrade your gear if you find an item or an effect you like.  You “can”, but your weapons scale with your character stats and can also be upgraded at a blacksmith, so if you find something you particularly like, you’re totally fine hanging onto that thing for the whole game.  This makes it much easier to focus on exploration and story instead of constantly babysitting your equipment.

There’s also lots of lore to be discovered, not all of it stated explicitly in-game.  Where Elder Scrolls uses in-game books to flesh out lore for curious players, Elden Ring uses item descriptions.  There are tons of interesting creatures and races of people, all of whom have their own history and lore fleshed out as you explore and collect items.  When you open your inventory there’s a “Recent” tab and exclamation points will be next to items you’ve picked up that you haven’t looked at yet.  Not only does this reveal details about the item and its stats, but every item has a detailed description of what it is, why it exists and its history.

[h2]Multiplayer[/h2]
The optional multiplayer works a lot like it did in Dark Souls where you’ll see and can leave messages for other players.  The messages must be composed from a pre-defined list of statements, but it has been fleshed out a lot to include up to two statements combined with a conjunction and an optional emote that your player phantom will play out when someone reads your message.  This seems like the kind of thing that, for someone like me who cares about lore and experiencing a game raw, would ruin the experience, but in reality, interacting with other players like this in a limited capacity thru short messages actually feels fun and engaging.

Directly interacting with other players in Elden Ring is explicitly opt-in.  There are specific items that you must find and use to summon others or invade their world, or to be invaded by other players.

There are also arenas that you can find and unlock as you play.  These serve as low-stakes battlegrounds where players can fight one another using various rules.

[h2]Audio and Graphics[/h2]
The music and audio design is one of those things that you don’t consciously notice is rewiring your brain until you hear a familiar jingle in a video or something and your ears pique.  They did an excellent job with environmental sound, and a great job scoring the soundtrack in just the right ways to manipulate me emotionally.

The visual presentation is pretty solid.  In an era where optimization seems non-existent, it’s refreshing to see a game that looks and runs this good on a handheld, with support for HDR so the colors and lighting look more natural and less artificially saturated.

One recommendation I would make is that, if you have the option, play this on a TV.  There are areas and situations that just hit different when you’re looking at them on a large screen, such as fighting atop the branches of the massive Haligtree.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
The game plays a lot like other souls games.  Coming from Dark Souls I was able to fall right in without having to spend too much time learning new systems or controls.  FromSoft definitely believes in not fixing what isn’t broken so if you’ve played other souls games, you’ll feel right at home here.  If you haven’t, here’s some tips.

Get used to roll dodging.  If you have a shield you can block, but even if a shield blocks 100% of incoming damage, it will still consume your stamina, and your stamina rebuilds slower while you’re holding your shield up, so if you just stand there trying to tank everything you may find yourself getting staggered, or with so little stamina you can’t counterattack.  So while a shield can be a useful tool, my most common method of avoiding damage is rolling.

On that note, pay attention to your gear.  On your equipment screen the game will tell you whether you’re “light”, “medium” or “heavy”.  “Heavy” changes your rolling to a “fat roll” where you basically just flop on the ground and take ages to get up, leaving you vulnerable.  All “equipped” items count towards your carry weight, even if they’re not currently in your hand, so there may be times where you need to adjust your loadout to prevent overloading yourself.

[h2]Summary[/h2]
I’ve fallen in love with Elden Ring.  I picked it up and had put 100 hours in before I even realized it.  The game looks, sounds and feels great, and has that difficult, yet immensely satisfying combat that souls games are known for.  There’s something to be said for attempting a boss several times, leaving to go level up, coming back later and finally “getting” it.  Too many games seem to want to paint the “correct” path in yellow paint or hand you victory on a silver platter because you’re the “chosen one” or whatever.  Elden Ring just is what it is; there is no difficulty setting and it doesn’t pull any punches.  But it has awoken something in me that I haven’t felt for years.  It has satisfying combat and a beautiful and interesting open world, for those with the patience to learn new things and pay attention to the small details.

After playing this game for 100 hours, I can certainly say, this is one of the best games I've ever played,
maybe even THE best. I already loved the first session and with more time my love steadily increased.
This game just blew me away and it felt like I was a kid again by being amazed of how good this game truly is.

However, the game is pretty difficult, as you would expect from a Souls game. Nevertheless it's the most
beginner friendly out of all the Souls games, because you can influence the difficulty way more by summoning spirits, requesting help from online players or exploring a diffrent part of the Open World. The graces (bonfires of Elden Ring) are also way more common and generously placed compared to the Dark Souls games. Additionally, there are also stakes of marika, at which you can respawn without having the other benefits of a grace (like leveling up). They increase respwan points even further. The beginning of the game can get quite frustrating, because you don't have a lot of equipment and items, potentially making progress more difficult. Try to be patient and give this game a chance, if you're struggling in the beginning. If you're hard stuck at one point, just explore the world, because exploration is often rewarded and will make you stronger.

You will need a PC with somewhat good hardware, it takes approximately 12 GB of RAM in 1080p, so go for 16+ and at least 4 GB VRAM. Keep in mind, the FPS in this game is capped at 60, so don't expect over 60 FPS (without mods). I personally played it on Windows, but I've heard that it runs better on Linux.

The only criticism I have is the unrealistic physics. If you chop through a small tree with an axe, nothing happens. Additionally you can't swim. The fall damage also doesn't make any sense, because sometimes it feels like this:
You fall off a 1m cliff: *no damage*
You fall off a 5m cliff: *no damage*
You fall off a 10m cliff: *no damage*
You fall off an 11m cliff: *instantly dies at full HP*
Imo this is rather a minor criticism, but the experience would've been slightly better with improved physics.

Overall I feel like Elden Ring is definitely worth the full $60, but if you're in doubt whether you will like it or not,
you can also wait for a discount, just keep in mind, this game is pretty rarely on sale (around 3 times per year).

Conclusion: Would I recommend buying this game? Absolutely.

Great game marred by some bad design choices: 9/10.

This is my first proper souls-like game. I only played DS1 a long long time ago, but never finished it. As such, the beginning of the game was a bit rough for me. Not because the game is too difficult, but because the movement is clunky and a bit sluggish which meant getting used to. Personally it feels like old games that today seem outdated - movement wise. There always seems to be some kind of lag, not only on dodges per se, but literally every action. HOWEVER, the biggest downside for me definitely has to be the camera. It is just so abysmal that it's mind boggling. It made segments of an otherwise great game really frustrating. Once you learn how to use the camera, some fights are somewhat better but in reality, the only time camera seems optimal is when you are fighting monsters the same size as you, which is almost never. Fighting Deathbirds has to be the pinnacle of design stupidity.

That being said, the game is huge and the world is gorgeus. There are so many secrets to explore, weapons, armors to find, and with that, builds to try. At first I didn't like that you basically don't change weapons and armor that often, or that everything seems to be balanced somewhat, but kind of got used to the fact that you rarely change anything. The game feels more catered towards replayability rather than one time playthroughs. It feels specifically catered for dark souls fanbase. Like a giant love letter with all their knowledge combined in one open world game. I don't particularly enjoy the "online" presence, messages, other ghosts and what not. They ruin the experience, but at the same time, the game is designed to be played as a collective, which I am not a fan of to be honest. There is no way you would be able to solve most of the nonsense puzzles and secrets. I actually skipped many as I didn't want to look for stuff online, but in some cases where the story was crucial I really didn't want to waste time.

It took me roughly 100 hours for the playthrough, and I probably missed some content. 90% of everything was solo found with some help with nonsense, primarily towards the end where the burn out started to creep in. I wanted to finish the game but didn't enjoy it as much as I did initially. I probably should have made a small pause from playing. But I didnt, so I started to use the mimic summon as soon as I got it just to finish the game and I just powered through the end game. Before that I didnt even use summons, as I only learned how to by the end of the game. With that in mind, the whole snow area could be removed and the game would be better for it. It's disappointing to see some great bosses get added later as copies, just to make the game longer. It kind of diminishes its uniqueness.

All in all, its one hell of an experience, make no mistake. Everything else trumps the shortcomings mentioned above.

EDIT: So after finishing DS3, I went back to play Elden Ring. I just kind of felt like it. Fresh playthrough, no summons, no cheesing, pure melee. And I got to say that I even enjoyed it far more than the first time. To my surprise, I killed every boss within a couple of tries at most with the exception of Mohg and Malenia (those took a bit more).

Overview
Elden Ring sets the player upon a journey through the shattered Lands Between, where grace has fled and ruin holds dominion. The tale unfolds like a grand tragedy, filled with ambition, betrayal, and the faint glimmer of hope that clings to the Tarnished who dares to rise.

Story and World
The world is broad as any kingdom sung by ancient bards. Each region bears its own sorrowful history. Storm shaken castles brood upon their cliffs, swamps murmur with forgotten curses, and golden fields lie haunted by the ghosts of former glory. To wander here is to tread upon a stage where every stone whispers of past deeds and future peril.

Gameplay and Combat
Combat is a fierce and noble contest. Blades meet with thunderous force, spells flare like stars torn from the heavens, and every foe demands wit and courage. Some enemies tower like giants from old tales, while others skulk with treachery in their hearts. Victory, when seized, feels as sweet as triumph before a roaring crowd.

Death and Difficulty
Death visits often, yet serves as a stern teacher. Each fall grants new wisdom, and each return to battle strengthens the resolve of the Tarnished. The challenge is great, but never unjust, and the player grows in both skill and spirit.

Traversal and Torrent
Torrent, the spectral steed, is a companion of rare worth. Swift as a winter gale and steadfast in every trial, he carries the Tarnished across plains, cliffs, and battlefields with grace that borders upon the divine.

Boss Encounters
The great foes of this realm stand as the finest actors in this grim play. Their presence commands awe, their battles stir the blood, and their defeat marks the turning of mighty chapters. Each encounter feels like a duel of fate itself.

Final Verdict
Elden Ring is a work of high art, worthy of any poet’s praise. Its world is rich, its trials profound, and its triumphs unforgettable. Were Shakespeare himself to walk the Lands Between, he would find tales enough to fill a lifetime of quills.

I genuinely think this is the best game ever made. Granted I'm a huge Souls series fan, but this game just has literally everything I could ever want from a game.

The story is incredible. In classic Fromsoft fashion, you aren't spoonfed the lore, you have to search for it and read descriptions of items. You have to talk to NPCs multiple times and do convoluted quests that might seem nonsensical, but if you pay close attention you should be able to figure out where you need to go or what you need to do. Not to mention the plethora of guides available now.

The gameplay is incredibly fun. Tons of cool enemies and bosses, many of which are extremely challenging, but always fair. If you learn the movesets and utilize the tools given to you, you will succeed. So many of the bosses aren't just fun to fight, but they're also visual spectacles, much like so many areas of the game.

The freedom to play the way you want is incredible. Whether you want to use only magic, miracles, or melee, you have a multitude of tools, weapons, and buffs to enable and enhance your chosen style of play. There's also a ton of incredible fashion, which is always a huge plus.

Overall, I genuinely could not recommend this game enough. If you're a fan of souls games or open-world adventure games, this is the game for you.

Plus, the DLC is enormous with even more incredible bosses, weapons, spells, and armor with an incredible story and even more of the best music you've ever heard.

This is a tentative recommendation.  

Elden Ring does not respect your time; the open world was a mistake.

That's not to say you cannot still have fun, find loot, kill bosses, cooperate, or kill.  It's just that there more empty time between all of that.  More so, once you have entered one of the sub-dungeons or side areas, you've seen them all, since many enemies are re-used and bosses go from one medium monster, to two medium monsters, etc. It's all repeated monsters and bosses, the tombs being the worst of it.  

It seemed like the devs wanted to go Souls, but to 11.  That's fine, but they also cranked up all the annoying stuff along with it.  Bad platforming, gimmick dungeons, stuff that is truly esoteric that you wouldn't find by accident, and more. 

That's not to say I didn't enjoy it, I just enjoying being in the forts, castles, and dungeons, like Dark Souls, more than in the winding open fields.  

There are some gorgeous vistas to behold, but there's also like four different swamp areas, where you're going to trudging cheeks deep in multiple shades of poisonous gunk.  Loved that before?  Do it MANY times!

Oh, and I have a quite capable machine, this game is locked at 60FPS 98% of the time.  That last 2% is when it's locked at 5 SPF... yes, 5 seconds per frame.  The game has several areas where it will just hang for a very long period of time and you gotta hope you're not dead or crashing. Beat the game when it came out and took a break, decided to wait until I 100%ed before reviewing. After roughly 93 hours of playtime 100% is mine and here are my thoughts as someone who has played ecery souls game. Elden Ring truly is the souls formula perfected, the boss variety and world design are both some of the best ever made, and the density of areas is astounding. I remember when the first Elden Ring teaser came out and everybody knew it was going to be a generation defining game, and it lived up to the hype. The diversity of build potential is unmatched by Elden Ring's predecessors. In the souls trilogy magic was very prominent, yet very difficult to get into early game especially in a blind playthrough. Needing extensive knowledge of the inner workings of the game, including quests, to achieve magic that rivals the physical weapons you can find around the world. Even if a player were to stumble across proper magic and transition to magic, their levels would likely already be built into strength or dex and they would be unable to change it. Elden Ring breaks this pattern, allowing for players to respec their stats, and find various magic items throughout the game world. This allows a player to transition to any build almost whenever they like, keeping the gameplay very fresh. Next there is the difficulty of Elden Ring. Elden Ring posits itself as a souls game, notoriously difficult, yet compared to the likes of Sekiro through to the original souls trilogy and bloodborne Elden Ring is not nearly as difficult. This is because of the nature of the open world, allow9ng players to become as strong as they need to be to pass a boss. This is not saying Elden Ring is easy, it will still rape your ass especially if this is your first souls game. Now on to the 100% grind, and honestly, not much to say. Elden Ring is not unfair — it is uncompromising. Once you stop rushing and actually learn its mechanics, the game becomes one of the most rewarding experiences in modern gaming.

At first, some encounters can feel brutal or overwhelming. But after understanding core systems—spacing, stamina management, invincibility frames, positioning, build synergy, and enemy pattern recognition—the difficulty feels deliberate. Every death teaches something, and every victory feels earned.

Boss fights are designed to punish impatience, not skill. When you adapt, read attacks, and commit only when it’s safe, the combat flows beautifully. The game gives immense freedom in how you approach challenges, and that flexibility is its greatest strength.

The open world is vast yet purposeful. Exploration is constantly rewarded, whether through gear, lore, or alternative paths that let you grow stronger before returning to tougher fights. The atmosphere, art direction, and music elevate every moment, making the Lands Between feel mysterious and alive.

Elden Ring respects player intelligence. It doesn’t explain everything—but it trusts you to learn. If you do, it delivers a sense of mastery and accomplishment few games can match.

A demanding masterpiece that rewards patience, skill, and curiosity.

Great Game, Bad PC Experience

Elden Ring is an incredible game held back by a frustratingly outdated PC implementation. Despite running on powerful modern hardware, the game is hard-locked to 60 FPS with no official option to uncap it. In modern PC gaming, this feels unacceptable.

On high-refresh monitors, the game feels sluggish, heavy, and choppy, especially compared to newer soulslike titles such as Lords of the Fallen or Lies of P, which fully support uncapped framerates and modern display technology. Camera movement lacks fluidity, input feels delayed, and traversal never feels as smooth as it should—none of which are limitations of my hardware, but rather the game’s design choices.

What makes this worse is that the 60 FPS cap isn’t just a technical limitation, it’s a deliberate decision tied to FromSoftware’s aging engine. Players who want smoother gameplay must resort to unofficial mods, disable anti-cheat, and play offline, which is ridiculous for a premium AAA title.

Yes, the art direction, world design, and combat depth are outstanding. But great design doesn’t excuse poor PC optimization. A modern PC game should respect modern PC standards, and Elden Ring simply doesn’t.

If you’re used to 120-144Hz (or higher) gameplay, be prepared: Elden Ring will feel slow and dated no matter how strong your system is.

Elden Ring revolutionizes open-world action RPGs with its seamless blend of brutal combat, vast exploration, and intricate build crafting in the breathtaking Lands Between. FromSoftware's masterpiece balances punishing challenge with triumphant discovery, making every victory earned and unforgettable. Its expansive design rewards curiosity without hand-holding, cementing it as a genre-defining triumph.

- Core Mechanics -
Combat evolves Soulsborne fundamentals with jumping attacks, mounted Torrent battles, guard counters, and crafting from gathered materials, emphasizing timing, poise breaks, and versatile weapon arts. Exploration thrives via reduced fall damage, spirit springs, and a sprawling map filled with secrets, bosses, and procedural threats that encourage multiple approaches. Summoning spirits and co-op adds strategic depth without easing the core tension.
​

- Atmosphere and Narrative - 
The mythic world brims with cryptic lore unveiled through environmental storytelling, NPC quests, and colossal ruins, fostering a sense of awe amid despair. Day-night cycles, weather, and dynamic encounters heighten immersion in a land shaped by gods and ambition. Soundtrack and visuals deliver epic scale with intimate ferocity.
​

- Technical Strengths -
Optimized for diverse hardware, it delivers fluid 60fps performance and intricate animations that elevate every clash. Intuitive controls scale from basics to advanced combos, with deep customization via stats, ashes of war, and upgrades.
​

- Award Worthiness -
Dominates "Game of the Year" and "Outstanding Open World" Steam Awards categories through unmatched freedom, replayability, and mechanical brilliance that influenced the industry.

[h2]The "Loser" Experience (aka The Mage Life)[/h2]

In the base game, I am "Maidenless." In our playthrough, I was "The Human Artillery." My partner was essentially a professional babysitter with a sword.

[list]
[*] [b]The Strategy:[/b] My partner did the "parrying" and "dodging." I stood three zip codes away, spamming blue pebbles and praying the boss didn't look at me.
[*] [b]The Questlines:[/b] My partner was reading lore and solving ancient mysteries. I was mostly following his cape like a lost duckling, asking "Are we there yet?"
[*] [b]The Combat:[/b] If a boss so much as sneezed in my direction, I folded like a lawn chair. My main contribution was "emotional support through panic-rolling."

Elden Ring is great, but not perfect and there are some things that ruin it.

Its too big. Its exhausting. Its quests are too complex and the only way to know how do to them and get the good reward items for your playstyle is to look at the wiki, why would I want to do that and just play the game as a checklist going through events until its complete, and also spoiling the game as I do it cause you cant use a wiki as a guide without spoiling it. The game gets boring after so many catacombs and crappy caves. Same issue with all these massive map type games. Doesnt have interesting level design. 

The weather and time of day system ruins the good look of the game. Its always raining or cloudy and looks boring. The game looks nice during a bright sunny day, but doesnt happen much. 

Level design isnt as good or long as other games like Dark Souls 1+3 so basically when you find an area you like, for example a certain castle or other building, it isnt as long and detailed as you'd want it to be most of the time. Some areas like Stormveil Castle, Volcano Manor and Leyndell are detailed and feel interesting, but many areas are just boring and fall short. They should have made the game smaller and just had more detail in the areas they kept. There are a number of small mini forts/castles that basically just have no reason to ever go to once you've ran in and got the item. 

Background music is a tedious, boring, depressing droning sound. Sounds really poor and effortless. Dark souls 1 firelink shrine music was very memorable and had a lot of the right emotion behind it to it to set the tone of the game as a bleak and lonely experience. Elden rings music says nothing and makes me instantly bored. 

[spoiler]By the time I was past the magic lakes area, I entered into the Altus Plateau and Mt Glemir, which was so boring and not needed in the game. It dragged and dragged and I just didn't want to play it at all. So boring. I honestly felt like quitting. [/spoiler]

Far too many bosses (mainly due to the caves, mines and catacombs just repeating them) 
Bosses should be much less so its more eventful when we fight a boss. A boss every 6 seconds gets really boring and makes me stop caring. 

The character screaming in an annoying and dramatic way every time I get hit is so annoying.

Rodrekia and Nepheli Loux have bad voice acting. I live in the part of the world where those women's voice actors are from and I can tell they just did their normal speaking voice, I literally heard that type of voice every single day - its not interesting and breaks emersion. Roderkia girl literally sounds like she works in my local corner shop and made no effort to make an interesting voice, just some generic modern day northern accent on a woman. Its so jarring and bad

Around the half way point of the game, the environment becomes in my opinion very boring and ugly. I havent played past this point yet so dont know if it improves. But im already getting bored of the game and now I have to slog through even more of it in an environment that's ugly. 

Boss design is great, build variety is great, graphics and special effects are great. Thats about it. Its got lots of good things about it, but its just too much. I didn't ask for this and don't need it. Dark Souls 1 & 3 were great video games with the right amount of content so I could play it multiple times. This game is just a marathon and I can't imagine doing it again with another character or in NG+

Before playing I had only seen a few clips. I assumed it was just a big open area to the south and a massive castle in the distance.
I was very wrong.

This is not just a map it is a world. One you live in struggle in and survive in. It feels endless like it exists whether you are there or not. Exploration is constantly rewarded danger feels meaningful and discovery never stops feeling exciting.

To Fromsoft, thank you for this wonderful experience.

Elden Ring is one of those rare games that keeps proving its value long after the credits roll, and even after I unlocked every achievement across every platform it’s available on. I have seen every ending, beaten every boss, explored every corner of the Lands Between, and somehow the game still feels alive. That alone says more than any score ever could. FromSoftware did not just make a difficult action RPG, they built a world that rewards curiosity, patience, and mastery in a way very few games ever manage.

What makes Elden Ring special is how much freedom it gives the player without ever feeling directionless. You can approach challenges in countless ways, whether through brute force, careful planning, strange builds, or self imposed limitations. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself experimenting with weapons, spells, and playstyles simply because the combat system is deep enough to support it. The open world never loses its sense of mystery either. Familiar areas still feel atmospheric rather than empty, and returning to them feels like revisiting a place rather than clearing a checklist.

Most games are finished once the achievements are done. Elden Ring is different. Even with nothing left to unlock, the game remains enjoyable because the core experience is strong. The art direction, music, enemy design, and sense of scale all work together to create something timeless. It is the kind of game you do not just complete, you live in it for a while. Maxing it out on every platform did not burn me out. It convinced me that Elden Ring is not just a great Souls game, but one of the best games ever made.

FromSoftware successfully merges its signature challenge with a truly expansive open-world structure.
The world design demonstrates a rare confidence, guiding players subtly rather than relying on intrusive markers.
Exploration is consistently meaningful, driven by curiosity instead of obligation.
Combat mechanics are refined, deliberate, and deeply rewarding for skilled players.
Enemy and boss design show exceptional creativity and mechanical depth.
Character progression offers flexibility without sacrificing balance or identity.
The game’s narrative approach favors environmental storytelling over exposition.
Lore is layered and intelligently fragmented, inviting long-term engagement.
Art direction reinforces the bleak yet majestic tone of the world.
Technical performance is largely stable given the scale of the experience.
Sound design and music are used sparingly but with strong emotional impact.
Difficulty feels demanding yet fair, respecting player improvement over time.
Replay value is high due to build variety and world non-linearity.
In conclusion, Elden Ring is not just a successful title, but a defining evolution of the Souls-like genre.

I want to start off by saying that this review will only focus on the base game and will not contain any information about Shadow of the Erdtree. The DLC is so big that I will make a separate review on that after this.

Elden Ring had a lot to live up to after I had played the entire Dark Souls trilogy for the first time in 2024. Those three games took up a majority of that year and I knew that as soon as I was done I would be moving on to Elden Ring. I was nervous and excited going in to this game as I didn't know how it would compare. After all, Elden Ring had no ties to the Dark Souls universe - its characters and world would be left behind as I ventured forth. 

When I first started playing I was happy to see that the movement and inventory system felt very familiar. The new jump mechanic did throw me off a little but it soon became second nature and something I wish Dark Souls had. In terms of controls, the only complaint that I have is the sneak function. By default, this is bound to pressing down the left joystick. Unfortunately, I appear to have a lead thumb and very often pressed this down on accident during fights causing my character to start sneaking which disrupted my rolls briefly. Because of this, I ended up just unbinding sneak for the entire game and never used it. There are some moments where sneaking is necessary however, so I did need to rebind it temporarily all the time. Ignoring that though, the controls of Elden Ring are immaculate, and one of my biggest woes with these games - camera lock on distance being too small - was finally answered. Overall, the game just feels intuitive and snappy.

Next, I want to address the biggest difference between this game and Dark Souls: the open world format. Truthfully by the time I made it through the first area I missed the structured, linear, and thoughtful feel of previous games. The world can sometimes feel too big and much of it is barren and only serves to give the world shape. That [i]would[/i] be a problem if not for the fact that somehow this game is filled to the brim with dungeons, caves, and secret loot that rewards exploration. Combined with the major POIs on the map FromSoft has done a shockingly good job at filling out the world, especially since this is one of their first games with such an expansive play area. Many of the smaller dungeons do feel very similar, but the fact that they are there at all did help me stay engaged. The larger or "legacy" dungeons which give players that classic Dark Souls level design really carry here. These locations most of the time are [i]huge[/i] and just by themselves contain enough secrets and loot to spend hours on.

Trying my best to keep this review short, the last topic I'd like to discuss is the boss fights. After all, it would be neglectful to review a souls-like game and not mention of the most important features. Somehow this game ends up being one of the easiest and hardest FromSoft games that I have played so far. One boss will be laughably easy while another one requires so many attempts that it stops being fun. While this variability does exist, thankfully most bosses fall somewhere in the middle and are challenging yet satisfying. There is a LOT of really cool stages and mechanics in this game during boss fights, at least for the major ones.

I have a lot left that I could talk about in this review, like how beautiful and complex the areas feel or how Miyazaki just couldn't help but put in like 12 poison swaps (all different status effects by the way). In the end though, there is just too much here to talk about in a single review. It took me around 200 hours to complete the base game being very thorough and that was spread out over most of 2025. If you choose to explore and try to find every secret, this game can easily last you a year or more like it did for me. And by the end of that? You'll be sad that you're saying goodbye to one of the greatest gaming experiences of all time.
