Pretty good game. I'm going to be a bit more critical than many others since it seems a lot of people have overlooked it's flaws. The game isn't perfect.

*Pros:

-Great graphics- 
The game is beautiful and the art design is impressive. There are a few times were I was just taking in the environment, really enjoying myself. Maybe it's getting harder to impress me, but I still wasn't as impressed as when I play OG Dark Souls back when it first came out.


-Build variety- 
There are so many options for builds, you can go through the game like I did with the Greatsword (Berserk fan, I had to), you could dabble in more magic, or you could be a spellsword. I think there are hundreds (?)  of weapons, which is crazy. There's just a ton of diversity in how you can play the game.

-Replayability- 
The diversity of builds allows for multiple playthrough using different weapons and builds. Add to that the multiple ending and numerous secrets and you get a game that you can play multiple times and still have a new experience.

-Enemy Variety- 
This is a big one. There are a lot of different enemies to fight, which helps things feel fresh and prevents the game from becoming too repetitive. I do wish there were a few more weird enemy types, but they did a pretty good job overall.

-Exploration- 
This is the main appeal to these games for me. I really enjoyed finding new areas, discovering secrets, learning the systems, and the overall world. I really did feel a sense of discovery that I don't get with most games.

-Progression- 
Having my character go from a total wimp to a badass god-slayer felt great. After struggling for so long, it felt great to be able to steamroll through enemies and feel like a force to be reckoned with.

-The lore-
This will be hit and miss for some, because the game barely explains anything, but the background for the world is really interesting. There's a reason why there's so many lore videos whenever these games come out. I like how it can be interpreted in multiple ways  depending on how you look at it.

*Cons:

-Boss design- 
Apparently, From Soft's modern approach to boss design is to have EVERY SINGLE ATTACK track  the player. You can be behind the boss and they will pivot 180 degrees IN THE MIDDLE OF THIEIR ATTACK and hit you. This was NOT the case in Demon's Souls and Dark Souls. 90% of the bosses are designed like this, making almost every boss fight a game of timing your dodge and then getting one or two hits in. That's not to say the fights can't be fun, but... when almost every boss is a slight variation of this design principle... it can get old.  I mean, you can use shields, but the boss design encourages a lot of dodging. And there are some bosses where you just can't get away with blocking much (Melania for example, since she'll heal every time she hits, even if you block...).

-Difficulty is a bit over-tuned-
I'm going to say something that might blow modern Souls fans' minds... difficulty was never the main appeal of the Souls games. With Demon Souls and Dark Souls, yes, they were difficult games. But the difficulty was just a side effect of having a more slow paced combat system and the game not explaining anything and letting you figure it out. I actually enjoy a difficult game, but the mechanics of these games don't support some of the decisions the devs have made here. It's not that fun to bash my head against the wall for an hour and make no progress. There should be a more strategic way you could mix things up with to overcome aside from "I'm going to do the same thing until I get lucky." Keep in mind that you can't respec until halfway through the game.
Oh, and before anyone says "git gud" I played Demon Souls and Dark Souls when they originally came out and I mastered those games. I've probably been a fan longer than you.

-Stop being weebs-
Why are katanas a weapon type in a medieval fantasy game? Why the hell is Melania activating her bankai in the middle of a fight? I get that the game is made by Japanese devs, but it's still supposed to be a medieval dark fantasy setting. Having a character come in and do some anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is fine if I'm playing Devil May Cry, but it just doesn't suite this setting or the series, even if it's kinda cool.

-The open world can be a bit empty-
Sometimes the open world feels great to explore and I find something interesting around every corner, but other times it's bland and empty. It feels like a lot of it could have been cut out or shortened so that you don't spend five minutes traveling from point A to point B. As far as open worlds go, it's still not bad, but a lot of it just feels like it's there to pad out playtime. And don't even get me started on how annoying it is to find a secret item only for it to be some useless crap.

-Crafting sucks-
I probably crafted items 5 times. The only really useful items to craft are the status ailment curing items. Most item pick ups are crafting materials and barely anything is worth crafting... At that point, just make consumable items pickups and ditch the crafting system. Crafting was obviously put in the game because every AAA game has it in some form. It's dumb, it's barely useful, and it doesn't belong in the game.

-The camera lock-on has issues-
The moment you try to fight a large enemy and you get up close to them, the camera doesn't know what to do. I've definitely been killed a few times from this and been hit even more. You can unlock the camera when you get close, but that's not a perfect solution since you're splitting your focus between fighting and managing the camera. I'm not sure how the Souls series has become this popular and they still can't get this right.

-PVP is lame-
I know some people love PVP... but Souls PVP sucks. It's extremely jank, it's intrusive when I'm just trying to play the game, and it's not fun when someone with ♥♥♥♥ internet warps behind me and backstabs me. I don't understand the appeal it has with some people and I never have.

-Secrets are a bit too obscure sometimes-
The secrets are fun, but you'll definitely miss a lot of them, learn about them online, and then say "how would anyone know to do that?"  After looking up some of the steps for finding the secrets I definitely wondered who would intuitively think to do some of these things. This has always been a thing for these games. I don't find looking up all the steps online to be a fun way to play, but it's basically required unless you want to waste hours trying to find.... whatever you're supposed to find.

*Conclusion*

I recommend Elden Ring with the disclaimer that the game is very imperfect and has issues. The boss design is a bit lazy and the difficulty gets annoying, but it's satisfying to overcome the challenge and gradually become OP with various weapons and builds helping to spice things up. Exploration is fun, even if it doesn't always rewarded. and the world is very pretty, if a bit empty at times. I'm glad I waited until a sale, but this is definitely a game worth playing and even if it's NOT a masterpiece like some people claim, it's certainly better than most modern games.

[h1] Overview [/h1]
I’ll be honest, I was never interested in souls games before. I can get frustrated easily, and I knew their reputation was built around their insane difficulty. Just figured it was a “not for me” situation. Even as everyone got swept up in Elden Ring around its release, I didn’t pay it much attention, just disregarding it as “one of those souls games that are too hard for me” 

Until some friends convinced me to try it, with the promise that the open world lets you simply walk away from difficult encounters and come back later, when you’re stronger or better equipped. 

Grabbed Elden Ring on a sale, thought “why not try it?”.

I made it up to Margit, and after 30 or so deaths I was wondering if I was right about the genre. But, I remembered what I’d been told – I packed up my things and left, exploring the world elsewhere. The world itself is gorgeous, and it invites you to explore every nook and cranny for whatever goodies may be inside. I found other bosses and realized not all of them were nearly as hard as Margit. A couple dozen hours later I came back, and though it wasn’t exactly easy, I finally managed to take Margit down after a couple attempts. It felt like I went off to do a training montage and came back for the rematch, and I stood up and cheered when he finally went down – I was hooked from there up to the moment I beat Malenia with no summons - it took me 74 attempts but is one of my favourite moments in gaming ever. 

Journeying through the Lands Between, the distant Erdtree getting closer with each step, every boss felled, was an unmatched experience. Playstyle is incredibly varied, and I love how armour and weapons look in this game, with a good mix of fantastical and historically-inspired. 

There are only a handful of flaws, I think. For starters, the complete lack of any kind of quest log. I don’t mind having to pay attention to dialogue, finding quest objectives without map markers, and piecing together hints from dialogue and item descriptions. I even took some of my own notes with pen and paper like an animal, but it was tough to go a few weeks or a month without playing and then try to piece together what I was doing when I came back, especially as you can’t typically get NPCs to repeat dialogue. 

Gideon in the Roundtable Hold does help provide info on the main quest throughout the game, but I found it easy to lose track of side quests after taking a break. Having to look up basic quest info and NPC names just added some friction to an otherwise smooth and immersive experience. 

The other flaw I would say are massive bosses. There are a lot of dragons and similarly-sized bosses in this game and I can’t say I enjoyed fighting them. They’re so big that you’re just zoomed in on their ankles as you’re poking their toes, not really sure what they’re doing until you suddenly get slammed by an attack you couldn’t see coming. Perhaps a ranged/magic playstyle would be better for these fights but that doesn’t really interest me. 
All things considered though, Elden Ring is without a doubt deserving of all the praise it has received since its release. I’ve never turned around on “I don’t really like this genre” to “this is one of my favourite games ever” so quickly and I’m suddenly interested in seeing what other souls games have to offer. 

[h1] Steam Deck [/h1]
Honestly I think there’s some sorcery here. I did mostly play on PC as I think this game really benefits from a bigger screen, you can more easily enjoy the beautiful visuals and see more of the arena during boss fights, but the fact that this runs as well as it does on the Steam Deck is pretty astounding. Settings are lowered and FPS won’t get any higher than 40, but that’s perfectly fine on the smaller screen. I mostly used the Steam Deck to idly farm runes or to practice certain bosses I was stuck on – I left exploration and “serious” boss attempts to the PC. 

[h1] Achievements [/h1]
Very straight forward. Achievements are almost all about story points and boss kills, many of which are optional side bosses but as long as you explore thoroughly you’ll come across most of them. The collectible hunt involves collecting every legendary weapon, spell, incantation, and summon. All but one of these can be hunted down after you’ve finished the game. A couple playthroughs are required to get the alternate endings, and you’ll be so powerful that New Game+ will be a breeze that you can stomp through in a couple hours. 

Would recommend playing blind, and cleaning up anything that was missed in a subsequent playthrough. Totally worth the experience over just being an achievement hunt.

[h1]Elden Ring — My first souls-like[/h1]

When my friend kept pushing me to try Elden Ring, I was hesitant at first. I already knew this genre isn’t made for fun — it’s basically built for moral humiliation. But curiosity got the better of me.

The gameplay is tough but fair. Every enemy and encounter made me think, adapt, and learn from mistakes. Honestly, I sometimes had to check the Wiki for certain items or quest steps — the world is huge, and not everyone wants to explore every single corner, me included. Even with that, exploring was a blast: frozen plains, dense forests, ruins, hidden areas — every corner had something to discover. That mix of freedom and direction made me feel the growth of both my character and myself.

What really stuck with me, though, was the music and the boss fights. The soundtrack creeps in subtly when danger is near and then explodes during tense fights — it makes every battle feel like an event. Bosses aren’t just tough enemies; they have their own personalities, attack patterns, and quirks. I found myself carefully timing moves, listening to the music, and almost dancing around attacks to survive. Those moments are what made the game unforgettable for me.

Even after finishing the game, I still remember moments when the world and the boss fights made me feel both fear and awe. The game is super replayable: trying out different classes — mage, knight — completely changes how you play. Personally, I’d recommend the co-op mod to play with friends if you tired of solo. Though the mod is still a bit rough around the edges.

[h1]  Мой первый Souls  [/h1]

 Не зная ни капельки ничего об игре и от предыдущих проектах Миядзаки, меня Елден поглотил с головой, огромнейший открытый мир, тонна разного оружия, разнообразие боссов, локаций, данжей, ну просто запрыгивай и исследуй не хочу. Я готов выделить несколько отдельных весовым плюсов и минусов:

[h3] Плюсы [/h3]

[b ] Открытый насыщенный мир [/b]
 Почти всегда ты что-то найдешь куда бы ты ни шёл, свернёшь с пути – найдешь крипту, не свернёшь – на дороге что-то произойдёт, а при этом если смотреть по сторонам, то в далеке увидишь огромную башню, к которой уже хочется прибежать, в близи пару домов с лутом, или высокую гору, где у подножья будет спуск в подземелье. Я выйти из первой локации не мог часов 20, на столько она насыщенна на контент, и игра не сбавляет обороты.

[b] Вооружение/классы [/b]
 Количество вооружения поражает, его на столько много, что буквально невозможно попробовать всё, очень огромный задел на реиграбельность через силу/ловкость/интеллект, ведь всё выкачать  за одно прохождение невозможно, я играл за силовика, и боже мой, сколько же я пропустил контента связанного с магией, буквально если начать НГ+ то геймплей поменяется полностью, и возможно, всё также интересно будет играть.
 
[b] Локации [/b]
  Их проработанность не только механически, но и эстетически, даже условные поля полей выглядят по-разному, и по своему завораживающе, локации с разной цветовой палитрой, с разными противниками, эмбиантом, буквально ощущение что попадаешь в другой мир, и оно прям работает, их не мало того что интересно исследовать, по ним просто передвигаться очень приятно, чего стоит только главный город, в котором я рассматривал отделку интерьера минутами.

[b] Боссы [/b]
 Главное что я хотел получить от этой игры, это не просто задрачивание боссов, а именно ощущение боевого танца, где ты просто завораживаешься тем, как босс анимирован, как ты его доджишь, и какой трек на нём играет, я это получил, я был безумно доволен постановкой боссов, на некоторых прям был абсолютный PEAK.

[h3] Минусы [/h3]

[b] Отсутствие системы прогрессии как таковой [/b]
 Самый жирный минус, игра буквально не заставляет менять оружие, ты можешь просто выкачать оружие полученное в первые часы игры и пробегать с ним вплоть до конца игры (???) Бред бредом, в игре 100+ оружия в которой ты будешь использовать до пяти, ибо ну как в нормальных играх оно должно работать, ты перешёл на новую локацию, начали появляться более сильные противники, ты чувствуешь что твоего оружия уже не хватает и надо искать получше, да? А Миядзаки так не думает, если выкачать условную алебарду на +5, то она уже будет сильнее оружия которое выпадает из финальных боссов, или хотя бы на равне.. Из-за этого ты буквально должен тратить лишние ресурсы, чтобы попробовать другой вид оружия, который по эффективности будет сопоставим с оружием из самой первой локации. (я уже молчу что придётся заного привыкать)

[b] Броня [/b]
Минус вытекает из предыдущего, опять таки баланса НЕТ, броня уже делется по тяжести, от тряпок до тяжеленных лат, но вот незадача, ЧЕМ ТЯЖЕЛЕЕ – ТЕМ ЭФФЕКТИВНЕЕ, то бишь, все средние, лёгкие, и прочие сеты бесполезные, тут даже нету условного бонуса, «Собрал сет – получил особый эффект», буквально ты собираешь кучу брони, которую бесполезно использовать, да тут есть некоторые баффы от шляп, но тут чисто символические либо +10% к заклинанием или вот тебе с барсокого Миядзакиевского плеча +2 к стату, класс, а резисты лучшие только у тяжёлых доспехов, которые типо «тяжелые», но с выкачкой они не тяжёлые,и из-за этого теряется смысл 95% брони в игре
  
[b] Кастомизация брони [/b]
Минус который СНОВА вытекает из предыдущего, Миядзаки-сан дал нам чуть-чуть кастомизировать броню, плащик добавить, ещё что-то, а почему нельзя просто внешний вид брони поменять, чтобы статы не менялись? Носишь сет А – а поставил скин сета Б (да может быть для онлайна оно бы вводила в заблуждние, но в сингле что с того?), просто проблема в том что сверхтяжёлая броня тут У%№!ЩНАЯ на внешний вид, мне буквально было плохо бегать в конце игры в «лучших» доспехах, где либо похож на кунг-фу панду либо на бомжа с гнилым доспехом, который весь в барнаклах. People gawk at the idea of these games having difficulty sliders, perhaps not realising that this game has the ultimate difficulty slider that you control yourself. Levelling up, getting spirit summons to aid you, and the order in which you engage with enemies all plays a massive part in how difficult the experience will be for you. Feel free to tailor it for your own enjoyment, giving yourself enough of a challenge that you keep playing and feel a sense of accomplishment - without hitting yourself against a brick wall until you quit. 

My main criticisms of the game are the lack of clarity with questlines - while they aren't essential to the story for the most part, they do add a lot, and when you don't do them you are certainly missing out a great deal. This game is designed so that either you miss out on loads of good content and make the game much harder for yourself, or you have the wiki up on your browser at all times. The game would absolutely benefit from an in-game wiki. 

The game can be glitchy at times, which can lead to unfair deaths. Thankfully the runbacks are typically short and you can usually pick up your lost resources. 

This game is not perfect, but it's very good and worth at least one run.

I originally played this game for a few hours, beat the first couple major bosses, got bored and forgot about it. Give or take a year later I picked the game back up and, well, I had exclusively played this game for the past month and logged over 200 hours in that time. Safe to say this is one of the best games I've ever played.

For context, this was my first ever soulsborne game, so learning the combat and other mechanics was quite a steep learning curve for me at first, but I powered through and had a blast with the different weapons at my disposal, and finally taking down a hard boss was always such a satisfying feeling; this is considering I've only really tried out 2 different builds throughout my playthroughs so far. There's still so many different ways to approach combat that I haven't even experienced yet, there truly is a build for everyone. All things considered this game has some of the best combat I've ever seen.

And don't even get me STARTED on the open world... I'm a sucker for metroidvanias, so naturally I found myself exploring every single corner of the map, and I'm STILL discovering places that I hadn't found previously! Right as I think I've found just about every secret the game has to offer, I stumble across 10 more, and that's not even taking the DLC into consideration. This game has one of the most beautifully interesting worlds that I've ever experienced in a game, and the fact that I got to explore it so thoroughly felt like nothing any game has ever done for me before.

And while I'm not normally a lore person, this game has some really interesting stories to tell. Even if I don't understand it fully, it's enough to make me take into consideration what characters are morally correct, if some villains are actually bad, if the main character is actually the "good guy" so to speak. Playing through this game blindly and experiencing this all first hand left me in awe several time, something that many games seldom do.

Even if you don't think you'd like this game, please, give it a try. I wouldn't have imagined that I'd like this game nearly as much as I do now, yet here I am, and I'm still having a blast re-exploring the world for the fourth time in NG+3.

[h1]BECOME MY BLADE ONCE MORE[/h1]

As someone who has poured thousands of hours into the Souls series, from the interconnectivity of Dark Souls 1 to the gothic aggression of Bloodborne... I thought I knew what the peak of this genre looked like. I was wrong.

[b]Elden Ring[/b] is not just a "sequel" in spirit; it is a paradigm shift. It takes the claustrophobic tension of a dungeon crawler and explodes it onto a canvas of epic fantasy that feels boundless. It manages to translate the "Souls" formula into an open world without diluting the difficulty or the mystery. It is, quite simply, the best game FromSoftware has ever made.

[list]
[*] [b]World Design:[/b] A masterclass in verticality and scale. The map keeps expanding in ways you cannot predict.
[*] [b]Combat Freedom:[/b] Power-stancing, jumping attacks, and Ashes of War create the most diverse build variety in the series.
[*] [b]Visuals:[/b] Every frame looks like a Renaissance oil painting. The art direction is unmatched.
[*] [b]Lore:[/b] George R.R. Martin’s mythos provides a grand, tragic history that makes the world feel ancient and lived-in.
[*] [b]Boss Spectacle:[/b] Fights like Radahn and Placidusax are not just battles; they are cinematic events.
[/list]
[list]
[*] [b]Late Game Balancing:[/b] The difficulty spike after the capital (Mountaintops of the Giants) feels slightly overtuned.
[*] [b]Dungeon Repetition:[/b] Some minor catacombs and caves reuse bosses and layouts a bit too often.
[/list]

[h1]THE LANDS BETWEEN[/h1]

Most open worlds feel like flat planes populated with icons. Elden Ring's world is a vertical labyrinth. You start in Limgrave, which feels like classic high fantasy, but the moment you accidentally stumble into [b]Caelid[/b], the sky turns blood-red, the music shifts to a horror drone, and you realize the environment itself is trying to kill you.

The brilliance here is the lack of hand-holding. There are no quest markers, no checklists, and no "towers" to climb to reveal the map. You reveal the map by finding map fragments, often deep in dangerous territory. The discovery is organic. Finding the elevator to the [b]Siofra River[/b] for the first time and realizing there is an entire galaxy of stars [i]underground[/i] is a gaming memory I will never forget.

[h1]COMBAT EVOLVED[/h1]

If you played Dark Souls 3, you will feel at home, but Elden Ring adds layers that change everything:

[b]1. Ashes of War:[/b] In previous games, weapon skills were fixed. Now, you can take a Greatsword and give it a magic projectile, or a dash-step, or a gravity pull. This allows for unparalleled build creativity.
[b]2. Spirit Summons:[/b] For solo players, the Mimic Tear or Black Knife Tiche act as a customizable difficulty slider. You can summon help without needing an internet connection, which makes the game more accessible without compromising the boss design for hardcore players who choose not to use them.
[b]3. Guard Counters & Jumping:[/b] The addition of a jump button isn't just for platforming; it allows for jumping heavy attacks that break enemy stances. Guard counters make shields viable and aggressive again.

[h1]THE BOSSES[/h1]

The boss roster contains some of the highest highs in gaming history.
[b]Starscourge Radahn[/b] is a festival of war where you summon an army of NPCs to charge a demigod holding back the stars. It is chaotic, epic, and emotionally resonant.
[b]Malenia, Blade of Miquella[/b], is the ultimate test of skill. She is arguably the hardest boss FromSoftware has ever designed, demanding perfection in dodging her "Waterfowl Dance."

While there are some repeat bosses in the minor dungeons (expect to fight a few too many Erdtree Avatars), the distinct "Demigod" fights are all masterpieces of visual and mechanical design.

[h1]ART & SOUND[/h1]

The collaboration with George R.R. Martin is evident in the history of the world, the political intrigue between the demigods, the shattering of the Ring, and the tragic fall of Queen Marika's lineage. It gives the world a sense of "history" that feels grounded despite the high fantasy setting.

Musically, the score shifts from the quiet, ambient tracks of exploration to bombastic, terrifying orchestral pieces during combat. The theme that plays when you enter the capital city, [b]Leyndell[/b], captures the majesty and sorrow of a fallen empire perfectly.

[h1]VERDICT[/h1]

Elden Ring is a triumph. It respects your intelligence, rewards your curiosity, and punishes your hubris. It captures the feeling of a grand adventure better than any game in the last twenty years. If you are a fan of the genre, this is the game you have been waiting for. If you are new, this is the best place to start.

[h1]Score: 10/10[/h1]

A sprawling, beautiful, and terrifying masterpiece that redefines what an open-world game can be. Essential playing for anyone who loves video games.
This is one of the best, most immersive open world RPGs ever made.  It's GOAT-tier and a must-play.

Overall, this is a good game. However, I think Elden Ring's flaws are hugely understated in contrast to previous FROMSOFT titles, and thus is a weaker title in my opinion.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]
[h2] Open World [/h2]
The reality is that the open-world formula does not add a positive twist to the souls-like genre. In reality, all it does is make you more reliant on external wikis and guide to find items that may be relevant to your build. In Dark Souls 3, replaying the game is a much tighter experience in part because every item will roughly be along the way to your ultimate goal of kindling the first flame. In Elden Ring, you very much have to spend a big amount of time doing side content to level your character before progressing. 
The mysterious nature of FROMSOFT quests are amplified because NPCs are spread throughout the gigantic world, meaning there is almost zero chance of naturally finishing a quest without external help. 
Because the map is so big, the boss roster suffers a lot. Repeat bosses are very frequent to fill the world, which is less than ideal.

[h2] Bosses [/h2]
The overall quality of the bosses is my biggest complaint, although it is a very mixed bag. I found the Fire Giant fight to be among the best FROMSOFT bosses. Then again, other bosses are much more forgettable or downright unfun to beat. Malenia is the perfect example of a difficult boss done wrong. Gimmicks like her flurry attack and her self-healing just aren't satisfying or rewarding to get over. Compare this to Sword Saint Isshin, a hugely difficult battle, with a wide variety of attacks, yet all of them can reasonably be learned and countered, sometimes in more than one way. 

[h1] The Good [/h1]
[list]
[*]Elden Ring has by far the most varied set of viable builds among FROMSOFT titles. There are easily dozens of different builds with a wide variety of weapons that can be very fun to explore.
[*]The visuals are simply stunning. 
[*]The addition of the jump is a straight upgrade from Dark Souls 3's combat. It just makes the movement mroe fluid and dynamic, especially compared to DS3's weird horizontal jump.
[*]The world building is very strong in this title. The story feels natural and it's clear from the moment you step into the lands between that the big tree is important. It's an enjoyable experience to learn more about this world.
[/list]
In the end, if you were a fan of other FROMSOFT games, definitely don't skip over this one. But if you're new, I would turn your attention to a tighter experience.

Yes, I said it. I will tell you what you need to hear... It has a lot of bugs, it is very generic souls-like game, it has some RPG elements and builds, which would be a really great, but in the time I was trying it out and doing a big research (trust me, I always do my research before and after starting any game), you could choose only a very few builds which actually felt great and they seem pretty repetetive. I need to make very clear that I wasn't expecting anything going into it, so it wasn't about feeling disappointed, because I was expecting the greatest game of all time.

Now, the disclaimer and why I don't feel like recommending it to anybody or random person. Souls-like games aren't exactly my "cup of tea"... that being said and out of the way, I played some. Elden Ring was overhyped and talking to people about it (even watching videos while researching) it feels like everybody is infected and/or smoked something. Everybody tells you that it's one of the best games (if not the best) of all time (or at least of the decade/recent years), you don't even need to know or like souls-like game, you WILL enjoy it -> Well, that's the biggest lie and overstatement. This game should feel the best when fighting or being in combat - does it? No, not even close. The game feels the best when you can skip a mob or even group of mobs, because you don't feel like slashing and dodging for 2 minutes, because a trash mob is in your way. + Very nice world(s)/map(s)
+ Good music
+ Big world
+ Big community (a lot of guides, builds, videos about it - and you'll need them)

- Boss fights either feel extremely long and repetetive (you are doing the same thing for minutes at the same boss), or feel weirdly easy with meta build(s) (You are hitting the floor around the boss and the boss is dead.)
- Overhyped and overrated
- No clear structure (*) 


(*) Yes, I know. It's part of the souls-like experience. So feel free to ingore it, but remember, this was supposed to be a great souls-like game (or starter game) for beginners of the genre, so...

But is it accessible to everyone? While the game can be brutally difficult for beginners, and there is no easy mode, players will find there are many ways to make the game easier and you can choose your own way to do so. That said, the nature of the game is to come up against a challenge that stops you in your tracks and makes you think you can't do it, but whether through sheer grit, or through leveling up and finding better gear, players will feel an amazing sense of accomplishment when they finally succeed. Seasoned veterans will find the re-playability is almost endless, with countless secrets, deep and rewarding mechanics, and self imposed hard modes to keep the game fresh.

I held off reviewing this until I finally beat it.

To be honest, my experience was mixed,  but there's no denying that Elden Ring is a magnificent achievement of gaming excellence. 

Let's get the positives out of the way.

 This is the peak SoulsBourne implementation mechanics wise. Combat is fast, fluid, and exceptionally polished. The only game with better combat would be Sekiro.

The visual quality of the game is absolutely stunning. World design is top notch. There's never been a more well designed or meticulously crafted world in any game.

The negatives:

1) Like most open world games, ER suffers from "Openworld-itis". Pacing is sporadic and uneven. Sometimes it gets to be excruciatingly difficult while other times it is way too easy. All of it depends on the order in which you do things. I find the pacing to be far worse than the more linear and branching nature of past games. I'd like to see the gaming industry realize that Open World isn't better. It's just a different way to design games. Many franchises in recent memory have suffered from the aimlessness of open world design. It would be nice to see a return to a more consistent and linear pacing personally.

2) While I appreciate the minimalist UI, the game is frustratingly quiet about key information. Of my 150+ hours, I spent a good 40 hours going in circles wondering where I should go next. For people who follow guides, this won't matter, but if you want a true gaming experience without any external information, this game is really frustrating at times. It only gives you vague indicators as to where you should go next, and the NPC dialogue is esoteric gibberish that does very little to explain anything at all. I have no idea what the lore means, and the "quest" system of the game is basically just reading between the lines of what NPCs say and hoping it makes sense later. 

The map shows the bare minimum information, and is often way too abstract to be accurate. There's no update for sites you've been to regarding their completion status, nor any indication that you may have more to do there. 

3) I'm just not a fan of the summon system. I miss the satisfaction of soloing bosses. While it's still possible to do, the bosses are clearly designed around using the summoning system. They are significantly overtuned to the point that it would take you 50+ tries or more , and a very specific build, to beat them without use of the summon system. Summons are presented as optional, but for anyone who expects to see meaningful progress in appropriate amounts of time, you will have to summon AI helpers, and it just doesn't feel as satisfying as previous titles in that regard.

Don't let my criticisms deter you though. Elden Ring is an exceptional product that stands head and shoulders above the competition in presentation, mechanics, and overall magnificent design. While it falls into some of the pitfalls as other games with its Open World presentation, it manages to minimize such pitfalls more than most other open world games.

Every area feels carefully crafted, and exploring never feels like a chore — there’s always something interesting to find, whether it’s a hidden dungeon, a terrifying boss, or a quiet, beautiful moment in the world.

What I loved most is how the game tells its story. It doesn’t spell everything out for you, but instead lets you uncover the lore at your own pace. That sense of discovery makes the world feel deeper and more alive, and it keeps you curious the entire time.

Overall, Elden Ring feels like a game made with real passion and care. It’s challenging, beautiful, and unforgettable — easily one of the most impressive and rewarding games I’ve ever played.

I have had a love hate relationship with this game for years, I even did my dissertation for my degree on how its community can sometimes be a cesspool but after this most recent playthrough something changed.

My issue with dark souls 3 was the reliance on twitch reflex boss designs which continued and I fear I just can not keep up in terms of pure skill but this brings me into what I adore about this game. The build crafting and build variety. You can play this game in so many ways, it just does not end. Sure there are some bosses that are total BS, such as a certain gank boss near the end of the game and there were some bosses I thought could have been top tier but were ruined by being needlessly punishing for no good reason (looking at you Malenia). Besides only a few optional bosses I can count on one hand, this game did strike a good balance in design philosophies, especially in the first half.

I used to think this game was unbalanced and to an extent I was right. Unlike previous souls games where you could get by with even a half decent build, this game out right requires an optimised one. That's not inherently a bad thing since you'll be most of the way there by the end game but I do feel as if it gimps the power fantasy to a slight extent. I also had to relearn my past souls experience. I was always of the mindset a hybrid build = certain death but Elden Ring has enough levels to go around meaning you HAVE to invest in survivability or you will hate it like I did on my first playthrough.

I've beaten this game 6 times across different platforms, most recently the steam deck and it is a perfect fit and now I can say that I understand Elden Ring. My advice if you want to dive into this game is for the love of god, take your time, explore, find runes and don't B-line the main story. Sounds simple but it was a harsh lesson for someone who's played the dark souls trilogy has much as I have. 

With my prior playthroughs being as painful as they were, I never bought the dlc out of fear that I just couldn't keep up and now after this last playthrough and finally beating BS Malenia I think I might have a chance as long as I remember to keep it slow and explore....

The game never ends. There is so much wrong with the game.

Okay first let me be clear the game really looks beautiful and has some amazing atmospheres but that is basically it.

Everything else just doesn't work. The controls are all over the place on the gamepad and on the mouse and keyboard. If you are playing on a gamepad you have to sometimes deform your hand to do the things at then same time and on the other hand if you can't do that then you just can't do the things you want to do. On the mouse and keyboard you have to physically let go of the mouse and use ARROWS?!?! to swap the items. I have never seen such an abomination of controls in a game.

The next problem is the camera. The locking system doesn't work and if you try to lock onto an enemy that is partially visible behind a wall you will fail and your camera will rotate 180 degrees which will result in deep frustration and probably death in a boss fight.

Enemy damage is just not fun. When you try to play something hard like V rising solo on brutal you will see what means hard and how something hard is executed. They give you a lot of health but the boss is just ruthless and also has a lot of health. It gives you some time in a boss fight to study the moves and not like elden ring where no matter the level you are basically one shot at every point in the game. The hard doesn't come from you being one shot, that is just called unfair and irritating, hard stems from consistency of hard moves and long lasting fights you can adapt and learn from. One shotting and attacks that cover entire arenas are not hard but fair but just unfair and frustrating.

The dodging system is boring. There are no interesting ways to dodge the attacks. Your dodge is always a roll. There are no movement patterns you are learning to the specific attacks. Its more like playing geometry dash but with bad camera. Its just precise timing simulator where you are multitasking some other random things. Again take a look at V rising where attacks have movement patters for dodging and also time based dodges and when mixed together its fun. Look at hollow knight for fun dodging. 

Next this game is not meant to be played as a sorcerer. It just doesn't have any interesting spells. You constantly find interesting looking and creative melee abilities but spells are just boring. Even when you find cool spells they either don't do a lot of damage or are just to slow to be used in a fight against a boss.

The game never ends. Even when you think you are near the ending the game tells you nahh and you have to go to some remote ass place where you have to open the way for the ending. Then you complete that but now there is an even farther away location where you have to go to find some other thing to unlock the game ending. And after all that and an extra 30 hours of playing you are given a very unfun boss rush where you basically have to defeat 2 bosses just to gain access to the back to back boss fight to finish the game. After delaying what should have been an ending for 40 hours you are just tired and want to finish the game. This extra stuff should have been something like a true ending in hollow knight and something just to finish the game. 

Sometimes the game really makes you feel like you are exploring something alive and real which is great. That feeling is the only good part of the game. Feeling of entering an ancient city that has culture, mobs, rituals and everything that goes alongside it but it is not enough to compensate for every other bad thing.

This game also doesn't have modern day pc support. No widescreen, no unlimited FPS, no anything that makes you feel like you can use the high end PC and on lower specs PC-s it just stutters and performs badly. Then my question is for what PC-s is this made for?

Of course someone will just say git gud but believe me there are much harder games and challenges than those of elden ring and I know your elitist elden ring brain can't comprehend that but just try.

Basically don't buy this game if you have anything to do other than get annoyed.
